Table 2.9. The thirteen systems of channels and their roots (after Ca.Vi. 5.8) Channels carrying Sanskrit Roots breath prāṇavaha heart; alimentary tract (mahāsrotas) water udakavaha palate; kloman (an organ of uncertain identity) food annavaha stomach; left side nutrient fluid rasavaha heart; the ten vessels attached to it blood raktavaha liver; spleen flesh māṃsavaha ligaments; skin fat medovaha kidneys; omentum bone asthivaha fat; hips marrow majjavaha bones; joints semen śukravaha testes; penis urine mūtravaha bladder; groins faeces purīṣavaha colon; rectum sweat svedavaha fat; hair follicles

Channels may be disordered in four ways: by excessive flow (atipravṛtti), obstruction (saṅga), the formation of nodules (sirāgranthi) or flow into the wrong path (vimārgagamana) (Ca.Vi. 5.24). The account of how disease develops—through the accumulation, aggravation and spread of the doṣas, their lodging in a weakened place, and the appearance of symptoms—is described in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 2.11 Regimen: The Day, the Seasons and Conduct
docs.text: Prevention occupies a large place in the compendia. Both Caraka (Ca.Sū. 5–7) and Vāgbhaṭa (AH Sū. 2–4) begin their works with detailed rules for daily life, for the seasons, and for the urges that must not be suppressed.

docs.title: 2.11.1 The Daily Regimen (Dinacaryā)
docs.text: Vāgbhaṭa’s chapter on the daily regimen opens: “a healthy person should rise at the hour of Brahmā (brāhme muhūrte), to protect his life” (AH Sū. 2.1). The regimen that follows includes the evacuation of the bowels and bladder; cleaning the teeth with twigs of astringent, pungent or bitter plants and scraping the tongue; applying collyrium to the eyes; nasal instillation of oil; holding oil or decoctions in the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa, kavala); smoking medicated wicks; massage with oil (abhyaṅga); exercise “to half one’s strength”; rubbing the body with powders; bathing; and the observance of good conduct. Several of these practices have counterparts in other traditions of hygiene. The particular effects that the texts claim for some of them, such as holding oil in the mouth, have not been confirmed by modern studies.

docs.title: 2.11.2 The Seasonal Regimen (Ṛtucaryā)
docs.text:
The year is divided into six seasons of two months each (Table 2.10). The three seasons from late winter to summer, when the sun moves northwards (uttarāyaṇa), are the period of “taking” (ādāna), when the sun and wind are thought to dry and weaken living beings; the three from the rains to early winter, when the sun moves southwards, are the period of “releasing” (visarga), when the moon is strong and strength increases. The regimen for each season aims to counter its effect on the doṣas.

Table 2.10. The six seasons and the general direction of the seasonal regimen (after Ca.Sū. 6 and AH Sū. 3) Season Approximate months General tendency of the regimen Period of “taking” (ādāna) śiśira (late winter) mid-January – mid-March nourishing, unctuous food; protection from cold and wind vasanta (spring) mid-March – mid-May light, dry food; exercise; measures against aggravated kapha grīṣma (summer) mid-May – mid-July sweet, cold, liquid food; rest; avoidance of exertion Period of “releasing” (visarga) varṣā (rains) mid-July – mid-September easily digested food; measures to protect the weakened digestive fire śarad (autumn) mid-September – mid-November sweet, bitter, cooling food; measures against aggravated pitta hemanta (early winter) mid-November – mid-January heavy, nourishing food, since the digestive fire is strong

docs.title: 2.11.3 Exercise
docs.text: Caraka defines exercise (vyāyāma) as bodily activity that produces steadiness and strength, and that should be undertaken in proper measure (Ca.Sū. 7). It brings lightness, capacity for work, firmness, tolerance of hardship, the reduction of excess doṣas and a strong digestive fire. The proper measure is reached when sweat appears, breathing becomes heavy, and the body feels light; Vāgbhaṭa specifies that the strong should exercise to half their capacity, especially in the cold seasons (AH Sū. 2). Excessive exercise is said to cause exhaustion, thirst, wasting, cough, fever and vomiting, and exercise is to be avoided by children, the old, those with vāta disorders and those who have just eaten. The doctrine of moderate, regular exercise adapted to the individual is one of the most widely endorsed parts of the classical regimen today.

docs.title: 2.11.4 Sleep
docs.text: Caraka discusses sleep at length in the chapter on the eight censured physiques (Ca.Sū. 21). Sleep comes, he says, when the mind, together with the senses, is exhausted and withdraws from its objects. Happiness and misery, nourishment and emaciation, strength and weakness, potency and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, life and death all depend on sleep: properly taken it brings health, improperly taken it destroys. Sleeping by day is generally forbidden, because it increases kapha, except in summer, when the nights are short, and for those exhausted by speech, travel, study, grief, fear, anger or illness, for the very young and the very old, and for some others. Insomnia is to be treated by massage, bathing, nourishing food, milk, wine in moderation, pleasant surroundings and peace of mind. The account is a good example of the compendia’s attention to the ordinary conditions of health.

docs.title: 2.11.5 Good Conduct (Sadvṛtta) and “Rejuvenation by Conduct”
docs.text:
Caraka’s rules of good conduct (Ca.Sū. 8) mix personal hygiene, social etiquette, religious duty and moral precepts: to honour gods, cows, brāhmaṇas, teachers and elders; to bathe, dress and groom with care; to speak the truth and speak kindly; to control the senses; to avoid quarrels, gambling and other men’s wives; and much else. The rules reflect the values of an upper-caste householder, and several of them presuppose the social hierarchy of their time.

In the chapter on rejuvenation Caraka goes further, and treats such conduct as itself a form of rejuvenation (ācārarasāyana; Section 8.7).

Summary

The theory of the compendia explains the body, its food and its drugs by the same few principles: five elements, three doṣas defined by their qualities, seven constituents built up by internal fires, and the rule that like increases like. Because the balance of these factors shifts with constitution, age, time of day, season and place, the same theory serves both for treating disease and for the regimen that is meant to prevent it. It is a humoral theory, comparable to but independent of Greek humoralism, and its terms are best read on their own terms rather than as anticipations of modern physiology.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The theory of the doṣas and constituents is best read in the Sūtrasthāna of Caraka, in Sharma’s translation (Sharma 1981–1994), and in Wujastyk’s selections (Wujastyk 2003). Filliozat compares the Indian and Greek humoral theories (Filliozat 1964). The genetic studies of prakṛti are reported in (Prasher et al. 2008; Aggarwal et al. 2010).

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Caraka Saṃhitā
docs.text:
dharmārthakāmamokṣāṇām ārogyaṃ mūlam uttamam rogās tasyāpahartāraḥ śreyaso jīvitasya ca Health is the supreme root of virtue, wealth, pleasure and liberation. Diseases destroy it, and destroy well-being and life itself.

— Caraka Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 1.15–16

docs.title: 3.1 The Work and Its Authors
docs.text:
The Caraka Saṃhitā is the oldest and most comprehensive surviving work of Indian general medicine (kāyacikitsā). It is also a work of considerable philosophical range, with discussions of the self, rebirth, causation, the means of knowledge and the rules of debate. For two thousand years it has been the foundation of Āyurvedic learning, and it remains the first text studied in Āyurvedic colleges.

The work describes its own history. Its teaching is presented as that of Punarvasu Ātreya, set down by his pupil Agniveśa; the text was “redacted” (pratisaṃskṛta) by Caraka; and, since a third of it had been lost, it was completed by Dṛḍhabala, son of Kapilabala, of the town of Pañcanada. Dṛḍhabala says that he supplied seventeen chapters of the Cikitsāsthāna and the whole of the Kalpasthāna and Siddhisthāna—41 chapters in all. Which seventeen therapeutic chapters are his is disputed, because the manuscripts order the Cikitsāsthāna in two different ways.

The dates of these figures are uncertain. Agniveśa’s original work, if it existed as a single book, cannot be dated. Meulenbeld’s careful review of the evidence places Caraka’s redaction somewhere between about 100 BCE and 200 CE, and Dṛḍhabala in the fourth or fifth century CE (Meulenbeld 1999–2002). A Buddhist story, preserved in a Chinese translation of the late fifth century, makes a physician named Caraka the doctor of the Kuṣāṇa king Kaniṣka; whether this is the same person is unknown. The text as we have it is thus a layered work, and even within Caraka’s own portion there are passages of different date and style.

The arguments behind this wide range show how such dates are reached (Section 1.7). The upper limit comes from later witnesses. The Bower Manuscript of the late fifth or sixth century cites Ātreya and his pupils as authorities (Section 1.7.1), and Vāgbhaṭa, about 600, draws on Caraka’s text, including the parts supplied by Dṛḍhabala, throughout. The lower limit, and Caraka’s place within the range, rest on the work’s intellectual setting. Its list of the terms of debate (Ca.Vi. 8) overlaps with the Nyāyasūtra but is less systematic, and many scholars take it to be the older of the two; the Sāṃkhya of its Śārīrasthāna lacks the separate conscious principle of the Sāṃkhyakārikā and looks like an earlier form of the school; and the Vaiśeṣika categories are already known to it. None of these comparisons yields a firm date, because the philosophical texts are themselves hard to date. Two traditional identifications point in different directions. The Buddhist story of Caraka as physician to Kaniṣka would place him in the Kuṣāṇa period, about the second century CE, if it refers to the same man. A verse at the opening of Cakrapāṇidatta’s commentary praises the serpent-lord who removed the faults of mind, speech and body through the Yoga, the Mahābhāṣya and the redaction of Caraka—that is, it makes the grammarian Patañjali (2nd century BCE) the redactor of the medical text as well—but this identification is late, and most historians reject it. Meulenbeld weighs these and other arguments and finds none of them decisive, which is why his range is so wide (Meulenbeld 1999–2002).

The standard Sanskrit edition is that of Jādavjī Trikamjī Ācārya, with the commentary of Cakrapāṇidatta (Trikamji Acharya 1941). Complete English translations include that of Priyavrat Sharma (Sharma 1981–1994); Wujastyk’s Roots of Āyurveda gives an accurate translation of selected chapters with an excellent introduction (Wujastyk 2003), and M. S. Valiathan’s The Legacy of Caraka retells the work section by section for the modern reader (Valiathan 2003).

docs.title: 3.2 The Structure of the Work
docs.text:
The Caraka Saṃhitā has 120 chapters in eight sections (sthāna), listed in Table 3.1 and compared by size in Figure 3.1.

Table 3.1. The eight sections of the Caraka Saṃhitā Section Chapters Subject Sūtrasthāna 30 General principles: drugs, regimen, diet, the physician, the classification of disease Nidānasthāna 8 Causes and signs of eight major diseases Vimānasthāna 8 “Specific measures”: tastes and diet, epidemics, channels, methods of examination, the training of physicians and the rules of debate Śārīrasthāna 8 The person and the self; embryology; the body; pregnancy and childbirth Indriyasthāna 12 Signs of approaching death Cikitsāsthāna 30 Therapeutics: rejuvenation, virility, and the treatment of particular diseases Kalpasthāna 12 Pharmaceutics of emetic and purgative drugs Siddhisthāna 12 The successful administration of the purification therapies, especially enemas Total 120 Figure 3.1. The eight sections of the Caraka Saṃhitā by number of chapters. The Kalpa- and Siddhisthāna and seventeen chapters of the Cikitsāsthāna are Dṛḍhabala’s.

docs.title: 3.3 The Sūtrasthāna
docs.text:
The thirty chapters of the Sūtrasthāna (Table 3.2) are arranged in seven groups of four (catuṣka) and a concluding pair, and the arrangement is itself an argument about what a physician must know and in what order. Chapters in works of this kind are usually named after their opening words or their main subject.

Table 3.2. The chapters of Caraka’s Sūtrasthāna Ch. Title Main subject 1 Dīrghañjīvitīya origin and definition of Āyurveda; categories; classes of drugs 2 Apāmārgataṇḍulīya drugs for purification of the head and body; gruels 3 Āragvadhīya external applications for skin diseases 4 Ṣaḍvirecanaśatāśritīya purgative drugs; the fifty great groups 5 Mātrāśitīya measure of food; daily regimen 6 Tasyāśitīya seasonal regimen 7 Navegāndhāraṇīya urges; exercise; habituation 8 Indriyopakramaṇīya the senses and the mind; good conduct 9 Khuḍḍākacatuṣpāda the four feet of treatment 10 Mahācatuṣpāda curability and incurability 11 Tisraiṣaṇīya the three desires; means of knowledge; three kinds of therapy 12 Vātakalākalīya debate on the properties of vāta, pitta and kapha 13 Sneha oleation 14 Sveda sudation 15 Upakalpanīya preparations and equipment for purification 16 Cikitsāprābhṛtīya the skilled physician; effects of proper and improper purification 17 Kiyantaḥśirasīya diseases of head and heart; combinations of doṣas 18 Triśothīya swellings 19 Aṣṭodarīya enumeration of diseases 20 Mahāroga diseases caused by single doṣas 21 Aṣṭauninditīya the eight censured physiques; obesity, emaciation; sleep 22 Laṅghanabṛṃhaṇīya lightening and nourishing therapies 23 Santarpaṇīya disorders of over- and under-nutrition 24 Vidhiśoṇitīya pure and vitiated blood; fainting and intoxication 25 Yajjaḥpuruṣīya the origin of the person; the foremost things 26 Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya tastes; incompatible foods 27 Annapānavidhi the properties of foods and drinks 28 Vividhāśitapītīya digestion and nourishment; diseases of the constituents 29 Daśaprāṇāyatanīya the ten seats of life; true and false physicians 30 Arthedaśamahāmūlīya the heart and the ten great vessels; the purpose of Āyurveda

The first group (chapters 1–4) is on drugs. After the story of the transmission and the definition of the science (Chapter 1), Caraka sets out the six categories, classifies drugs by origin and by the part used, and lists those most needed for purification—among them four “great fats” (ghee, oil, muscle fat and marrow), five salts, eight kinds of urine and eight of milk. Twenty-eight medicated gruels follow, a reminder that much classical therapy was given in the form of food, and the group ends with the fifty “great groups” (mahākaṣāya) of ten drugs each, defined by their action (Chapter 6). Only then, in the second group (5–8), does Caraka turn to the healthy person: the measure of food, which “depends on the strength of the digestive fire” (mātrāśī syāt; āhāramātrā punar agnibalāpekṣiṇī, Ca.Sū. 5.3), the daily and seasonal regimen, the senses and good conduct (Chapter 2). Chapter 7 lists the thirteen natural urges whose suppression causes disease—urination, defecation, ejaculation, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, belching, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, and heavy breathing after exertion—and, against them, the impulses that should be restrained: rash action, greed, grief, fear, anger, vanity, shamelessness, envy, excessive passion and covetousness. Health is framed from the start as a matter of what one does.

The third group (9–12) asks what medicine is and whether it works. Chapter 9 sets out the four “feet” of treatment—physician, drugs, attendant and patient, each with four qualities. Chapter 10 opens with one of the most remarkable passages in the work. A sage named Maitreya argues that medicine is useless, since some patients who are treated die and some who are not treated recover. Ātreya answers that diseases differ: some are easily curable, some curable with difficulty, some only controllable and some incurable, and failure in the last kinds, or through defective treatment, does not show that treatment is useless (Section 10.4). The compendia were thus aware of the most basic problem in judging a treatment—that patients may recover without it—even if they lacked the means to solve it. Chapter 11, on the three desires for life, wealth and the other world, defends rebirth against sceptics with Caraka’s four means of knowledge, sets out the three kinds of therapy and the three supports of life (Section 1.3), and distinguishes impostors and hangers-on from true physicians, the “givers of life” (Ca.Sū. 11.50–53); the concern with impostors reflects a world without formal qualifications, in which a patient’s only protection was the physician’s reputation. Chapter 12 is cast as a debate among sages on the properties of vāta, and Chapter 25 later as another, on the origin of the person: the self, the mind, the tastes, the elements, the parents, past action, inherent nature, the creator and time are each proposed, and Ātreya concludes that the person, like disease, arises from wholesome and unwholesome food. In these chapters doctrine is presented as the outcome of argument, with rival views heard before the teacher gives his own.

The fourth group (13–16) turns to the preparatory therapies of oleation and sudation and to the conduct of purification (Chapter 7). Its chapter on “preparations” (Upakalpanīya, Ca.Sū. 15) describes what a physician needs before purifying a king or a wealthy patient: a house built by an expert architect, sheltered from wind, smoke, dust and unpleasant sights and sounds and supplied with water, a mortar and pestle, a privy, a bathing place and a kitchen; attendants of good conduct skilled in cooking, bathing, massage, lifting and nursing the patient and preparing medicines; singers, musicians, panegyrists and storytellers to keep the patient cheerful; milch animals; and a store of grains, oils, salts, fruits, drugs and instruments. This “house of treatment” is the closest thing in the compendia to a description of an inpatient facility, though it is designed for a single wealthy household rather than a public hospital.

The fifth group (17–20) surveys diseases: those of the head and heart, the possible combinations of the doṣas, swellings, the enumeration of diseases by their numbers, and finally the disorders caused by a single doṣa alone (nānātmaja), of which Caraka counts eighty of vāta, forty of pitta and twenty of kapha (Ca.Sū. 20). The sixth (21–24) is on the planning of treatment. It opens with the eight “censured” physiques—the excessively tall, short, hairy, hairless, dark, fair, fat and thin—and a long analysis of obesity, in which fat blocks the channels so that the other constituents are starved while the trapped digestive fire produces constant hunger; the same chapter discusses sleep (Section 2.11). Chapter 22 then reduces all therapy to six actions (ṣaḍupakrama)—lightening, nourishing, drying, oleating, sweating and checking—each defined by the qualities of the substances used; Chapter 23 sets the diseases of over-nutrition against those of under-nutrition and treats each by its opposite; and Chapter 24 deals with pure and vitiated blood, bloodletting, and the graded states of intoxication, fainting and coma.

The seventh group (25–28) is on food and drink. Chapter 26 gives the theory of the six tastes (Table 3.3), with the calculation that they can be combined in sixty-three ways, and the eighteen kinds of “incompatibility” (viruddha) in food, of which fish with milk, and honey with an equal quantity of ghee, are the best-known examples. Chapter 27 describes the properties of foods and drinks in twelve groups (Section 6.5), and Chapter 28 relates nourishment to the diseases of the bodily constituents. The concluding pair (29–30) returns to the physician: the ten seats of life; the true physician, “a saviour of life” (prāṇābhisara), against the quack who poses as one to make money (rogābhisara); the heart and ojas; the purpose of the science, which is declared eternal because the nature of things is eternal (Ca.Sū. 30.27); and the instruction to declare allegiance to the Atharvaveda if asked.

Read as a whole, the Sūtrasthāna moves from substances to the healthy person, from the physician’s means of knowledge to procedures and diseases, and back through food to the physician. It is less a summary of the rest of the work than a training of judgement: almost every later chapter applies a rule first stated here.

Table 3.3. The six tastes: elements and effects on the doṣas (after Ca.Sū. 26) Taste Predominant elements Decreases Increases Examples madhura (sweet) water (earth) vāta, pitta kapha ghee, milk, sugar, rice amla (sour) earth, fire vāta pitta, kapha sour fruits, curd lavaṇa (salt) water, fire vāta pitta, kapha rock salt kaṭu (pungent) air, fire kapha vāta, pitta pepper, ginger tikta (bitter) air, space pitta, kapha vāta neem, turmeric kaṣāya (astringent) air, earth pitta, kapha vāta myrobalan

docs.title: 3.4 The Nidānasthāna
docs.text:
The eight chapters on causes (Table 3.5) deal with fever (jvara), bleeding disorders (raktapitta), abdominal swellings (gulma), urinary disorders (prameha), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), wasting (śoṣa), insanity (unmāda) and epilepsy (apasmāra). The first chapter sets out the five means of knowing a disease (nidānapañcaka, Ca.Ni. 1.6): its cause (nidāna); its premonitory signs (pūrvarūpa); its manifest signs (liṅga or rūpa); what relieves or aggravates it, used as a diagnostic test (upaśaya); and the course of its development (saṃprāpti).

Fever is treated first, both here and in the Cikitsāsthāna, as the “king” of diseases: the first to arise, accompanying birth and death. Caraka recognises fevers caused by each doṣa, by pairs and by all three together, and fevers due to external causes, including injury, poison and emotion.

Raktapitta, “blood-bile”, is a bleeding disorder in which blood vitiated by pitta escapes through the upper orifices (mouth, nose, eyes, ears), the lower (anus, urethra, vagina) or both. Caraka judges the upward form curable, the downward form only controllable, and bleeding in both directions incurable. Gulma is a hard, often mobile swelling in the abdomen, of five kinds—one for each doṣa, one for all three, and one “of blood” that occurs only in women and must be distinguished from pregnancy. Śoṣa, “drying up”, is the wasting disease treated in the Cikitsāsthāna as rājayakṣman (below).

Caraka’s account of prameha distinguishes twenty kinds by the appearance of the urine: ten caused by kapha, six by pitta and four by vāta. Among the last is madhumeha, in which the urine is “like honey”. The texts associate prameha with overeating, heavy and sweet food, curd, idleness and sleeping by day, and they recognise an inherited form. The account is a striking clinical description; it is not, however, a description of diabetes mellitus in the modern sense, since the category includes other conditions in which the urine is abnormal.

The last chapter of the section, on epilepsy, adds a general discussion of how diseases interact. One disease may be the cause of another: fever and bleeding disorders may lead to wasting, for example, and enlargement of the spleen to abdominal swelling. A disease may also be the cause of another while itself disappearing, or may persist alongside it. The physician must therefore understand the whole history of an illness, not only its present signs.

docs.title: 3.5 The Vimānasthāna
docs.text: The “section on specific measures” is the most intellectually varied part of the work.

docs.title: 3.5.1 Diet (Ca.Vi. 1–2)
docs.text:
The first chapter lists eight factors that determine the effect of food (āhāra­vidhi­viśeṣa­āyatana; Table 3.4).

Table 3.4. The eight determinants of the effect of food (Ca.Vi. 1.21) Factor Meaning prakṛti the natural qualities of the food karaṇa its preparation (washing, heating, churning, storing and so on) saṃyoga combination with other foods rāśi quantity, of the whole meal and of each item deśa place, both where the food grows and where it is eaten kāla time of day, season and the state of the eater upayogasaṃsthā the rules of eating upayoktṛ the eater, whose habituation determines what suits him

The second chapter teaches that the stomach should be thought of in three parts: one to be filled with solid food, one with liquid, and one left for the doṣas.

docs.title: 3.5.2 Epidemics (Ca.Vi. 3)
docs.text:
The third chapter, “On the destruction of communities” (Janapadoddhvaṃsanīya), asks how a single disease can strike many people of different constitutions at once. The answer is that some factors are common to all the inhabitants of a region: air, water, land and season. When these are vitiated—the wind unseasonable or foul, water discoloured or stinking, the land infested and its plants withered, the seasons out of order—whole populations fall ill. The root of such vitiation, Caraka says, is unrighteousness (adharma), above all of rulers, which corrupts the natural order; war and curses are named as further causes. As remedies he recommends rejuvenating drugs collected before the land is spoiled, the purification therapies, and truthfulness, compassion, charity, worship and the company of the good.

The chapter is notable for treating disease as a matter of shared environment as well as individual constitution, and for linking public health to just government. It is not a theory of contagion, and its causal account is moral as much as natural. The same chapter contains a debate on whether the span of life is fixed by past actions or can be changed by present effort; Ātreya concludes that both play a part, and that the physician’s work therefore matters.

docs.title: 3.5.3 Diseases, Channels and Patients (Ca.Vi. 4–7)
docs.text:
The middle chapters of the Vimānasthāna deal with method. Chapter 4 explains the three means of knowing a disease—instruction, perception and inference—and how each applies. Chapter 5, on the channels, has been summarised in Chapter 2. Chapter 6, “On the hosts of diseases” (Rogānīka), shows that diseases can be classified in many ways: as curable or incurable, mild or severe, mental or bodily, endogenous or exogenous, arising in the stomach or the colon, and so on, and that the number of diseases is in principle unlimited, since they can be named and classified without end. The lesson is that the physician should not be troubled if he cannot name a disease, provided he understands its doṣas, site and causes.

Chapter 7 (Vyādhitarūpīya) warns against judging by appearances: some patients look gravely ill but have only a mild disease, while others look well but are seriously ill. It also describes twenty kinds of “worms” (krimi), external and internal—those of the skin and hair, and those arising from blood, phlegm and faeces—and their treatment by extraction, measures against their source, and the avoidance of their causes. The account includes what are clearly lice and intestinal worms, alongside other, more speculative “worms” supposed to cause disease.

docs.title: 3.5.4 The Training of Physicians and the Rules of Debate (Ca.Vi. 8)
docs.text:
The last chapter of the Vimānasthāna is a manual of medical education. It describes how to choose a text, a teacher and a student; the three means of learning—study, teaching and discussion with other experts; the initiation of the student and the teacher’s address to him (Chapter 1); and the conduct of discussions. Discussion (sambhāṣā) may be friendly, between colleagues seeking the truth, or hostile, against an opponent to be defeated; Caraka gives practical advice on when to engage in each, and on how to win. He then defines forty-four technical terms of debate (vādamārgapada): thesis, counter-thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion, fallacies, quibbles, points of defeat and the like. This list is one of the oldest surviving treatments of the subject in Sanskrit and overlaps substantially with the early Nyāya tradition.

The chapter ends with the tenfold examination of the patient (Chapter 10) and the examination of drugs.

docs.title: 3.6 The Śārīrasthāna
docs.text:
The section on the body begins with a long philosophical chapter on the nature of the person (Katidhāpuruṣīya, Ca.Śā. 1), discussing the self, the mind, the elements, the evolution of the world in a form related to Sāṃkhya, action and rebirth, suffering and liberation. Chapters 2–4 and 8 deal with conception, the development of the embryo, pregnancy and birth; chapters 5–7 with the correspondence of person and world, the constituents of the body, and the enumeration of its parts—Caraka counts 360 bones, including teeth and nails.

Table 3.5. The chapters of the Nidāna-, Vimāna- and Śārīrasthāna Nidānasthāna Vimānasthāna Śārīrasthāna 1 fever (jvara) tastes (rasa) “how many kinds of person” (katidhāpuruṣīya) 2 bleeding disorders (raktapitta) the three parts of the stomach “of unequal lineage” (atulyagotrīya) 3 abdominal swellings (gulma) destruction of communities the descent of the embryo (short) 4 urinary disorders (prameha) the three means of knowing disease the descent of the embryo (long) 5 skin diseases (kuṣṭha) the channels (srotas) examination of the person 6 wasting (śoṣa) the hosts of diseases examination of the body 7 insanity (unmāda) the forms of the sick enumeration of the body’s parts 8 epilepsy (apasmāra) disease, physician and treatment “the thread of birth” (jātisūtrīya)

docs.title: 3.6.1 Conception and Heredity
docs.text: The second chapter of the Śārīrasthāna, “Of unequal lineage”, begins by asking why a couple may fail to conceive, and why children differ from their parents. Its title refers to the rule that a man should marry a woman of a different gotra (clan lineage). Caraka discusses defects of semen and uterine blood, the conditions under which conception occurs, the causes of twins and of children of indeterminate sex, and the influence of the parents’ diet and conduct and of the child’s own past actions. Chapter 6, “Examination of the body”, discusses the factors that promote the growth of the body—a good season, good soil, the parents’ health, suitable food, and the absence of injury—and the causes of its decline. (Elsewhere, in the Sūtrasthāna, Caraka states the doctrine that things come into being through causes but perish of their own nature, without a cause of destruction (svabhāvoparama); the physician’s task is therefore to supply the causes of balance, not to destroy imbalance directly.)

docs.title: 3.6.2 The Person, Rebirth and Liberation
docs.text:
The first chapter of the Śārīrasthāna is one of the most important philosophical texts in Sanskrit outside the works of the philosophical schools. It describes the person as composed of twenty-four principles: the unmanifest (avyakta), the intellect, the ego and the five elements, which are the eight “evolvents” (prakṛti); and the sixteen “evolutes” (vikāra)—the ten faculties of sense and action, the mind, and the five sense objects. Unlike classical Sāṃkhya, Caraka does not set a separate conscious spirit over against these principles; consciousness belongs to the unmanifest. Historians of philosophy regard this as evidence of an early stage of Sāṃkhya thought, before the school’s doctrines were fixed in the Sāṃkhyakārikā (Wujastyk 2003).

The chapter goes on to discuss action and its fruit, rebirth, the causes of suffering, and liberation. Suffering arises from the conjunction of the self with the body and senses, driven by desire; it ends when desire is eliminated through knowledge, detachment and yogic discipline. Caraka describes the eight powers of the accomplished yogin and the path to final release, in which the self is freed from all connection with the body. A medical work thus ends its account of the person not with health but with liberation from embodiment altogether.

docs.title: 3.6.3 Embryology
docs.text: The embryo, according to Caraka (Ca.Śā. 3), is formed from six factors: what derives from the mother (soft parts such as skin, blood, flesh, heart and liver), from the father (hard and fixed parts such as hair, nails, teeth, bones and semen), from the self, from habituation, from the nutrient fluid, and from the mind. The fourth chapter describes the development of the embryo month by month, from a jelly-like mass in the first month to a firm body with differentiated limbs, and the appearance of the “longings” of pregnancy (dauhṛda) in the fourth month, when the foetus’s heart is formed and its desires are expressed through the mother. The account combines careful observation of miscarried foetuses with theory and ritual belief.

docs.title: 3.6.4 Pregnancy and Birth (Ca.Śā. 8)
docs.text: The last chapter of the section, “On the thread of birth” (Jātisūtrīya), prescribes rites and conduct for conception, the care of the pregnant woman, preparation of a lying-in house, management of delivery and the care of the newborn and the mother (Chapter 8). It includes a rite to obtain a male child (puṃsavana) and rules intended to influence the sex and character of the child.

docs.title: 3.7 The Indriyasthāna
docs.text:
The twelve chapters on the “senses” are devoted to prognosis, and specifically to the signs (ariṣṭa) that death is near. They are drawn from changes in complexion, voice, smell, taste and touch; from the patient’s shadow and reflection; from dreams; from the behaviour of the messenger who comes to call the physician; and from omens on the way to the patient’s house. Some examples give the flavour of the section. A patient whose reflection in a mirror or in water appears deformed, headless or without its natural colour is near death; so is one who sees the sun at night or the moon by day, who no longer perceives smells, or whose body gives off the smell of flowers without cause. Dreams are ominous when the sleeper sees himself riding a donkey or a camel towards the south, being dragged by a dark woman, or eating and drinking with the dead (Ca.In. 5). The physician’s messenger is also examined: if he arrives dirty, weeping, carrying a weapon or at an inauspicious time, the patient will not recover; and omens on the way to the patient’s house—a sneeze, a crow’s call, a broken pot—are interpreted in the same way (Ca.In. 12).

The purpose was practical: a physician who undertook a hopeless case would bring discredit on himself. The texts advise him, when he perceives such signs, not to announce death but to withdraw tactfully. Much of this material belongs to the world of omens rather than of clinical observation.

docs.title: 3.8 The Cikitsāsthāna
docs.text:
The Cikitsāsthāna, the largest section, opens with two chapters on rejuvenation (rasāyana) and virility (vājīkaraṇa), which are described with the rest of these branches in Sections 8.7 and 8.8, and continues with the treatment of particular diseases (Table 3.6).

Table 3.6. The chapters of the Cikitsāsthāna (order of the Trikamjī edition) Ch. Subject Ch. Subject 1 rejuvenation (rasāyana) 16 anaemia and jaundice (pāṇḍu, kāmalā) 2 virility (vājīkaraṇa) 17 hiccup and dyspnoea (hikkā, śvāsa) 3 fever (jvara) 18 cough (kāsa) 4 bleeding disorders (raktapitta) 19 diarrhoea (atisāra) 5 abdominal swellings (gulma) 20 vomiting (chardi) 6 urinary disorders (prameha) 21 spreading skin eruptions (visarpa) 7 skin diseases (kuṣṭha) 22 thirst (tṛṣṇā) 8 consumption (rājayakṣman) 23 poisons (viṣa) 9 insanity (unmāda) 24 alcoholism (madātyaya) 10 epilepsy (apasmāra) 25 wounds (dvivraṇīya) 11 chest injury and wasting (kṣatakṣīṇa) 26 the three vital organs (trimarmīya) 12 oedema (śvayathu) 27 stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha) 13 abdominal enlargement (udara) 28 disorders of vāta (vātavyādhi) 14 haemorrhoids (arśas) 29 vātarakta (a disorder of the joints) 15 disorders of digestion (grahaṇī) 30 gynaecological disorders (yonivyāpad)

docs.title: 3.8.1 Some Major Diseases
docs.text:
The treatment chapters follow a common plan: the origin of the disease (often told as a myth), its causes, signs and varieties, its prognosis, and its treatment by stages. A few examples show the range.

Fever (Ca.Ci. 3). Fever is said to have arisen from the anger of Śiva at the sacrifice of Dakṣa. Caraka distinguishes fevers by their doṣas, by their causes and by their course, including the “irregular” fevers (viṣamajvara) that are continuous, recur once or twice a day, every other day, or every fourth day. The last two correspond closely to the tertian and quartan periodicity of malaria, which the ancient Greeks also described. In early fever the patient is to fast and to drink boiled water; drugs are given only when the fever has “ripened”.

Consumption (Ca.Ci. 8). The “king’s disease” (rājayakṣman) takes its name from a myth: the Moon, married to the twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa, favoured one of them, and was cursed by his father-in-law with a wasting disease from which the Aśvins cured him. Caraka names four causes of the disease in human beings—rash overexertion, the suppression of natural urges, the depletion of bodily constituents, and irregular eating—and describes a wasting illness with cough, fever, pain in the side, hoarseness and bloody sputum. Treatment is by nourishing food, especially meat, by rejuvenating drugs and by careful regimen.

Skin diseases (Ca.Ci. 7). Caraka recognises seven major and eleven minor forms of kuṣṭha, and attributes them not only to incompatible food and the doṣas but also to sinful acts, including disrespect towards brāhmaṇas and teachers. The category, which includes leprosy, and the stigma that this moral explanation helped to create are discussed in Chapter 8.

Alcoholism (Ca.Ci. 24). Caraka’s chapter on the disorders of drinking is a remarkable mixture of praise and warning. Wine taken in the right way, in moderation, with food, by a suitable person, is said to bring pleasure, appetite, strength and good spirits; Caraka describes the three stages of intoxication with evident literary pleasure. But taken in excess, by the wrong person or in the wrong way, it causes a set of disorders—pānātyaya, paramada, pānājīrṇa and pānavibhrama—affecting digestion, the mind and the whole body, and in the end death. The treatment, characteristically, includes the gradual reduction of drinking rather than sudden withdrawal.

Wounds (Ca.Ci. 25). Caraka’s chapter on “the two kinds of wound”—those arising from the doṣas and those caused by injury—summarises the surgical school’s treatment in a form usable by the general physician, and refers the more complex procedures to the surgeons.

Insanity, epilepsy and poisons (Ca.Ci. 9–10, 23). Caraka’s chapters on madness and epilepsy, and his chapter on poisons of plant, mineral and animal origin, including snakebite, compound poisons administered by others (gara) and latent poisons (dūṣīviṣa), are described with the rest of these subjects in Sections 8.5 and 8.6.

Gynaecological disorders (Ca.Ci. 30). The last chapter of the section describes twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract (yonivyāpad), with disorders of breast milk and of semen, and ends with a summary of the whole work.

docs.title: 3.9 The Kalpasthāna and Siddhisthāna
docs.text:
The twelve chapters of the Kalpasthāna, added by Dṛḍhabala, describe the emetic and purgative drugs. The first six deal with emetics, beginning with madanaphala (the fruit of Randia or Catunaregam spinosa), which is regarded as the best; the next six with purgatives, among them trivṛt (Operculina turpethum), āragvadha (Cassia fistula) and the milky latex of snuhī (Euphorbia). The full sequence of emetics is madana, jīmūtaka, ikṣvāku, dhāmārgava, vatsaka (kuṭaja) and kṛtavedhana, several of them bitter gourds; the purgatives are śyāmā and trivṛt, caturaṅgula (āragvadha), tilvaka, sudhā (snuhī), saptalā with śaṅkhinī, and dantī with dravantī. For each drug the text gives its synonyms and the signs of good material, and then a long series of preparations—powders, decoctions, confections, medicated ghees and others—so that a single drug could be adapted to different patients, seasons and diseases. The section is thus as much a treatise on pharmacy as on purification. The Siddhisthāna, also by Dṛḍhabala, deals with the successful administration of the purification therapies (Chapter 7), their complications and their correction, and above all with enemas. Its final chapter lists the thirty-six “devices of composition” (tantrayukti) by which a scientific text is constructed and should be interpreted (Section 5.6.2).

The Siddhisthāna is a strikingly practical book. Its chapters deal with the planning of a course of purification and the signs of its right and wrong performance (Si. 1), the indications and contraindications of the five therapies (Si. 2), the enema apparatus (Si. 3) and the faults of its nozzle and bag (Si. 5), the complications of emesis and purgation (Si. 6) and of enemas (Si. 7), and, in a chapter of wider interest, the three vital organs—heart, head and bladder—whose disorders are approached largely through enemas and nasal therapy (Trimarmīya, Si. 9). The closing chapter (Si. 12) is devoted to further enemas before the list of tantrayukti. Much of the section is concerned with what goes wrong: over- and under-action of a purgative, an enema that is retained or returns too fast, a nozzle that injures. The attention to complications reflects a clinical tradition that knew these procedures to be dangerous and reserved them for the trained physician.

Health and Safety Note

The regimens for conception and pregnancy, the treatments for poisoning and the purification procedures described in this chapter are history, not advice; some of them are now known to be unsafe. See the consolidated note in Section 12.7.

docs.title: 3.10 The Commentators
docs.text:
The Caraka Saṃhitā attracted commentaries from an early date, though many are lost or survive only in part (Table 3.7).

Table 3.7. Principal commentaries on the Caraka Saṃhitā Commentary Author and date Notes Carakanyāsa Bhaṭṭāra Hariścandra (date uncertain; early) The oldest known commentary; survives in fragments Nirantarapadavyākhyā Jejjaṭa (Kashmir; perhaps 9th century) Partly preserved Āyurvedadīpikā Cakrapāṇidatta (Bengal; 11th century) The standard commentary, complete and authoritative Jalpakalpataru Gaṅgādhara Rāy (Bengal; 19th century) Extensive; based on a revised text Carakopaskāra Yogīndranāth Sen (Bengal; early 20th century) A clear modern commentary

The Caraka Saṃhitā was also known beyond India. The tenth-century Arabic bibliographer Ibn al-Nadīm records an Arabic translation of a book of “Sharak the Indian”, made from a Persian version, and the physician Abū Bakr al-Rāzī (d. c. 925) quotes “Sharak” in his great compilation al-Ḥāwī.

docs.title: 3.11 Assessment
docs.text:
The Caraka Saṃhitā is a remarkable document. Its insistence on examination before treatment, on the individuality of the patient, on diet and regimen, and on the testing of knowledge by reasoning has impressed every modern reader. Its ethics of practice are serious and humane. At the same time it is a work of its age. Its anatomy and physiology are speculative; its causal accounts mix the natural, the moral and the supernatural; its remedies were not tested in any way that would now count as evidence; and it was written for and by a narrow social group. To read it well is to read it as one of the great achievements of ancient science, not as a modern textbook.

Summary

The Caraka Saṃhitā is a layered work of 120 chapters, a third of them added by Dṛḍhabala, whose date can be fixed only within a wide range. Its Sūtrasthāna trains the physician’s judgement before it describes diseases; its Vimāna- and Śārīrasthāna join medicine to epistemology, debate and an early Sāṃkhya account of the person and of liberation. Its ethics and its insistence on examination have impressed every modern reader, while its anatomy and therapeutics belong to its own age.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The Sanskrit text with Cakrapāṇidatta’s commentary is in Trikamjī’s edition (Trikamji Acharya 1941); the complete translation by Sharma (Sharma 1981–1994); selected chapters in Wujastyk (Wujastyk 2003). Meulenbeld discusses the date and redaction of the work in detail (Meulenbeld 1999–2002).

docs.title: Chapter 4: The Suśruta Saṃhitā and Indian Surgery
docs.text:
yathā kharaś candanabhāravāhī bhārasya vettā na tu candanasya evaṃ hi śāstrāṇi bahūny adhītya cārtheṣu mūḍhāḥ kharavad vahanti As a donkey carrying a load of sandalwood knows its weight but not the sandalwood, so those who have studied many treatises without grasping their meaning carry them like donkeys.

— Suśruta Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 4.4

docs.title: 4.1 The Work and Its History
docs.text:
The Suśruta Saṃhitā is the great classical work of Indian surgery (śalyatantra). Like the Caraka Saṃhitā, it covers the whole of medicine, but its distinctive contribution lies in its account of surgical training, instruments and operations, of wounds and their care, of anatomy learned by dissection, and of the “vital points” of the body. It is among the most detailed surgical texts to survive from the ancient world, and the reconstructive operations it describes for the nose and the ear lobe have made it famous far beyond India.

The work presents itself as the teaching of Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his pupil Suśruta. Like Caraka’s compendium, it is composite. Current scholarship treats it as an older core—perhaps of the last centuries BCE—that was revised and enlarged, above all by the addition of the Uttaratantra (“later book”; Table 4.1 and Figure 4.1), and that had approximately its present form by about 500 CE (Meulenbeld 1999–2002; Wujastyk 2003). The twelfth-century commentator Ḍalhaṇa names a “Nāgārjuna” as its redactor; who this was is unknown, and there is no good reason to identify him with the Buddhist philosopher of the same name. A Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript of 878 CE preserves a version that differs in many places from the one printed in modern editions (Section 5.6.4). The traditional dating of Suśruta to the second millennium BCE has no historical basis.

The standard edition is that of Jādavjī Trikamjī Ācārya and Nārāyaṇ Rām Ācārya, with the commentary of Ḍalhaṇa (Trikamji Acharya and Acharya 1938). The complete English translation of Kunja Lal Bhishagratna is old but still useful (Bhishagratna 1907–1916); Wujastyk translates important chapters (Wujastyk 2003), and Valiathan summarises the whole work for the modern reader (Valiathan 2007). Guido Majno’s history of wound treatment in the ancient world gives a fair assessment of Suśruta’s surgery alongside Egyptian, Greek, Roman and Chinese practice (Majno 1975).

Table 4.1. The six sections of the Suśruta Saṃhitā Section Chapters Subject Sūtrasthāna 46 General principles; training; instruments; alkalis and cautery; leeches; wounds; diet Nidānasthāna 16 Causes and signs of diseases, especially those requiring surgery Śārīrasthāna 10 Embryology, anatomy (including dissection), vessels, vital points, pregnancy Cikitsāsthāna 40 Treatment, including operations, fractures and the purification therapies Kalpasthāna 8 Toxicology: poisons, snakes, insects and their treatment Uttaratantra 66 Diseases of the eye, ear, nose and head; children’s diseases; general medicine; possession; method Total 186

docs.title: 4.1.1 Beyond Surgery
docs.text:
Although surgery is its distinctive subject, the Suśruta Saṃhitā also contains a full system of medicine. Its Sūtrasthāna includes a long chapter on foods and drinks (Su.Sū. 46), the longest in the work, and chapters on the classification of drugs, the qualities of land and water, the seasons and the regimen of health. Suśruta’s account of the doṣas gives blood a special place: in discussing the origin of disease he treats blood almost as a fourth doṣa, alongside wind, bile and phlegm, and he regards the vitiation of blood as the cause of many skin diseases, swellings and abscesses—which is why bloodletting is so important in his school. The Cikitsāsthāna includes the purification therapies, rejuvenation and virility, and a chapter on the prevention of disease (Su.Ci. 24) that describes the daily regimen, exercise and massage.

Suśruta’s chapter on liquids (Su.Sū. 45) contains a notable discussion of drinking water. It describes the properties of rain water, river water, well water and water from tanks and springs, the signs of polluted water—discoloured, foul-smelling, slimy, full of insects or decaying leaves—and the diseases it causes, and methods of purifying it: boiling, heating in the sun, plunging heated iron or stones into it, and clarifying it with the crushed seeds of the kataka tree (Strychnos potatorum), a method still used in parts of rural India to settle muddy water. The water is then to be cooled and kept in clean vessels.

Figure 4.1. The six sections of the Suśruta Saṃhitā by number of chapters. The Uttaratantra, a later addition, is the largest.

docs.title: 4.1.2 Learning and Teaching
docs.text: The opening chapters of the Sūtrasthāna describe the student’s initiation and study. As in Caraka, the teacher instructs the newly initiated student in the conduct expected of him, and the text describes how a text is to be learned: by reciting it with the teacher, phrase by phrase and verse by verse, until it is memorised, and then by understanding its meaning. Suśruta is scornful of learning without understanding: in the verse quoted at the head of this chapter he compares the student who has memorised a text without grasping its meaning to a donkey carrying sandalwood (Su.Sū. 4.4). The same chapter recommends that the student learn from other sciences as well, since no single science contains everything.

docs.title: 4.2 The Scope of Surgery
docs.text:
The word śalya means a dart or thorn, anything lodged in the body that causes pain. Surgery is the art of removing such things: arrows, splinters, stones, dead foetuses, pus and diseased tissue. Suśruta distinguishes foreign bodies that arise within the body (śārīra)—such as stones, hair or pus—from those that enter it from outside (āgantu), and gives detailed instructions for locating and extracting arrows, which reflects the importance of war wounds in early surgery.

He classifies all operations into eight kinds (Su.Sū. 5; Table 4.2).

Table 4.2. The eight kinds of surgical operation (Su.Sū. 5) Operation Meaning Operation Meaning chedya excision eṣya probing bhedya incision āhārya extraction lekhya scraping visrāvya drainage vedhya puncture sīvya suturing

Alongside the knife, Suśruta gives great importance to two other means of treatment: caustic alkali (kṣāra), which he calls superior to cutting instruments because it can be applied where knives cannot, and the actual cautery (agnikarma), which he considers superior still because diseases treated by fire do not recur (Su.Sū. 11–12). He also describes bloodletting by leeches, horn, gourd and venesection (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 4.2.1 Alkali and Cautery
docs.text: Suśruta’s chapters on alkali and cautery (Su.Sū. 11–12) are among the most detailed in the work. Caustic alkali (kṣāra) was prepared from the ashes of particular plants dissolved in water and concentrated. It was graded as mild, medium or strong, and applied externally to growths, haemorrhoids, fistulae and skin diseases, or given internally in diluted form. Suśruta describes the signs of proper and excessive application and its neutralisation with sour liquids. Actual cautery (agnikarma) was performed with heated rods, probes and other instruments of metal, or with heated substances such as honey, oil, wax or treacle, and was used to stop bleeding, to treat pain in the joints and ligaments, warts, sinuses and haemorrhoids, and after excision. The text describes several forms of cauterisation—in rings, dots or lines, or by rubbing—and four degrees of accidental burns, with their treatment.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Leeches
docs.text: Suśruta’s chapter on leeches (Su.Sū. 13) describes where suitable leeches are to be found, how they are to be caught, kept and fed, how they are applied, how they are made to let go, and how they are made to vomit the blood they have taken so that they may be used again. He distinguishes twelve kinds, six venomous and six not, by their colour, shape and habitat. Leeches were preferred for the delicate, the young, the old and the timid, because their use is gentle. Medicinal leeches, whose saliva contains anticoagulant substances, are still used in modern reconstructive surgery to relieve congested tissue.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Arrows and Foreign Bodies
docs.text: War made the extraction of arrows one of the surgeon’s principal tasks. Suśruta describes the kinds of arrowhead, the signs by which the position of a buried arrowhead can be inferred—swelling, pain, bleeding, the patient’s posture—and many methods of extraction: pulling it out the way it entered, pushing it through to the other side, cutting down upon it, or using magnets for iron points. He also describes the removal of foreign bodies from the eye, ear, nose and throat, and of food lodged in the throat by a blow on the shoulders.

docs.title: 4.3 Surgical Training
docs.text:
One of the most admired passages of the work is its account of surgical practice on models (yogyā, Su.Sū. 9). A student who has learnt the texts but has not practised, Suśruta says, is unfit to operate. He is to practise each operation on objects that resemble the tissues in question (Table 4.3).

Table 4.3. Practice on models (after Su.Sū. 9) Operation Practised on excision gourds, cucumbers, melons and other fruits and vegetables incision a leather bag, bladder or pouch filled with water or mud scraping a stretched hide with the hair still on it puncture the vessels of dead animals; lotus stalks probing worm-eaten wood, bamboo, reeds, the mouths of dried gourds extraction the pulp of jack-fruit and other fruits; the teeth of dead animals drainage a plank of silk-cotton wood smeared with beeswax suturing the edges of thick and thin cloth and of soft leather bandaging model human figures made of cloth or other material ear-lobe repair soft flesh, or lotus stalks cautery and alkali pieces of soft flesh

docs.title: 4.4 Instruments
docs.text:
Suśruta describes 101 blunt instruments (yantra) and 20 sharp instruments (śastra); modern reconstructions of both are shown in Figures 4.2–4.4. He adds that the hand is the chief of all instruments, since none can be used without it, and that the physician may devise others as circumstances require.

The blunt instruments fall into six groups (Su.Sū. 7): forceps shaped like the heads of animals and birds (svastika, 24), tongs (saṃdaṃśa, 2), flat instruments (tāla, 2), tubes (nāḍī, 20), rods and probes (śalākā, 28) and accessory instruments (upayantra, 25), among which the text counts such things as cords, bandages, leather, bark, creepers, stones, hammers, magnets, the tongue and the teeth. The tubes include instruments for examining fistulae and haemorrhoids and for administering enemas.

The twenty sharp instruments (Su.Sū. 8) are named mostly after their shapes (Table 4.4). Instruments are to be made of good iron by a skilled smith, kept sharp, clean and in boxes, and the text describes how they should be held, what operations each is used for, and the qualities of a good edge.

Table 4.4. The twenty sharp instruments (Su.Sū. 8) Name Meaning Name Meaning maṇḍalāgra round-tipped knife āṭīmukha “bird’s-beak” knife karapatra saw śarārimukha scissors vṛddhipatra razor-shaped knife antarmukha knife with inward-curved edge nakhaśastra nail-shaped knife trikūrcaka three-pointed instrument mudrikā ring-knife, worn on the finger kuṭhārikā small axe utpalapatra lotus-leaf knife vrīhimukha “rice-grain” lancet ardhadhāra single-edged knife ārā awl sūcī needle vetasapatra cane-leaf knife kuśapatra grass-leaf knife baḍiśa hook eṣaṇī probe dantaśaṅku dental scraper Figure 4.2. A plate of modern drawings reconstructing sharp instruments (śastra) named in the Suśruta Saṃhitā. Such reconstructions are conjectural: the text describes the instruments in words, and the drawings often borrow the forms of modern European instruments. Plate: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita, vol. 1 (1907), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 4.3. A plate of modern reconstructions of blunt instruments (yantra), including tongs, probes and forceps. The same caution applies. Plate: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita, vol. 1 (1907), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

No surgical instrument described in the text has been securely identified among archaeological finds in India. By contrast, sets of Roman surgical instruments—scalpels, forceps, probes, hooks and specula—have been excavated at Pompeii and elsewhere, and some resemble the forms described by Suśruta, as one would expect of tools made for similar tasks. Modern reconstructions of the Indian instruments, such as those in Mukhopadhyaya’s pioneering study (Mukhopadhyaya 1913–1914), are based on the textual descriptions and on the instruments used by Indian practitioners in the early twentieth century.

Figure 4.4. A further plate of modern reconstructions of blunt instruments, including probes, forceps named after the beaks of birds and the mouths of animals, and the hook (garbhaśaṅku) used to extract a dead foetus. The same caution applies. Plate: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita, vol. 1 (1907), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 4.5 Anatomy and Dissection
docs.text:
Suśruta holds that a surgeon must know the body by direct observation as well as by the texts, and prescribes the dissection of a corpse (Su.Śā. 5). The body chosen should be complete, not of a very old person, and not of one who died of poison or a long illness. After the intestines have been emptied, it is wrapped in grass, bark or hemp, placed in a cage in a slow-flowing stream in a hidden place, and left to decompose for seven days. Its layers are then rubbed away gently with brushes of grass roots, hair or bamboo so that each part can be observed in turn.

The text gives no reason for its method of maceration rather than cutting. Modern writers often explain it by a taboo on touching a corpse with a knife, but that is an inference, not something the text says; what is clear is that the method would have revealed some structures better than others. Human dissection had also been practised, briefly, by Herophilus and Erasistratus in Hellenistic Alexandria in the third century BCE; there is no evidence of contact between the two traditions, and claims that Suśruta was “the first” to dissect cannot be established.

Suśruta’s enumerations of the parts of the body are partly the result of observation and partly of system (Table 4.5):

Table 4.5. Some anatomical enumerations of the Suśruta Saṃhitā Structure Number Notes bones (asthi) 300 Caraka counts 360, including teeth and nails (Su.Śā. 5) joints (sandhi) 210 ligaments (snāyu) 900 muscles (peśī) 500 twenty more in women vessels (sirā) 700 carrying vāta, pitta, kapha and blood (Su.Śā. 7) “pulsating” vessels (dhamanī) 24 arising from the navel (Su.Śā. 9) vital points (marman) 107 Su.Śā. 6

docs.title: 4.5.1 Reading the Dissection Passage
docs.text:
The instruction to dissect closes Suśruta’s chapter on the enumeration of the body (Śarīrasaṃkhyāvyākaraṇa, Su.Śā. 5), and its place there matters. The chapter is first of all a list: of the body’s layers, receptacles, bones, joints, ligaments, muscles and vessels, given by number and by region. The passage on the corpse explains how such a list is to be made one’s own. Knowledge of the body, the text argues, comes from two sources together, the teaching of the authoritative texts and direct seeing (pratyakṣa), and a surgeon who wants to be certain must combine them, since neither is enough alone. In the language of the philosophical schools this is an appeal to perception as a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) alongside testimony, and it matches the weight that Caraka gives to examination by the physician’s own senses (Chapter 10).

The details of the procedure show what kind of knowledge was expected. The body is to be whole, of a person neither very old nor dead of poison or of a long illness: a body, that is, whose parts are in their ordinary state. A week in water loosens the tissues, and gentle scraping removes them layer by layer, so that skin, fat, flesh, vessels, ligaments and finally bones can be seen in place. A method of this kind shows layers, cavities, the larger vessels and the arrangement of the skeleton far better than it shows small structures, and the anatomy of the Śārīrasthāna has exactly this character. The seven layers of the skin, the membranes and the receptacles of the trunk are described with care. Nerves in the modern sense are absent, and the vessels are classified by what they are thought to carry rather than traced one by one.

Some things are not said. The text gives no sign that dissection was done regularly, or by a teacher before a class, or that its results were used to correct the received lists, and nothing in the later literature points to a continuing practice. Later compendia repeat the enumerations without adding observations of their own, and the commentators explain the passage as they explain the rest of the text. Whether Suśruta’s instruction records the practice of an earlier surgical school or an ideal set down by an author who valued direct observation cannot now be decided. What is clear is that the instruction itself was transmitted with respect for more than a thousand years, and that it gave later reformers a classical warrant for teaching anatomy from the dead body (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 4.5.2 How Many Bones?
docs.text:
No question of classical anatomy has received more scholarly attention than the number of the bones. Caraka counts 360 (Ca.Śā. 7), and his list includes, besides the bones of the limbs, trunk and head, the thirty-two teeth, the thirty-two sockets in which they sit, and the twenty nails. The law book of Yājñavalkya gives the same total with a closely similar list. The number is older than either. A passage of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, in the Vedic ritual literature, matches the 360 bones of the person to the 360 days of the ritual year, one of the many correspondences between the body and the cosmos that the Brāhmaṇas draw. Suśruta knows this tradition and departs from it. He reports that those who follow the Veda (vedavādin) speak of 360 bones, but states that in the science of surgery there are 300, and he distributes them by region and classifies them by form (Table 4.6).

Table 4.6. Suśruta’s count and classification of the bones (Su.Śā. 5) Region or kind Number or examples By region the four limbs 120 (thirty in each) pelvis, flanks, back and chest 117 neck and head 63 total 300 By form kapāla (“plate”) flat bones, as of the knee, hip, shoulder, cheek, palate, temple and skull rucaka (“bright”) the teeth taruṇa (“tender”) soft, cartilaginous parts, as of the nose, ears, neck and eye sockets valaya (“ring”) curved bones of the hands, feet, flanks, back, abdomen and chest nalaka (“tube”) all the rest: the hollow, tubular bones

Neither total agrees with the 206 bones of the adult skeleton in modern anatomy, and the reasons are instructive. Both lists count the teeth, which modern anatomy does not include among the bones, and Caraka counts their sockets and the nails as well. Suśruta’s “tender” bones include cartilages. Several bones that are single in the adult, such as the hip bone, the sacrum and the breastbone, form from separate parts that fuse during growth, and an observer of a young or macerated skeleton could reasonably count those parts separately. Some numbers, finally, were reached by rule rather than by looking. A tradition for which 360 was already a significant number, or one that gave three bones to every toe, the great toe included, would arrive at round totals whatever the corpse showed. Classical anatomy, in other words, was neither fantasy nor a simple record of observation, and both the dismissal of the counts and the claim that they match modern anatomy point by point miss what they are.

The comparison was first worked out in detail by A. F. Rudolf Hoernle, the editor of the Bower Manuscript, in his Osteology of 1907 (Hoernle 1907). Hoernle collated the lists of Caraka, Suśruta, Yājñavalkya and Vāgbhaṭa with their commentaries and identified as many of the named bones as he could with those of modern anatomy. He argued that two systems lay behind the texts. One was older, shared by the Ātreya school of Caraka and by the Vedic and legal tradition. The other was a surgical count associated with Suśruta. Hoernle also argued that Suśruta’s list had been disturbed in transmission, and proposed emendations to restore it. His collation remains indispensable. His emendations are more debatable, since they assume that the original text must have agreed with what a careful anatomist would see, and later scholars have been readier to accept that the classical counts were partly conventional. The commentators had faced the problem long before: they knew that the two compendia disagreed and tried to reconcile them by explaining what each count included.

The debate shows that a number in a Sanskrit compendium could be at once a datum of observation, an inherited convention and a point of doctrine, and that readers from the commentators onwards argued about which it was. Suśruta justifies the attention he gives the bones with an image: as trees stand by the hard core within them, so bodies are held up by the bones, which remain when the flesh has perished (Su.Śā. 5). The count of the bones proved as durable as the bones themselves. It was copied from text to text, debated by commentators, and revised only when modern anatomy entered the Āyurvedic curriculum in the twentieth century.

docs.title: 4.5.3 Embryology and the Layers of the Body
docs.text: Suśruta’s Śārīrasthāna begins, like Caraka’s, with the evolution of the world and the nature of the person, and then turns to conception and the development of the embryo (Su.Śā. 3–4). The embryo is formed from semen, uterine blood and the self; its parts develop month by month, the heart being formed in the fourth month, when the foetus begins to express desires through its mother. Suśruta describes seven layers of the skin, from the outermost, “shining” layer (avabhāsinī) to the innermost, which holds the flesh; seven membranes (kalā) that separate the bodily constituents; and the various “receptacles” (āśaya) of the body, such as the stomach, colon and bladder. Organs such as the liver and spleen are said to arise from blood, the lungs from the foam of blood, the intestines, bladder and anus from the essence of blood and phlegm cooked by bile, and the kidneys from the essence of blood and fat. These accounts combine observation with speculative theory.

docs.title: 4.5.4 The Vital Points (Marman)
docs.text: A marman is a place where flesh, vessels, ligaments, bones and joints meet, and where injury is especially dangerous. Suśruta lists 107 such points (Su.Śā. 6), which the surgeon must know in order to avoid them. He classifies them by the tissue that predominates—flesh (11), vessels (41), ligaments (27), bone (8) and joints (20)—and by the consequence of injury: immediately fatal (19), fatal after an interval (33), fatal on removal of the foreign body (3), disabling (44) and painful (8). The vital points are distributed over the whole body: eleven in each limb, twelve in the chest and abdomen, fourteen in the back, and thirty-seven in the head and neck. Among them are the heart (hṛdaya), the navel (nābhi) and the bladder (basti), all “immediately fatal”, the temples (śaṅkha), the crown of the head (adhipati) and the point between the eyebrows (sthapanī). The size of each is given in finger-breadths, and the surgeon is told how far from each he must keep his knife. The doctrine of vital points was also important in the martial traditions of South India, where it developed into the marmam and varmam lore of Kerala and Tamil Nadu (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 4.5.5 Anatomy after Suśruta
docs.text:
The anatomy of the compendia changed little over the following centuries. Vāgbhaṭa reorganised the material of Caraka and Suśruta in his own Śārīrasthāna, and the later handbooks condensed it, but no Sanskrit author is known to have revised the enumerations on the basis of fresh observation. Anatomy remained a body of numbers and names to be learned, and the arguments about it were arguments about texts.

Other traditions present in India approached the body differently. Unani physicians inherited Galen’s anatomy, learned from the dissection of animals and set out in Arabic and Persian textbooks. A Persian treatise on anatomy by Manṣūr ibn Ilyās, written in Shiraz at the end of the fourteenth century, was illustrated with full-page figures of the bones, nerves, muscles, veins and arteries, and was copied in India. Tibetan physicians, as Chapter 11 shows, sometimes appealed to what could be seen at sky-burial grounds to test the inherited descriptions. None of these traditions practised systematic human dissection before modern times.

The decisive change came with the colonial medical colleges and the dissection performed by Madhusudan Gupta at Calcutta in 1836 (Chapter 12). Later Indian writers often cited Suśruta’s instruction to show that the dissection of the dead was no offence against Indian tradition. Some eighty years after Gupta, Āyurvedic reformers wrote new Sanskrit textbooks of anatomy based on modern dissection (Chapter 12), and the modern Āyurvedic degree course teaches anatomy from the cadaver. The dissection passage had become a charter for a practice that its author may never have seen carried out as a routine.

docs.title: 4.5.6 Pictures of the Body
docs.text: Classical Sanskrit medical manuscripts are almost never illustrated: the body was carried in words and numbers, not in drawings. Pictures of the body appear late and outside the Sanskrit medical texts. The Tibetan medical paintings commissioned by Desi Sangye Gyatso at the end of the seventeenth century include anatomical plates of the bones, organs, vessels and vital points (Chapter 11). From about the eighteenth century, painters in Nepal and northern India also produced figures of the human body marked with channels, vital points and the centres of the yogic body. Dominik Wujastyk has studied one such painting in the Wellcome Collection in London. He shows that its labels combine the vocabulary of the medical texts with that of yoga and tantra, so that the picture represents a body understood through several bodies of learning at once (Wujastyk 2009). Images of this kind are not records of dissection. They are diagrams of the body as the texts and practices of their time described it, and they are valuable precisely for that reason.

docs.title: 4.6 The Surgeon
docs.text:
Suśruta describes the qualities required of a surgeon at the moment of operation: courage, speed, sharp instruments, freedom from sweating and trembling, and presence of mind (Su.Sū. 5). More generally, the physician should be learned, experienced, skilful, clean, well-dressed, gentle in speech and friendly to all. Like Caraka, Suśruta speaks of four “feet” of treatment—physician, patient, drugs and attendant—and holds the physician to be the most important of the four (Su.Sū. 34). The same chapter describes the place of the physician in war: with his drugs and instruments he is to be stationed near the king’s tent, where he can be seen and reached by the wounded, and the text gives instructions for protecting the army’s food and water against poison by the enemy.

A physician who had completed his studies was to begin practice only after obtaining the king’s permission (Su.Sū. 10)—one of the earliest references in India to a form of licensing. Suśruta also describes the omens to be observed on being called to a patient, the signs of a good or bad messenger, and the auspicious and inauspicious dreams of the sick (Su.Sū. 29), in terms similar to Caraka’s Indriyasthāna.

Suśruta’s classification of diseases (Su.Sū. 24) is notable. He divides them into seven groups according to their origin: hereditary diseases transmitted through the parents’ reproductive fluids; congenital diseases arising during pregnancy; diseases of the doṣas; diseases caused by injury; seasonal diseases; diseases sent by gods or other supernatural agents; and “natural” conditions such as hunger, thirst, old age and death. The scheme recognises heredity and congenital disease as distinct categories.

Suśruta also warns against the half-trained. A surgeon who knows only the texts but has no practical skill is like a coward on the battlefield; one who has practical skill but lacks learning should be punished by the king; and both are unfit to practise, like a bird with only one wing (Su.Sū. 3). The ideal is the physician who knows both, who is compared to a chariot with two wheels.

docs.title: 4.7 The Surgical Patient
docs.text: The surgeon prepares by assembling his instruments, cotton, bandages, oils, honey, decoctions, cold water and hot water and the attendants needed to hold the patient. Light food is given before most operations, but the patient is kept fasting before some, such as operations in the abdomen or mouth. To dull pain the text recommends wine; it does not describe anaesthesia in the modern sense. After the operation the wound is cleaned, dressed and bandaged, and the patient is placed in a clean, sheltered room. Here Suśruta’s instructions combine practical hygiene—protection from wind, dust, flies and smoke, cleanliness of bed and attendants, a regulated diet—with fumigation and protective rites against “night-wanderers” and other spirits thought to attack the wounded (Su.Sū. 19).

docs.title: 4.7.1 Wounds and Bandaging
docs.text:
Suśruta distinguishes chronic or inflamed wounds (vraṇa) arising from the doṣas from fresh traumatic wounds (sadyovraṇa), which he classifies by shape into six kinds: incised, perforated, punctured, lacerated, crushed and abraded. He lists sixty measures (upakrama) for the treatment of wounds, from fasting and poultices through cleansing, incision, suturing and bandaging to the restoration of normal skin colour and the regrowth of hair (Su.Ci. 1). He describes the signs of a clean wound and of a healed wound with great care, and fourteen kinds of bandage (Su.Sū. 18), to be chosen according to the part of the body (Table 4.7). He also describes the materials of bandages—linen, cotton, wool, silk, bark and leather—and three degrees of tightness, to be chosen according to the site and the doṣas involved.

Table 4.7. Suśruta’s fourteen bandages (Su.Sū. 18), with the literal sense of their names Name Literal sense Name Literal sense kośa sheath yamaka twin dāma garland khaṭvā cot svastika cross cīna (a bandage for the eye corners) anuvellita spiral vibandha binding pratolī street, passage vitāna canopy maṇḍala circle gophaṇā sling sthagikā cap pañcāṅgī five-limbed

docs.title: 4.8.1 Piercing of the Ears
docs.text: The chapter that contains the repair of the nose begins with the piercing of a child’s ears (karṇavyadha), which Suśruta prescribes in the sixth or seventh month after birth, on an auspicious day, for protection and for ornament (Su.Sū. 16). He describes how the child is to be held and distracted, where the lobe is to be pierced, the complications of piercing in the wrong place—pain, swelling, fever and damage to vessels—and the gradual stretching of the hole with progressively larger plugs. The custom of stretching the lobes with heavy ornaments explains why torn lobes were so common and why so much of the chapter is devoted to repairing them. Suśruta distinguishes the shapes of torn lobes and devises a method of repair for each, using local tissue and, where necessary, a flap from the cheek; he also describes the after-care of the repaired lobe and the signs of failure.

docs.title: 4.8.2 Reconstruction of the Nose and the Ear Lobe
docs.text:
In ancient India cutting off the nose was a punishment and a form of humiliation. Besides his fifteen ways of joining torn ear lobes (karṇasandhāna), Suśruta describes a method of rebuilding the nose (nāsāsandhāna, Su.Sū. 16.27–31). Its essentials are these: the surgeon takes a leaf the size of the nose, cuts a matching flap of skin from the cheek, leaving it attached at one end, freshens the edges of the stump, turns the flap over and sutures it in place; two tubes are inserted to keep the nostrils open, the area is dusted with powdered drugs, and the wound is dressed with oil. When the flap has taken, the attached end is cut. The operation is a pedicled flap, the principle of much modern reconstructive surgery. The text also describes repair of the lip.

Suśruta’s descriptions are among the oldest written accounts of reconstructive surgery anywhere. “Firsts” in this field, however, are hard to establish, and the history of the operation in modern times is more complicated than popular accounts suggest. In October 1794 the Gentleman’s Magazine of London published a letter, signed “B. L.”, describing an operation performed near Poona on Cowasjee, a Maratha bullock-driver with the British army whose nose and one hand had been cut off by soldiers of Tipu Sultan. The operation, witnessed by two Bombay surgeons, Thomas Cruso and James Findlay, was performed by a local practitioner described as belonging to the “brick-maker” caste, and it used a flap from the forehead, not from the cheek. Whether this living craft descended from Suśruta’s text is unknown; there is no written link. The report stimulated European interest: Joseph Constantine Carpue performed two operations by the “Indian method” in London and published them in 1816, and the forehead flap is still known as the “Indian flap”. European surgeons, however, already had their own tradition of nasal reconstruction, using a flap from the arm, which goes back to the Branca family in fifteenth-century Sicily and was published by Gaspare Tagliacozzi in 1597.

docs.title: 4.8.3 Couching of Cataract
docs.text: In the Uttaratantra (Su.Utt. 17), Suśruta describes the treatment of one form of cataract (kaphaja liṅganāśa) by couching: with the patient seated and looking at his nose, the surgeon inserts a lancet-shaped probe at the side of the eye, between the black and the white, at a “natural opening”, and pushes the opaque lens down and out of the line of sight. Couching was also practised in the Greco-Roman world and is described by Celsus in the first century CE. It was performed by itinerant couchers in India into the twentieth century. It can restore some sight, but without a lens the eye cannot focus, and infection and other complications were common.

docs.title: 4.8.4 Abdominal and Urinary Surgery
docs.text: Suśruta describes the removal of bladder stones through an incision in the perineum (Su.Ci. 7)—an operation also known to Greek surgeons, who were forbidden by the Hippocratic Oath to perform it themselves—and treatments for intestinal obstruction and perforation (Su.Ci. 14). In the last, the abdomen is opened and the edges of a perforated intestine are brought together by the bites of large black ants, whose bodies are then cut off, leaving the heads as clips; the intestine is replaced and the abdomen sutured.
