The text is clear that these operations are dangerous; for the removal of a stone, it advises the surgeon to obtain the king’s permission first, since the patient may die.

docs.title: 4.8.5 Obstructed Labour
docs.text: Su.Ci. 15 deals with the obstructed foetus (mūḍhagarbha). When the foetus is dead, the surgeon is to extract it by hand, by hook or by cutting it in pieces, to save the mother’s life; the text describes the different positions of the foetus and the manoeuvres for each. The text does not describe a caesarean section on a living mother, as is sometimes claimed.

docs.title: 4.8.6 Fistula, Haemorrhoids and the Alkaline Thread
docs.text: Suśruta classifies fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) into five kinds (Su.Ni. 4) and treats it and haemorrhoids by surgery, alkali and cautery. For sinuses (nāḍīvraṇa) in weak patients or in delicate places he mentions a thread smeared with alkali, tied through the track and tightened gradually. In the twentieth century this was developed, chiefly at Banaras Hindu University, into the “alkaline thread” (kṣārasūtra) treatment of fistula-in-ano, which has been compared with conventional surgery in clinical trials and is used in some surgical units in India.

docs.title: 4.8.7 Swellings, Tumours and Other Surgical Diseases
docs.text: Much of the Nidāna- and Cikitsāsthāna deals with conditions that we would still regard as surgical: abscesses (vidradhi), which are to be opened when they “ripen”, and Suśruta gives careful signs for judging when the pus has formed; inflammatory swellings (śopha); nodules (granthi) and tumours (arbuda), for which he prescribes excision, cautery and caustics; scrofulous swellings of the neck (gaṇḍamālā); haemorrhoids (arśas), which he treats by drugs, alkali, cautery and excision according to their type; scrotal enlargements (vṛddhi), including hydrocele and hernia; and sinuses and non-healing ulcers. The variety of procedures—and the emphasis on choosing the least drastic that will work—is characteristic of the text.

docs.title: 4.8.8 Fractures and Dislocations
docs.text: Suśruta distinguishes six kinds of dislocation (sandhimukta) and twelve kinds of fracture of the shaft (kāṇḍabhagna) (Su.Ni. 15), among them comminuted, crushed, split, bent and transverse fractures. Treatment (Su.Ci. 3) involves traction and reduction, immobilisation with splints of bark or bamboo bound with bandages, cold applications, and a regimen to promote healing.

docs.title: 4.9 The Uttaratantra
docs.text: The Uttaratantra, the “later book”, was added to the older five sections to make the work cover all eight branches of medicine. Its 66 chapters deal with diseases of the eye (chapters 1–19), ear (20–21), nose (22–24) and head (25–26), which Suśruta treats together as śālākya; with the seizers (graha) that afflict children (27–37); with gynaecological disorders (38); with a series of general diseases—fevers, diarrhoea, wasting, cough, vomiting and others (39–59); with possession by spirits, epilepsy and insanity (60–62); and with the classification of tastes, the regimen of health, the thirty-two “devices of composition” (tantrayukti; Section 5.6.2) and the varieties of the doṣas (63–66). Suśruta classifies seventy-six diseases of the eye by the part affected: the lids, the junctions, the white, the black, the whole eye and the “seeing” part.

docs.title: 4.10 Toxicology
docs.text:
The eight chapters of the Kalpasthāna form the classical treatise on toxicology (agadatantra). They begin with the protection of the king against poisoners and go on to the poisons of plants and minerals, the classes of snakes and the stages of envenomation, and the bites of rats, insects, spiders, scorpions and rabid animals. Suśruta’s account is the fullest in the compendia; it is described, together with Caraka’s, in Section 8.6.

Health and Safety Note

Neither the operations described in this chapter nor the classical treatments for snakebite and poisoning should be attempted. Couching of cataract, still practised by some traditional healers, carries a high risk of permanent blindness, whereas modern cataract surgery is widely available in India, often free of charge. See Section 12.7.

docs.title: 4.11 Commentaries and Transmission
docs.text:
The most important commentaries are those of Jejjaṭa (perhaps 9th century, now fragmentary), Gayadāsa (Nyāyacandrikā, perhaps 11th century, partly preserved), Cakrapāṇidatta (Bhānumatī, 11th century, on the Sūtrasthāna) and Ḍalhaṇa (Nibandhasaṃgraha, 12th century), whose complete commentary is printed with the standard edition and quotes his predecessors extensively.

The tenth-century bibliographer Ibn al-Nadīm records that a book of “Susrud” was translated into Arabic by an Indian physician called Manka for the Barmakid vizier Yaḥyā ibn Khālid in Abbasid Baghdad; Arabic medical writers such as al-Rāzī cite Indian authorities among others. The extent of Indian influence on Arabic surgery, however, is not well established.

docs.title: 4.12 Surgery after Suśruta
docs.text:
The Suśruta Saṃhitā continued to be copied, taught and commented on, but surgery itself seems to have declined among the learned physicians of the medieval period. Vāgbhaṭa kept the surgical material in condensed form. The later handbooks describe the surgical diseases but treat them more and more with drugs, alkali and cautery, and Meulenbeld’s survey of the literature records few later works devoted to surgery (Meulenbeld 1999–2002). Historians have offered several explanations: the brahmanical concern with purity, which made contact with blood, pus and corpses polluting; the growing prestige of mineral and mercurial pharmacy (Chapter 9); and the lack of institutions in which surgical skill could be taught to many students at once. None of these explanations can be proved, and the decline may be partly an illusion created by the texts, which record what learned physicians wrote rather than what all healers did.

Surgery did not disappear; it passed into the hands of craftsmen. Barbers let blood, lanced abscesses and pulled teeth. Bonesetters treated fractures and dislocations (Chapter 11). Specialist couchers of cataract, often itinerant, travelled from village to village, and other specialists removed bladder stones. The practitioner who rebuilt Cowasjee’s nose near Poona in 1794 belonged to such a world of hereditary craft. These skills were learned by apprenticeship within families, not from Sanskrit texts, and they are known mainly from the reports of European travellers and colonial officials, who described them with a mixture of curiosity and disdain.

Colonial surgery competed with these practitioners directly. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries surgeons of the Indian Medical Service performed cataract extractions and operations for stone on a very large scale, and the success of these operations did much to win acceptance for Western medicine among the Indian public. The same surgeons condemned the couchers, whose patients often lost the eye to infection or inflammation after an initially successful operation. Studies of traditional couching in parts of Africa and South Asia in the late twentieth century found that it often ends in blindness.

In the twentieth century the Āyurvedic colleges revived surgery as a subject. Departments of śalya (surgery) and śālākya (diseases of the head and the senses) teach the classical texts together with modern surgery, the alkaline thread for fistula (above) was developed and tested, and the question of what operations Āyurvedic graduates may perform has become a matter of public controversy (Chapter 12). The heritage of Suśruta is now claimed both by the modern surgeon, who honours him as a predecessor, and by the Āyurvedic surgeon, who sees himself as his successor.

docs.title: 4.13 Suśruta and Ancient Surgery Elsewhere
docs.text: Surgery was practised in all the major civilisations of antiquity, and comparison helps to place Suśruta’s achievement. Egyptian papyri of the second millennium BCE describe the treatment of wounds, fractures and dislocations. The Hippocratic writings (fifth and fourth centuries BCE) include treatises on fractures, joints and head wounds, and the Roman encyclopaedist Celsus (first century CE) describes operations for bladder stone, cataract (by couching), hernia and the reconstruction of lips, ears and noses using advancement flaps from adjacent skin. Galen, in the second century, wrote extensively on anatomy, based largely on the dissection of animals. In this company the Suśruta Saṃhitā stands out for the systematic nature of its surgical teaching—especially its insistence on practice on models, its classified instruments and its careful attention to wound care—and for its rotation flap for the nose. Guido Majno, a pathologist and historian of ancient wound care, gave it an important place in his comparative survey, while noting that its theory of wounds, like that of the Greeks, rested on humoral ideas (Majno 1975).

docs.title: 4.14 Assessment
docs.text:
Suśruta is often called “the father of surgery”. The title is a modern honorific; it is not a historical finding, and claims that international bodies have formally conferred it should be treated with caution. What can be said is that the Suśruta Saṃhitā contains one of the most systematic and detailed accounts of surgical teaching and practice to survive from antiquity: a curriculum that required practice on models, a classified armamentarium, anatomy learned from the dead body, careful wound care, and a repertoire of operations that included the reconstruction of the nose and ear, the removal of stones, the couching of cataract and the extraction of an obstructed foetus. It deserves its place in the history of world surgery on its own merits, without exaggerated claims of priority.

It should also be remembered that surgery in pre-modern India, as everywhere before the nineteenth century, was performed without effective anaesthesia, without knowledge of infection and without blood transfusion. Operations were painful and dangerous, and many patients must have died of bleeding, shock and sepsis. The texts’ careful attention to speed, cleanliness and the selection of patients reflects these realities. The transformation of surgery in the modern world came with anaesthesia (from the 1840s), antisepsis (from the 1860s) and later advances, which Indian surgeons have taken up and contributed to as fully as any others.

Summary

The Suśruta Saṃhitā, an older core revised and enlarged by about 500 CE, is the classical work of Indian surgery: it requires practice on models, classifies its instruments, prescribes the study of a macerated corpse and describes operations from the repair of the nose and ear to lithotomy and the extraction of a dead foetus. Its anatomy combines observation with inherited numbers, as the debate over its 300 bones shows, and its later history passed from the learned physician to the craftsman. It deserves its place in the history of surgery on its own merits, without the modern claims of priority made for it.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the text see Trikamjī and Ācārya’s edition (Trikamji Acharya and Acharya 1938) and Bhishagratna’s translation (Bhishagratna 1907–1916); for selected chapters and an introduction, Wujastyk (Wujastyk 2003); for comparison with other ancient surgery, Majno (Majno 1975). On the count of the bones see Hoernle (Hoernle 1907); on later images of the body, Wujastyk (Wujastyk 2009).

docs.title: Chapter 5: Vāgbhaṭa and the Later Medical Literature
docs.text:
rāgādirogān satatānuṣaktān aśeṣakāyaprasṛtān aśeṣān autsukyamohāratidāñ jaghāna yo ’pūrvavaidyāya namo ’stu tasmai Homage to that unprecedented physician who destroyed all the diseases—passion and the rest—that cling constantly, pervade the whole body, and bring longing, delusion and discontent.

— Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, Sūtrasthāna 1.1

docs.title: 5.1 Vāgbhaṭa
docs.text:
The third member of the “great triad” is the work of Vāgbhaṭa, who lived in Sindh, probably around 600 CE (Meulenbeld 1999–2002). Two compendia bear his name: the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha (“Compendium of the Eight Branches”), written in mixed prose and verse, and the shorter Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (“Heart of the Eight Branches”), written entirely in verse. The colophons of the Saṃgraha name its author as Vāgbhaṭa, son of Siṃhagupta and grandson of another Vāgbhaṭa. Whether the same man wrote both works, or whether the Hṛdaya is a later condensation by a namesake, has been long debated, and the question is not settled; the two texts are closely related, and many verses are shared.

The opening verse of the Hṛdaya, quoted above, praises an “unprecedented physician” who has destroyed passion, delusion and the other afflictions. The language of the verse—“passion and the rest” (rāgādi) are the defilements of Buddhist thought—has led many scholars to read it as an homage to the Buddha, and other passages of the Saṃgraha invoke Buddhist deities. Vāgbhaṭa was in all probability a Buddhist; but his work was accepted without difficulty by physicians of all communities, and it became the most widely used medical text in India.

docs.title: 5.1.1 The Two Compendia
docs.text:
Vāgbhaṭa’s aim was to bring together the teachings of Caraka and Suśruta, with additions from later practice, in a form that could be learnt and used. The Saṃgraha, of 150 chapters, is the fuller work; the Hṛdaya, of 120 chapters in six sections (Table 5.1), is concise, clear and memorable. Its verse form suited a tradition in which students learned texts by heart. A complete English translation of the Hṛdaya is available (Srikantha Murthy 2012), and Valiathan has summarised it for the general reader (Valiathan 2009).

Table 5.1. The six sections of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya Section Chapters Subject Sūtrasthāna 30 General principles; daily and seasonal regimen; foods and drinks; tastes; doṣas; drugs; procedures Śārīrasthāna 6 Embryology, anatomy, constitution, prognosis Nidānasthāna 16 Causes and signs of diseases Cikitsāsthāna 22 Treatment of diseases Kalpasiddhisthāna 6 Purification therapies: drugs, administration and complications Uttarasthāna 40 Children and seizers; insanity and possession; eye, ear, nose, mouth and head; surgery; poisons; rejuvenation; virility Total 120

docs.title: 5.1.2 The Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha
docs.text: The Saṃgraha is the larger and, in some respects, the more interesting of the two works. Its prose passages preserve discussions and explanations omitted from the Hṛdaya, and it quotes or paraphrases older authorities more extensively. It is more open about its religious context: it invokes the Buddha and Buddhist deities, and some of its prescriptions include Buddhist protective formulae. Like Vāgbhaṭa’s other work, it gives a place among the rejuvenating remedies to garlic, which brahmanical orthodoxy regarded as forbidden food but which the physicians valued highly—one of the texts of the Bower Manuscript is devoted to it (Section 1.7.1). The Saṃgraha was commented on by Indu in the Śaśilekhā. Because it is longer and less memorable, it was less widely studied than the Hṛdaya, but it is an important witness to the medicine of its time.

docs.title: 5.1.3 Character and Influence
docs.text:
The Hṛdaya’s Sūtrasthāna begins with the daily regimen—“a healthy person should rise at the hour of Brahmā to protect his life” (AH Sū. 2.1)—and continues with the seasons, the urges, the properties of foods and drinks, the protection of food from poison, the tastes, the doṣas and their subdivisions, and the principles of therapy. Its systematic arrangement made it the preferred textbook in many regions, above all in Kerala (Section 5.3).

The Hṛdaya was translated into Tibetan in the eleventh century, by the translator Rin chen bzang po and the Indian scholar Janārdana, and is preserved in the Tibetan Buddhist canon together with several commentaries. Its structure and much of its content are reflected in the Four Tantras (rGyud bzhi), the foundational text of Tibetan medicine, which also draws on other sources (Chapter 11). The principal commentaries on Vāgbhaṭa’s works are listed in Table 5.2.

Table 5.2. Principal commentaries on Vāgbhaṭa’s works Commentary Author and date Notes Padārthacandrikā Candranandana (Kashmir; perhaps 10th century) On the Hṛdaya; one of the oldest Śaśilekhā Indu On the Saṃgraha Sarvāṅgasundarā Aruṇadatta (13th century) On the Hṛdaya; widely studied Āyurvedarasāyana Hemādri (13th century) On the Hṛdaya; survives in part

docs.title: 5.1.4 The Contents of the Hṛdaya
docs.text:
A brief survey shows how Vāgbhaṭa reorganised the inherited material. The thirty chapters of the Sūtrasthāna move from the healthy person (regimen, seasons, urges, the prevention of disease) to foods and drinks, the protection of food against poison, the tastes, the doṣas, the classification of drugs, and then to the procedures of therapy: oleation and sudation, emesis and purgation, enemas, nasal treatment, smoking, gargles, eye treatments, bloodletting, the extraction of foreign bodies, alkali and cautery. The six chapters of the Śārīrasthāna treat embryology, the complications of pregnancy, the parts of the body, the vital points, constitution and signs of death. The Nidāna- and Cikitsāsthānas follow the order of diseases established by Caraka, starting with fever. The Kalpasiddhisthāna combines Caraka’s pharmaceutics of emetics and purgatives with the management of complications of purification. The forty chapters of the Uttarasthāna cover the remaining branches: children and their “seizers”, insanity and possession, the eye, ear, nose, mouth and head, wounds and fractures, fistulae and swellings, poisons and bites, and finally rejuvenation and virility.

In each area Vāgbhaṭa chooses, condenses and harmonises. He presents Suśruta’s surgery in abbreviated form, adds material from later practice—for example on the treatment of eye diseases—and gives a coherent theoretical framework throughout. It is this combination of completeness, order and brevity that explains the work’s success.

docs.title: 5.1.5 How the Commentators Worked
docs.text: Much of what we know about the history of the classical texts comes from their commentators. A Sanskrit commentary explains difficult words, supplies the implied subject of terse statements, resolves apparent contradictions between passages, connects the text with other authorities, and often records alternative readings found in other manuscripts. Ḍalhaṇa, for instance, frequently notes that “some read” a verse differently, and rejects passages that he regards as interpolations; Cakrapāṇidatta argues with earlier commentators such as Jejjaṭa and defends his own interpretations at length. Commentators also brought the texts up to date, explaining classical drug names by the names in use in their own time and region, and adding practical details from their own experience. For the modern editor, the commentaries are both a guide to meaning and evidence for the state of the text at the time they were written, and the variant readings they report are one of the main tools for reconstructing the history of the compendia.

docs.title: 5.2 The Medieval Literature
docs.text: After Vāgbhaṭa the medical literature in Sanskrit grew steadily. Its main genres were commentaries on the classics; handbooks of diagnosis; collections of formulae for practice (yoga, cikitsā works); lexicons of drugs (nighaṇṭu); works on particular subjects such as pulse, urine or children’s diseases; and, from about the tenth century, works on mercurial and metallic pharmacy (Chapter 9). Three later works came to be known as the “lesser triad” (laghutrayī).

docs.title: 5.2.1 Mādhava’s Nidāna (c. 700 CE)
docs.text:
Mādhavakara’s Rogaviniścaya (“Determination of Diseases”), generally called the Mādhavanidāna, collected the descriptions of the causes, premonitory signs, signs and course of diseases from the earlier compendia into a single diagnostic handbook arranged by disease, adding conditions that the older works had not described as separate diseases. Among these is āmavāta, a painful swelling of the joints attributed to āma and vāta, which modern Āyurvedic writers often equate with rheumatoid arthritis, though the correspondence is not exact. The work was enormously influential: it fixed the arrangement of diseases followed by most later handbooks, and it was itself commented on, notably in the Madhukoṣa of Vijayarakṣita and Śrīkaṇṭhadatta (c. 12th–13th century). Meulenbeld’s annotated translation of its first ten chapters with that commentary remains the fullest study of how such a handbook was read (Meulenbeld 1974).

Mādhava’s work runs to some seventy chapters, beginning with the five means of knowing a disease and fever, and proceeding through the diseases in an order that later handbooks followed closely. Besides āmavāta, he gives separate chapters to conditions that the older compendia had treated only briefly or not at all: acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), an itching rash attributed to cold wind (śītapitta), and a pox disease (masūrikā), which Suśruta had listed among the minor diseases (Su.Ni. 13) but which Mādhava describes in a chapter of its own. His method was to compile, quoting the earlier authorities verbatim and adding his own verses where needed, and the work is therefore also an important witness to the text of the compendia as they were read in his time.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Cakrapāṇidatta (11th century)
docs.text: The Bengali physician Cakrapāṇidatta, whose father served at the court of the Pāla king Nayapāla, was the most important medical author of the eleventh century. Besides his authoritative commentary on Caraka (Chapter 3) and his partial commentary on Suśruta, he wrote a formulary arranged in the order of Mādhava’s diseases, the Cikitsāsaṃgraha (known as Cakradatta), which became the standard practical handbook of eastern India, and a work on drugs (Dravyaguṇasaṃgraha). His commentaries are among the main sources for the history of the earlier literature, since they quote many lost works.

docs.title: 5.2.3 The Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā (c. 13th–14th century)
docs.text:
The compendium of Śārṅgadhara, son of Dāmodara, is a manual of pharmacy and practice in three sections (khaṇḍa) and thirty-two chapters. The first section deals with weights and measures, the preparation and timing of medicines, the pulse, the doṣas, the body and the classification of diseases; the second with the forms of medicine—juices, pastes, decoctions, infusions, powders, pills, confections, medicated oils and ghees, fermented preparations, and preparations of metals and minerals; and the third with the purification therapies, eye treatments and other procedures. It is one of the earliest works to describe examination of the pulse (Chapter 10), and it reflects the growing place of metals and mercury in practice. Its clear, practical arrangement made it the standard text on pharmacy, and modern Āyurvedic colleges still teach pharmaceutics largely on its model. It also contains one of the early mentions in Sanskrit medical literature of opium (ahiphena), which reached India through the Arab trade and became a common ingredient of later formulae.

The pharmaceutical works also discuss the times at which medicines should be taken. Suśruta lists ten such times, and Śārṅgadhara five: early in the morning on an empty stomach, before or after a meal, with each mouthful, at intervals, and at night. Each is related to the doṣa and the part of the body to be treated—a medicine taken before a meal, for example, was thought to act on the lower body. These rules, like the system of measures, are part of the history of pharmacy; they are not a guide to the use of any medicine.

docs.title: 5.2.4 Bhāvamiśra’s Bhāvaprakāśa (16th century)
docs.text:
Bhāvamiśra’s large compendium, written in the sixteenth century, summarises the whole of medicine for practitioners and contains an extensive section on drugs (the Bhāvaprakāśanighaṇṭu) that is still widely used for identifying medicinal plants. It is notable for describing new diseases and drugs. It gives the first Sanskrit account of phiraṅgaroga, “the disease of the Franks”, that is, syphilis, which reached India with the Portuguese; Bhāvamiśra treats it with preparations of mercury and with copacīnī, the “China root” (Smilax species) that had become popular in Asia and Europe as a remedy for the disease.

The Bhāvaprakāśa is also a valuable witness to the way the materia medica changed in the early modern period. Drugs introduced through Arab, Persian and Portuguese trade—among them opium, “China root” and other new items—appear in it alongside the old ones, and later lexicons added plants from the Americas, such as tobacco and chilli, that had arrived in India in the sixteenth century. Indian medicine, in other words, was never a closed system; it absorbed new diseases and new drugs as they appeared.

docs.title: 5.2.5 Medicine as Poetry
docs.text: Not all medical works were dry manuals. In the seventeenth century the Maharashtrian poet-physician Lolimbarāja composed the Vaidyajīvana, a short handbook of remedies written in elegant and playful verse, many of whose stanzas are addressed to a beloved woman. The work became very popular and was widely memorised, which shows that medical knowledge could also be a form of literary culture. Other authors put formularies into verse to aid memory, and commentators often displayed considerable literary learning.

docs.title: 5.2.6 Other Works
docs.text:
Table 5.3 lists some other important medical works.

Table 5.3. Some other important medical works (dates approximate) Work Author and date Character Kāśyapa Saṃhitā attributed to Mārīca Kaśyapa; c. 7th century Children’s diseases and obstetrics (Chapter 8) Siddhayoga Vṛnda; c. 9th–10th century Formulary arranged by disease, following Mādhava Cikitsāsaṃgraha (Cakradatta) Cakrapāṇidatta; 11th century Formulary; long the standard handbook in eastern India Cikitsāsārasaṃgraha Vaṅgasena; c. 12th century Large compendium of therapeutics Dhanvantarīyanighaṇṭu, Rājanighaṇṭu, Madanapālanighaṇṭu various; c. 10th–15th century Lexicons of drugs (see below) Yogaratnākara anonymous; Maharashtra, c. 17th–18th century Popular compendium; gives the eightfold examination of the patient Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī Govindadāsa; 18th–19th century Formulary, much expanded in modern editions Sahasrayoga anonymous; Kerala Formulary in Malayalam and Sanskrit, central to Kerala practice

docs.title: 5.2.7 Medicine in the Regional Languages
docs.text:
From the early second millennium medical works were also composed in the regional languages. Tamil medical literature developed into the Siddha tradition (Chapter 11). In Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam, Marathi, Bengali, Oriya, Gujarati, Hindi and other languages, physicians produced translations and adaptations of the Sanskrit classics, verse formularies, and works on particular subjects such as children’s diseases and snakebite. Many of these texts remain unpublished in manuscript collections. They were the means by which classical medicine reached practitioners who did not read Sanskrit, and they often record local plants, diseases and practices that the Sanskrit works ignore. Kerala developed a particularly rich medical literature in Malayalam (Section 5.3). Much of this vernacular literature has never been edited, and its history remains to be written. From the fourteenth century, Persian works presented Indian medicine to the Persian-reading elite, and Unani works in turn absorbed Indian drugs (Chapter 11).

A few examples show the range of this literature. In Kannada, Jain authors were prominent. Jagaddala Somanātha rendered Ugrāditya’s Kalyāṇakāraka (Chapter 1) into Kannada in the twelfth century, and Maṅgarāja’s Khagendramaṇidarpaṇa (fourteenth century) is a Kannada treatise on poisons and their treatment. In Sri Lanka the chronicle known as the Cūḷavaṃsa presents King Buddhadāsa (fourth century) as a physician-king who appointed doctors for the villages and composed a medical compendium, the Sārārthasaṅgraha; the attribution belongs to tradition, but the work itself became a standard text of the island’s Āyurveda. A Pali compendium, the Bhesajjamañjūsā (thirteenth century), adapted the classical teaching for a Buddhist readership. In north India the Vaidyamanotsava of Nayanasukha (1592), in Braj verse, is one of the earliest medical works in a form of Hindi. Such works were seldom original in their theory. Their value lies in their choice of material, in their local drugs and diseases, and in the evidence they give of the communities in which medicine was practised and read, such as the Jain households of Karnataka and the Buddhist monasteries of Sri Lanka.

docs.title: 5.2.8 Medicine, Karma and the Stars
docs.text: From the late first millennium a genre of works on “the ripening of deeds” (karmavipāka) linked particular diseases to particular sins in past lives and prescribed expiations, gifts and rites to remove them. Leprosy, for example, was attributed to the killing of a brāhmaṇa, and other diseases to theft, adultery or the neglect of ritual duties. Some works combined this doctrine with astrology and medicine. The Vīrasiṃhāvaloka, composed in 1383 under a ruler of the Tomara dynasty, treats each disease from three points of view—the astrological, the karmic and the medical—and prescribes for it planetary rites, expiations and drugs. Such works show that in late medieval India the rational, humoral explanation of disease and the religious explanation in terms of past deeds and the planets were not felt to be in conflict. The connection between medicine and astrology was also institutional: astrologers and physicians often belonged to the same learned families.

docs.title: 5.2.9 Specialised Sciences: Animals and Plants
docs.text: The model of Āyurveda was extended to animals and plants. Treatises on the medicine of horses are attributed to Śālihotra, and on the medicine of elephants to the sage Pālakāpya, whose Hastyāyurveda is cast as a dialogue with King Romapāda of Aṅga; both traditions were important to kings whose armies depended on these animals. The extant texts are medieval in their present form, though they draw on older material. A “science of the life of trees” (vṛkṣāyurveda) is represented by chapters in the encyclopaedic Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (6th century) and by later treatises such as that of Surapāla, which apply the doctrine of the doṣas to the cultivation and treatment of plants. These works are discussed in Volume 15 of this series.

docs.title: 5.2.10 Manuscripts and Their Preservation
docs.text: Almost all of this literature survives only because it was copied by hand, generation after generation. Medical manuscripts were kept in the houses of physicians, in temple and monastery libraries, and in the collections of rulers. Large collections are now held in Indian libraries and research institutes—among them the Sarasvati Mahal Library at Thanjavur, the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library in Chennai, the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, the Oriental Research Institute in Thiruvananthapuram and the national archives of Nepal—and in European collections, notably the Wellcome Collection in London, which holds one of the largest collections of Indian medical manuscripts outside India. Since 2003 the National Mission for Manuscripts has worked to survey and catalogue India’s manuscript heritage. Much remains unread: many medical works known from catalogues have never been edited, and the history of Indian medicine after the classical period is still being written from these sources.

docs.title: 5.3 Medicine in Kerala
docs.text: Kerala holds a special place in the history of Āyurveda. Its physicians kept a living tradition of learned practice into the twentieth century, and much of modern institutional and international Āyurveda comes from it. The tradition rests on three foundations: the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, a large medical literature in Malayalam, and hereditary lineages of physicians of several communities.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Vāgbhaṭa and the Aṣṭavaidyas
docs.text: Nowhere was Vāgbhaṭa’s influence greater. The traditional physicians of Kerala took the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya as their principal text, learned it by heart, and commented on it in Sanskrit and Malayalam; the Sanskrit commentary Vākyapradīpikā of Parameśvara is one of the Kerala commentaries on the work. Among these physicians a group of Nampūtiri brāhmaṇa families known as the Aṣṭavaidyas (“physicians of the eight branches”) held a special position. Their number is given differently in different sources, and only a few of the families continued to practise in the twentieth century. Each kept its own manuscripts, formulae and specialities and passed them from father to son, together with the standing to treat. Their rank was bound up with the caste order: as brāhmaṇas they stood at the head of the medical profession, and the rules of purity shaped whom they treated and how.

docs.title: 5.3.2 Physicians beyond the Brāhmaṇas
docs.text: Learned medicine in Kerala was never confined to the Aṣṭavaidyas. Physicians of the Īḻava community maintained their own lineages of learning and practice, used Sanskrit as well as Malayalam texts, and were renowned for their knowledge of plants; it was an Īḻava physician, Itty Achuden, whose testimony underlies the Hortus Malabaricus (Section 11.6). Specialists in poisons (viṣavaidya), many of them from non-brahmin families, treated snakebite with their own texts and formulae (Section 8.6). Bonesetters, and the masters of the martial art kaḷarippayaṟṟu, who knew the vital points (marmam), treated injuries, dislocations and fractures (Section 4.5.4). Medical knowledge thus ran across the boundaries of caste, though not on equal terms.

docs.title: 5.3.3 The Malayalam Medical Literature
docs.text: Kerala produced a large medical literature in Malayalam and in the mixed Malayalam–Sanskrit idiom called Maṇipravāḷam. Its best-known works are practical. The formulary Sahasrayoga (“Thousand Formulae”) gives the recipes of many preparations still made by Kerala pharmacies; verse handbooks such as the Cikitsāmañjarī were memorised by students; and a literature on poisons, of which the Jyotsnikā is the best known, served the viṣavaidyas. These works take their theory from Vāgbhaṭa and add recipes, procedures and local drugs. Their value lies in that record of how the classics were applied in one region over several centuries. Most of them have never been critically edited, and their history, like that of the other regional medical literatures, remains to be written.

docs.title: 5.3.4 Procedures and Institutions
docs.text:
Kerala practice is also distinctive in its procedures. The oil therapies now known as keraḷīya cikitsā—the continuous pouring of liquids over the head or body (dhārā), bathing in streams of warm oil (piḻiccil), massage with boluses of medicated rice (ñavarakkiḻi) and others—developed in the households of Kerala physicians (Section 7.8). They elaborate the external therapies of the classical texts rather than the five classical purifications.

In the twentieth century Kerala became one of the main centres of institutional Āyurveda. The state of Travancore opened a school of Āyurveda at Thiruvananthapuram in 1889 (Section 12.2). P. S. Vāriyar founded the Arya Vaidya Sala at Kottakkal in 1902, a manufacturing pharmacy that grew into a hospital, a school and a publisher of texts. Physicians of the old families, Aṣṭavaidya and others, joined or founded colleges and pharmacies of the modern kind. Kerala thus became the source of much of the “pañcakarma” now offered to visitors from India and abroad (Section 12.4), and for many people outside India its oil therapies have come to stand for Āyurveda as a whole.

docs.title: 5.4 Lexicons of Drugs (Nighaṇṭu)
docs.text: The nighaṇṭus are lexicons of materia medica. They list drugs under their many Sanskrit synonyms—which often describe a plant’s appearance, habitat or properties—and give their taste, qualities, potency, post-digestive effect and actions. The synonyms were essential for identifying drugs across regions with different vernacular names, but they also make identification difficult today, since the same name may refer to different plants in different places and periods. Among the most important are the Dhanvantarīyanighaṇṭu (one of the earliest surviving, perhaps 10th–13th century), the Madanapālanighaṇṭu (composed in 1374), the Kaiyadevanighaṇṭu (15th century), the Rājanighaṇṭu of Narahari (14th–15th century) and the Bhāvaprakāśanighaṇṭu (16th century).

docs.title: 5.5 Weights and Measures (Māna)
docs.text: The pharmaceutical works describe a system of weights and measures (māna) used for compounding medicines. The smallest units were derived from seeds and grains—the mustard seed (sarṣapa), the barley grain (yava) and the bright red-and-black seed of Abrus precatorius (guñjā, the jeweller’s rattī). Above these came the māṣa, the karṣa (later equated with the tolā) and the pala, and, for volumes, the kuḍava, the prastha, the āḍhaka and the droṇa, each of the last three being four times the one before. The texts record two systems, the Māgadha and the Kāliṅga, which differ in the values of some units, and the commentators discuss how the measures of the older compendia should be converted. The modern metric equivalents used in India are conventions adopted in the twentieth century, and historians of science have shown that the actual values varied by region and period. The system is described here as part of the history of pharmacy; it should not be used to prepare or dose any medicine.

docs.title: 5.6 How the Texts Were Transmitted
docs.text: Every classical medical work reached the modern world through a chain of handwritten copies, and the text read today is the product of that chain. Its history explains why verse numbers differ between editions, why some passages are doubted, and why the oldest manuscripts and translations matter so much.

docs.title: 5.6.1 Copying, Variants and Commentators
docs.text:
A palm-leaf manuscript in the humid climate of southern and eastern India seldom lasts more than a few centuries; birch bark and paper in the north fare a little better. A text that was to survive had to be recopied again and again, and every copy could introduce errors: a misread letter, a line skipped where two lines ended alike, a marginal note copied into the text. Medical texts were also working books. Their users added formulae that had served them well, glossed obscure words, and supplied verses where they thought something was missing. The wording of the Vedic texts was fixed by oral techniques of preservation, but the medical compendia were never closed in that way. They grew and changed as they were used.

The commentators were the first textual critics of the tradition. Cakrapāṇidatta on Caraka and Ḍalhaṇa on Suśruta regularly report that “some read” a passage otherwise, discuss which reading is right, and note that certain verses are not accepted by earlier authorities or are later additions. Ḍalhaṇa names commentators before him, among them Jejjaṭa and Gayadāsa, and his remarks show that he had several versions of the text in front of him and chose among them. In practice the Suśruta printed today is the text as Ḍalhaṇa established it in the twelfth century, and the Caraka is the text known to Cakrapāṇidatta in the eleventh. What lies behind those versions has to be recovered from older witnesses.

docs.title: 5.6.2 Rules for Reading: The Tantrayukti
docs.text:
The physicians did not only copy their texts; they also had explicit rules for reading them. Both great compendia include, near their end, a list of “devices of composition” (tantrayukti): thirty-two in Suśruta (Su.Utt. 65) and thirty-six in the list of Dṛḍhabala in the Caraka (Ca.Si. 12; Chapter 3). A closely similar list of thirty-two closes the Arthaśāstra, and the Tamil grammatical tradition has its own counterpart (see Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā). The devices were thus a shared method of the learned sciences, not a peculiarity of medicine.

Many of them name the ordinary moves of a technical text: the topic under discussion (adhikaraṇa), the meaning of a word (padārtha), a brief statement (uddeśa) and its detailed exposition (nirdeśa), the giving of a reason (apadeśa), an exception (apavarga), the author’s own technical terms (svasaṃjñā), an objection (pūrvapakṣa), and statements that are categorical (ekānta) or admit of exceptions (anekānta). Others are licences for the reader. Yoga allows words separated in a verse to be construed together; vākyaśeṣa allows an elliptical sentence to be completed; atideśa extends a rule stated for one case to others not yet mentioned; anāgatāvekṣaṇa and atikrāntāvekṣaṇa refer the reader forward and back; and ūhya marks what the intelligent reader is expected to work out for himself. Dṛḍhabala’s chapter compares the devices to the sun that opens a bed of lotuses and to a lamp that lights up a house: with them, a reader can find in a compact text what is not stated on its surface.

The devices explain much about how the compendia were used. A verse text that had to be memorised could not say everything, and the tantrayukti gave teachers and commentators an accepted way of supplying what was missing, of reconciling passages that seemed to conflict, and of extending a rule to new diseases and new drugs. They also gave commentators considerable freedom. An apparent gap or contradiction could always be read as intended—as an ellipsis to be completed, or a rule to be extended—and so the authority of the text was preserved while its meaning was adapted. The history of the medical texts is thus a history of reading as well as of copying: of a tradition that kept its words while it changed their application.

docs.title: 5.6.3 Lost Works and Single Witnesses
docs.text:
Much of the early medical literature has not survived. Of the six pupils of Ātreya who, according to Caraka’s account, each composed a treatise (Chapter 1), only Agniveśa’s survives in full, through Caraka’s redaction. The Bheḍa Saṃhitā hangs on a single incomplete manuscript, preserved in the Sarasvati Mahal Library at Thanjavur. The works of Jatūkarṇa, Parāśara and Kṣārapāṇi are known only from quotations in the commentaries and from the Bower Manuscript, which cites them as authorities (Section 1.7.1). The Hārīta Saṃhitā now extant is a much later work that borrows an old name. The same is true of many commentaries: Jejjaṭa’s and Gayadāsa’s survive only in part, and others are known only by name.

Quotations are therefore an important source. The commentators and later compilers cited earlier authorities by name, and these citations preserve passages of lost works and older readings of extant ones. They must be used with care, since a commentator could quote from memory, from an intermediate source, or from a version of a work that differed from any now known. The chance survivals—a birch-bark bundle in Kucha, a palm-leaf manuscript in Kathmandu, a single copy at Thanjavur—are a reminder of how much depended on luck, and of how partial the surviving record is.

docs.title: 5.6.4 The Nepalese Manuscripts
docs.text:
The dry valleys of Nepal and its royal and monastic libraries preserved many of the oldest manuscripts of north Indian works, and medicine is no exception. Among them is a palm-leaf copy of the Suśruta Saṃhitā in the Kaiser Library at Kathmandu (MS KL 699, filmed by the Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation Project), dated to 878 CE, centuries older than any other substantial witness. Its text differs in many places from the version on which Ḍalhaṇa commented. It lacks some passages of the familiar text, arranges others differently, and in places has readings that look older. A research project at the University of Alberta led by Dominik Wujastyk has been editing and translating this Nepalese version. Its results so far suggest that the Suśruta known since Ḍalhaṇa is a revised text, and that the history of the work in the first millennium can be traced more closely than was once thought possible. The Kāśyapa Saṃhitā, known only from quotations until its single Nepalese manuscript was published in 1938 (Chapter 8), owes its survival to the same libraries. The main stages in the history of the Suśruta’s text are set out schematically in Figure 5.1.

Figure 5.1. The transmission of the Suśruta Saṃhitā (schematic). The relations are simplified: the Nepalese version and the text known to Ḍalhaṇa descend from a common ancestor by routes that are not yet fully understood, and many intermediate copies are lost. The dashed box marks a lost text.

docs.title: 5.6.5 Central Asia and the Islamic World
docs.text:
Medical texts also travelled with Buddhist monks, merchants and physicians, and some survive earliest, or only, outside India. The Bower Manuscript (Section 1.7.1) is the oldest of them. Others are later, and they show which Indian works were valued abroad. The Siddhasāra of Ravigupta, a concise Buddhist handbook of about the seventh century, was translated into Tibetan and into Khotanese, the Iranian language of the Buddhist kingdom of Khotan, and fragments of it are known in Uyghur. R. E. Emmerick edited its Sanskrit text and Tibetan version (Emmerick 1980–1982). A bilingual collection of formulae in Sanskrit and Khotanese, the Jīvakapustaka, was found among the manuscripts of the cave library at Dunhuang, and fragments of the Yogaśataka have been identified among the Tocharian manuscripts of the Kucha region. The Siddhasāra was little read in India in later centuries, yet it became one of the main channels by which Indian medicine reached Tibet and the Silk Road. Its fortune abroad is a reminder that the history of a text is not only the history of its homeland.

In the Islamic world, the catalogue of books compiled by the Baghdad bookseller Ibn al-Nadīm (the Fihrist, 987) records Arabic translations of Indian medical works made under the patronage of the Barmakid viziers, among them books under the names of Suśruta and Caraka, and names Indian physicians who worked in Baghdad, among them one called Manka. None of these translations survives complete. Extracts are preserved in later Arabic works, above all in the summary of Indian medicine in al-Ṭabarī’s Firdaws al-ḥikma (Chapter 11).

The translations matter for the Sanskrit texts as well. A careful, literal translation made from a manuscript older than any now extant in Sanskrit can preserve readings that the Sanskrit tradition later lost. Modern editors use the Tibetan Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya in this way (Chapter 11), and the Tibetan and Khotanese versions of the Siddhasāra are essential witnesses to its text.

docs.title: 5.6.6 From Manuscript to Print
docs.text:
Printing changed the medical texts more in a century than copying had in a millennium. From the 1830s the presses of Calcutta printed Sanskrit medical works; the first printed Suśruta Saṃhitā, edited by Madhusudan Gupta, appeared there in 1835–36. In the second half of the century editions with Bengali, Hindi and Marathi translations made the classics available to practitioners who could not read the Sanskrit commentaries.

The most influential editions were those of Jādavjī Trikamjī Ācārya, published by the Nirṇaya Sāgar Press in Bombay: the Caraka Saṃhitā with Cakrapāṇidatta’s commentary, and the Suśruta Saṃhitā with Ḍalhaṇa’s commentary and the surviving part of Gayadāsa’s (Trikamji Acharya 1941; Trikamji Acharya and Acharya 1938). The verse numbers used in this volume follow them (see the Preface), and they have served for nearly a century as the standard texts of teaching and scholarship. They are not, however, critical editions in the modern sense. They rest on a small number of manuscripts, do not record variants systematically, and follow the text of the commentators. No critical edition of the Caraka Saṃhitā or of the complete Suśruta Saṃhitā yet exists.

Translation into the modern Indian languages and into English went hand in hand with print. Bengali, Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati versions of the compendia appeared from the late nineteenth century, often with the translator’s own explanations, and English versions followed. Kunja Lal Bhishagratna’s translation of the Suśruta appeared in 1907–16 (Bhishagratna 1907–1916). After independence the Shree Gulabkunverba Ayurvedic Society at Jamnagar published the Caraka Saṃhitā with translations into Hindi, Gujarati and English (1949), and complete English translations of the Caraka and of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya have since been made by Priyavrat Sharma and K. R. Srikantha Murthy (Sharma 1981–1994; Srikantha Murthy 2012). Translation raised problems of its own, since the technical vocabulary had to be rendered by modern words that carry modern meanings (Chapter 1). For most students today the classics are read through such translations and through modern textbooks rather than through the Sanskrit commentaries, and the translator’s choices have become part of the tradition.

Print also changed how the texts were used. A printed edition gives one text where the manuscripts gave many, and its page and verse numbers become the references that teachers, examiners and later authors cite. Print made the classics cheap and widely available and supported the colleges and examinations of the revival (Chapter 12). At the same time it fixed, for practical purposes, one state of texts that had always been changing. The editing of the medical classics from their manuscripts, on which their history depends, is still in progress.

docs.title: 5.7 The Spread of Indian Medicine Beyond India
docs.text:
Indian medical learning travelled with Buddhism, with trade and with the movements of physicians (Figure 5.2). The routes to Central Asia and to the Islamic world have been followed above through their manuscripts and translations. To China, Indian medical ideas came in Buddhist translations, which present the Buddha as a “king of physicians” and include the stories of Jīvaka and accounts of the four elements and their disorders; Indian specialists in eye surgery were known in Tang China, and Pierce Salguero has traced how these ideas were translated and adapted (Salguero 2014). In Tibet, Indian works, above all the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, were translated and shaped the development of Tibetan medicine (Chapter 11). Indian medicine also travelled with Buddhism and Brahmanical culture to Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand, Cambodia and Indonesia; in Sri Lanka Āyurveda has coexisted for centuries with an indigenous medical tradition (deśīya cikitsā). And within India, Persian works from the fourteenth century onwards drew on Sanskrit medicine: the Maʿdan al-Shifāʾ-i Sikandar-Shāhī of Miyān Bhuwa (1512), for example, presents Āyurvedic knowledge to Persian-reading physicians (Section 11.3).

Figure 5.2. Routes by which Indian medical learning travelled, and by which Greco-Arabic medicine reached India (schematic).

In South-east Asia Indian medicine merged with local and Buddhist traditions rather than being transplanted whole. The hospitals founded by the Cambodian king Jayavarman VII (Chapter 1) were described in Sanskrit inscriptions that use the vocabulary of Indian medicine. In Thailand, traditional medicine describes the body in terms of the four elements of Buddhist doctrine rather than the three doṣas, honours Jīvaka as its founder, and uses much Pali and Sanskrit vocabulary. In the 1830s, under King Rama III, medical texts and figures showing the lines and points used in massage were inscribed on stone at the monastery of Wat Pho in Bangkok, so that the knowledge would be available to all. In Bali, palm-leaf texts called usada combine Indian ideas of the humours and of drugs with local ritual healing. In each case Indian learning supplied vocabulary, texts and prestige, while practice took a local form.

Similarities between Indian and Greek humoral medicine—three or four humours, the importance of balance, the treatment of excess by opposites—have long interested historians. Jean Filliozat argued for early contacts (Filliozat 1964). Contacts between the Greek and Indian worlds certainly existed after Alexander, but no direct borrowing in either direction has been demonstrated, and the two systems may have developed largely independently.

Summary

Vāgbhaṭa’s synthesis, above all the verse Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, became the most widely used medical text in India and abroad, and the later literature—Mādhava’s diagnosis, Cakrapāṇidatta’s commentary and formulary, Śārṅgadhara’s pharmacy, Bhāvamiśra’s compendium and the works in the regional languages—kept the tradition open to new diseases and new drugs. The texts reached the modern world through copying, commentary, translation and print, and the oldest witnesses, from Kathmandu to Kucha, show how much they changed on the way; the standard printed editions are not yet critical editions.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Srikantha Murthy translates the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (Srikantha Murthy 2012). Meulenbeld is indispensable for the later literature (Meulenbeld 1999–2002); Salguero studies the transmission of Indian medicine to China (Salguero 2014). Emmerick’s edition of the Siddhasāra shows how a Sanskrit handbook was carried into Tibetan and Khotanese (Emmerick 1980–1982).

docs.title: Chapter 6: Dravyaguṇa: Materia Medica and Pharmacy
docs.text:
anenopadeśena nānauṣadhibhūtaṃ jagati kiṃcid dravyam upalabhyate tāṃ tāṃ yuktim arthaṃ ca taṃ tam abhipretya By this teaching, no substance is found in the world that is not a medicine, when it is used with the proper reasoning and for a definite purpose.

— Caraka Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 26.12

docs.title: 6.1 Substances and Their Properties
docs.text:
The study of “substances and their qualities” (dravyaguṇa) is the classical Indian science of materia medica. It describes the plants, animal products and minerals used as food and medicine, classifies them, and explains their action on the body in terms of the theory set out in Chapter 2. Caraka states its premise boldly in the passage quoted at the head of this chapter: there is no substance in the world that cannot be used as a medicine. Everything is made of the five elements; everything therefore has qualities that can increase or decrease the qualities of the body.

The number of substances described is very large. The great compendia name several hundred plants; the later lexicons (Chapter 5) list well over a thousand, with many synonyms. A large share of the Indian flora has some use in one or another of the medical traditions, learned or folk.

docs.title: 6.2 The Five Pharmacological Properties
docs.text: The action of a substance is analysed under five headings (Figure 6.1).

docs.title: 6.2.1 Taste (Rasa)
docs.text:
Taste is the first property, perceived directly by the tongue. There are six tastes—sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter and astringent—each predominantly composed of two elements (Table 3.3, Chapter 3). Taste is the physician’s chief clue to a substance’s nature and action. Sweet substances are nourishing and increase kapha; sour substances stimulate appetite and increase pitta; salty substances soften and moisten; pungent substances stimulate digestion and dry up kapha; bitter substances are cooling and reduce pitta and kapha; and astringent substances are binding and drying.

Figure 6.1. The five headings under which the action of a substance is analysed.

Caraka also describes the effects of each taste in excess (Ca.Sū. 26). Too much sweet food causes obesity, lethargy, heaviness, loss of appetite, swellings, urinary disorders and worms; too much sour, thirst, looseness of the body and inflammation; too much salt, baldness, greying, wrinkles, thirst and skin disease; too much pungent, weakness, fainting, thirst and burning; too much bitter, dryness, emaciation and disorders of vāta; too much astringent, constipation, distension, heart pain and stiffness. The lesson is that no single taste is wholesome by itself, and that a balanced diet contains all six (Table 6.1).

Table 6.1. The six tastes: properties and effects (after Ca.Sū. 26) Taste Properties in proper use Effects of excess sweet nourishing, strengthening; pleasing to the senses; good for the young, the old, the wounded and the emaciated obesity, heaviness, lethargy, swelling, urinary disorders sour stimulates appetite and digestion; moistens thirst, looseness, inflammation, burning salt softening, digestive; removes obstruction greying, baldness, wrinkles, thirst, skin disease pungent kindles digestion; dries kapha; clears the channels weakness, thirst, burning, tremor bitter cleansing; reduces pitta and kapha; relieves itching and fever dryness, emaciation, vāta disorders astringent binding, healing; stops discharge and bleeding constipation, distension, stiffness

docs.title: 6.2.2 Qualities (Guṇa)
docs.text: The twenty physical qualities in ten pairs (Table 2.2) describe how a substance acts: heavy or light, cold or hot, unctuous or dry, and so on. The qualities follow the rule of similarity and dissimilarity: heavy substances increase heaviness in the body, light substances decrease it.

docs.title: 6.2.3 Potency (Vīrya)
docs.text: Potency is the property through which a substance acts. Caraka reports a view that there are eight potencies (soft, sharp, heavy, light, unctuous, dry, hot and cold), but the view that prevailed is that there are two: hot (uṣṇa) and cold (śīta). Hot substances increase pitta and reduce vāta and kapha; cold substances do the reverse.

docs.title: 6.2.4 Post-digestive Taste (Vipāka)
docs.text: At the end of digestion, a substance’s taste is transformed. Sweet and salty substances usually become sweet, sour substances remain sour, and pungent, bitter and astringent substances become pungent. The post-digestive taste determines the substance’s effect on the doṣas, the bowels and the reproductive fluid.

docs.title: 6.2.5 How the Properties Relate
docs.text: The five properties do not always agree, and the texts give rules for resolving conflicts. In general, a later property overrides an earlier one when they conflict: post-digestive taste overrides taste, potency overrides post-digestive taste, and specific action overrides all the others. There are many exceptions, which the texts list. Thus most sweet substances are cooling, but the meat of some animals is said to be heating; most sour substances are heating, but the emblic myrobalan is cooling. The commentators discussed these rules at length, and the debates—for instance on whether potency is really two-fold or eight-fold—show a lively tradition of argument within the theory.

docs.title: 6.2.6 Specific Action (Prabhāva)
docs.text: Some effects cannot be explained by the four preceding properties. Caraka’s example is the pair citraka (Plumbago zeylanica) and dantī (Baliospermum montanum): both are pungent in taste and in post-digestive taste and hot in potency, yet dantī is purgative and citraka is not. The difference is due to specific action (Ca.Sū. 26.67–68). Prabhāva served as a catch-all for effects observed in practice that the theory could not account for.

docs.title: 6.3 Classifications of Drugs
docs.text:
Substances are classified by origin into those from animals (jaṅgama), plants (audbhida) and the earth (pārthiva). Plants are further divided by habit (trees, shrubs, creepers, herbs) and by the part used (root, bark, heartwood, resin, latex, leaf, flower, fruit, seed).

More important for practice are classifications by action. Caraka’s fifty “great groups” (mahākaṣāya, Ca.Sū. 4; Table 6.2) each list ten drugs with a common effect; Suśruta arranges drugs in thirty-seven groups (gaṇa), each named after its first member and used together in compound formulae (Su.Sū. 38).

Table 6.2. Some of Caraka’s fifty great groups (Ca.Sū. 4), with examples Group Action Examples of members jīvanīya life-promoting jīvantī, medā, kākolī, liquorice lekhanīya reducing (“scraping”) mustā, turmeric, vacā dīpanīya kindling the digestive fire long pepper, citraka, ginger balya strengthening balā, atibalā, aśvagandhā varṇya improving complexion sandalwood, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā kaṇḍūghna relieving itching sandalwood, neem, mustard kṛmighna destroying worms viḍaṅga, black pepper viṣaghna countering poison turmeric, śirīṣa, sindhuvāra stanyajanana promoting breast milk rice and certain grasses

docs.title: 6.3.1 Plants in the Vedas
docs.text: Many plants of the later pharmacopoeia already appear in the Vedic hymns, though their uses there are magical and ritual as much as medical. The Atharvaveda invokes kuṣṭha (Saussurea costus, an aromatic root from the Himalaya) against fever, apāmārga (Achyranthes aspera) against sorcery and disease, arundhatī (a creeper) for healing wounds and fractures, and pippalī as a remedy against “wind-disease”. The plant called soma, pressed in the Vedic sacrifice and praised as a drink of immortality, has never been securely identified, and its identity remains one of the most debated questions in Vedic studies.

docs.title: 6.3.2 Substitution
docs.text: The texts themselves allowed substitution when a drug was unavailable, and later authors drew up lists of approved substitutes (pratinidhi). Bhāvamiśra, for example, lists substitutes for the rare plants of the aṣṭavarga. Substitution was a practical necessity for physicians working far from the Himalaya or the forests where many drugs grew, and it is one reason why the same classical name may refer to different plants in different regions today.

docs.title: 6.3.3 The Problem of Identification
docs.text: Many classical drug names cannot be identified with certainty. The lexicons give numerous synonyms, the same name may designate different plants in different regions, and some drugs of the classical texts had become unavailable by the medieval period. The group of eight “life-promoting” plants known as the aṣṭavarga (jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, mahāmedā, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, ṛddhi and vṛddhi) is a well-known example: already in Bhāvamiśra’s time they were said to be rare (see above). The plant called brāhmī is identified as Bacopa monnieri in some regions and as Centella asiatica in others; śaṅkhapuṣpī is applied to several different species. For the historian, these problems mean that modern studies of a “classical” drug may not be studying the plant the classical author meant.

docs.title: 6.4 Some Important Plants
docs.text:
The following notes describe a few of the most widely used plants (two are illustrated in Figures 6.2 and 6.3), giving their properties according to the classical system and a brief indication of what modern research has and has not shown. They are not recommendations. Several of these plants have known adverse effects, and commercial products may be adulterated or contaminated.

Herbal Knowledge: Aśvagandhā (Withania somnifera)

Classical properties: bitter and astringent; hot potency; reduces vāta and kapha. Classed as strengthening, rejuvenating and promoting virility. Modern notes: Small clinical trials have reported effects on stress and sleep, but most are short, of limited quality and often industry-funded. Cases of liver injury associated with aśvagandhā products have been reported from several countries (Björnsson et al. 2020).

Figure 6.2. Fruits of aśvagandhā (Withania somnifera), each enclosed in a papery calyx. The root is the part chiefly used. Photo: Roger Culos, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Herbal Knowledge: Haridrā, turmeric (Curcuma longa)

Classical properties: bitter and pungent; hot potency. Used in skin diseases, wounds and urinary disorders, and classed as countering poison. Modern notes: Curcumin, its best-known constituent, has been the subject of thousands of laboratory studies, but it is poorly absorbed and clinical trials have produced inconsistent results; no curcumin product is an established treatment for any disease. Turmeric is a food and is generally safe in culinary amounts; concentrated supplements have been associated with liver injury, and turmeric powder in some markets has been found adulterated with lead compounds.

Herbal Knowledge: Tulasī, holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum, syn. O. sanctum)

Classical properties: pungent and bitter; hot potency; reduces vāta and kapha. Used in cough, dyspnoea and fever, and sacred to Viṣṇu. Modern notes: Laboratory and small clinical studies exist; the evidence is not sufficient to establish therapeutic effects.

Figure 6.3. Holy basil (tulasī) in flower. Photo: Joydeep, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Herbal Knowledge: Āmalakī, emblic myrobalan (Phyllanthus emblica)

Classical properties: has five tastes, lacking only salt, with sour predominant; cold potency; sweet post-digestive taste; reduces all three doṣas. One of the three “myrobalans” of triphalā and the chief ingredient of the confection of Cyavana. Modern notes: The fruit is a rich source of vitamin C and is widely eaten. Claims for rejuvenating effects are not established.

Herbal Knowledge: Guḍūcī (Tinospora cordifolia)

Classical properties: bitter and astringent; hot potency; reduces all three doṣas; called amṛtā, “immortal”. Used especially in fevers and as a rejuvenating drug. Modern notes: During and after the COVID-19 pandemic, when it was widely promoted as an “immunity booster”, Indian hepatologists published case series of liver injury in people taking guḍūcī products (Nagral et al. 2021). Claims of immune effects in humans have not been substantiated.

Herbal Knowledge: Guggulu (resin of Commiphora wightii)

Classical properties: bitter and pungent; hot potency; “scraping” (lekhana); used in obesity, joint diseases and swellings. Modern notes: A randomised controlled trial in the United States, published in 2003, found that guggulipid did not lower “bad” (LDL) cholesterol—it raised it slightly—and caused skin rashes in some participants (Szapary et al. 2003). The plant is endangered in the wild through over-tapping.

Herbal Knowledge: Brahmī (Bacopa monnieri; the name is also applied to Centella asiatica)

Classical properties: bitter; cold potency; classed as beneficial to the intellect (medhya). Modern notes: Some small trials of Bacopa extracts in healthy adults have reported modest effects on memory tests; the evidence is limited, and the products tested differ widely.

Herbal Knowledge: Śatāvarī (Asparagus racemosus)

Classical properties: sweet and bitter; cold potency; reduces vāta and pitta. Classed as nourishing, rejuvenating, promoting virility and breast milk; one of the most important drugs in the texts’ treatment of women. Modern notes: Widely sold as a “women’s tonic” and galactagogue. Clinical evidence for these uses is weak, and safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established.

Herbal Knowledge: Arjuna (Terminalia arjuna)

Classical properties: astringent; cold potency. In the compendia the bark is used chiefly for wounds, fractures and bleeding; its use as a “heart tonic” is emphasised in later works, notably in Cakrapāṇidatta’s formulary. Modern notes: Some small trials have studied it in heart disease. It is not a substitute for proven treatments, and it may interact with cardiac drugs.

Herbal Knowledge: Pippalī, long pepper (Piper longum)

Classical properties: pungent; potency described as neither hot nor cold (anuṣṇaśīta), and post-digestive taste sweet; reduces vāta and kapha. One of the three pungents (trikaṭu) and a classical rejuvenating drug, taken in an increasing and then decreasing course. Modern notes: Contains piperine (see below). Large quantities irritate the stomach.

Herbal Knowledge: Nimba, neem (Azadirachta indica)

Classical properties: bitter; cold potency; reduces pitta and kapha. Used for skin diseases, wounds, fevers and worms, and as a tooth-cleaning twig. Modern notes: Neem extracts have insecticidal properties and are used in agriculture. Neem oil taken by mouth has caused severe and sometimes fatal poisoning in infants and young children.

Herbal Knowledge: Yaṣṭīmadhu, liquorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra)

Classical properties: sweet; cold potency; reduces vāta and pitta. One of the four “intellect-promoting” drugs in Caraka’s list, used for cough, hoarseness, wounds and ulcers, and as a vehicle in many formulae. Modern notes: Liquorice root contains glycyrrhizin, which in substantial amounts causes salt and water retention, raised blood pressure and loss of potassium; regular use is unsafe for people with heart disease, hypertension or kidney disease and in pregnancy.

Herbal Knowledge: Vacā, sweet flag (Acorus calamus)

Classical properties: pungent and bitter; hot potency; an emetic and a drug for the voice, the intellect and disorders of the mind. Modern notes: Some varieties of the plant contain \(\beta\)-asarone, which has caused cancer in laboratory animals; regulators in several countries restrict or prohibit its use in food and medicines.

Herbal Knowledge: Triphalā, the three myrobalans

Classical properties: a combination of the fruits of harītakī, bibhītakī and āmalakī, regarded as balancing all three doṣas; used as a mild laxative, an eye wash and a rejuvenating drug. Modern notes: It has a laxative effect; claims of wider benefits are largely based on laboratory studies.

docs.title: 6.4.1 A Short List of Classical Drug Plants
docs.text:
Table 6.3 lists some of the plants most often named in the classical texts, with their usual modern identification and the part chiefly used. It is given for reference in reading the texts, not as a guide to treatment. Several identifications are disputed, and several of the plants are toxic.

Table 6.3. Some plants of the classical materia medica Sanskrit name Usual identification Part used; notes harītakī Terminalia chebula fruit; one of the three myrobalans bibhītakī Terminalia bellirica fruit; one of the three myrobalans āmalakī Phyllanthus emblica fruit; one of the three myrobalans pippalī Piper longum (long pepper) fruit and root marica Piper nigrum (black pepper) fruit śuṇṭhī Zingiber officinale (ginger) dried rhizome haridrā Curcuma longa (turmeric) rhizome nimba Azadirachta indica (neem) bark, leaf; neem oil is poisonous to small children guḍūcī Tinospora cordifolia stem; liver injury reported aśvagandhā Withania somnifera root; liver injury reported śatāvarī Asparagus racemosus root yaṣṭīmadhu Glycyrrhiza glabra (liquorice) root; raises blood pressure and lowers potassium in excess arjuna Terminalia arjuna bark kuṭaja Holarrhena pubescens bark and seed vāsā Justicia adhatoda leaf punarnavā Boerhavia diffusa root or whole plant bilva Aegle marmelos (bael) fruit and root mustā Cyperus rotundus tuber vacā Acorus calamus (sweet flag) rhizome; some varieties contain the toxic compound \(\beta\)-asarone citraka Plumbago zeylanica root; strongly irritant eraṇḍa Ricinus communis (castor) seed oil and root; the seeds contain the poison ricin mañjiṣṭhā Rubia cordifolia root candana Santalum album (sandalwood) heartwood uśīra Chrysopogon zizanioides (vetiver) root khadira Senegalia catechu heartwood extract kaṭukī Picrorhiza kurroa rhizome; threatened in the wild sarpagandhā Rauvolfia serpentina root; source of reserpine (Chapter 12) guggulu Commiphora wightii gum resin; endangered

docs.title: 6.4.2 Poisonous Plants in the Pharmacopoeia
docs.text:
The classical pharmacopoeia includes a number of highly poisonous plants, grouped as “poisons” (viṣa) and “minor poisons” (upaviṣa). They include vatsanābha (aconite, Aconitum species), dhattūra (Datura), kupīlu (nux vomica, Strychnos nux-vomica), bhallātaka (the marking nut, Semecarpus anacardium), guñjā (Abrus precatorius), karavīra (oleander, Nerium), lāṅgalī (Gloriosa superba) and the latex of arka (Calotropis) and snuhī (Euphorbia). The texts prescribe “purification” (śodhana) of these substances before use.

Health and Safety Note

The plant poisons named here can cause severe poisoning and death, and classical “purification” does not reliably remove their toxicity. This book gives no dose, preparation or method of purification for any of them; see Section 12.7.

docs.title: 6.5 Food and Drink
docs.text:
For the compendia there is no sharp line between food and medicine: both are substances whose qualities act on the body, and diet is the first instrument of therapy. Caraka’s chapter on food and drink (Ca.Sū. 27) and Vāgbhaṭa’s parallel chapters (AH Sū. 5–6) describe the properties of hundreds of foods, and the treatment of almost every disease begins with what the patient is to eat and to avoid.

Grains and pulses. Rice is the most praised grain, and the texts distinguish many varieties, the red śāli rice being among the best; barley and wheat are also discussed. Green gram (mudga) is the best of pulses; black gram (māṣa) is heavy and nourishing.

Meat. Classical Āyurveda is not vegetarian. Caraka’s list of meats is long and detailed. It sorts animals by their habitat and habits into eight groups—among them the animals that seize their prey, the burrowers, the birds that peck and those that scratch, the deer and birds of the dry country, and the animals of marshes and waters—and the qualities of each meat follow from its habitat. The meat of dry-land (jāṅgala) animals, light and wholesome, is prescribed for wasting diseases, for convalescence and for the weak, while that of marsh and water animals is heavy and increases kapha. Meat soup (māṃsarasa) is the most characteristic of these preparations: it is given to the emaciated and the convalescent, to patients returning to ordinary food after purification (Section 7.5), in “nourishing” enemas (Section 7.3.3) and in the treatment of consumption. Francis Zimmermann’s The Jungle and the Aroma of Meats takes its title from this dietetics. The healthiest landscape is the dry, open jāṅgala, its antelopes and birds give the most wholesome meat, and food is graded by the qualities of the land it comes from (Zimmermann 1987). The meat of the cow is described as fit for those with strong digestion and as useful in some vāta disorders. The Jain medical tradition and much later Hindu practice rejected meat, and modern Āyurvedic writing often presents the tradition as vegetarian, but that is not what the classical texts teach.

Milk and its products. Milk, curd, buttermilk, butter and ghee are described in detail, with the milk of cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, camels, elephants and human beings distinguished.

Ghee and honey. Ghee receives special praise. Caraka calls it the best of the fats, values its capacity to take on the properties of drugs cooked with it, and describes it as promoting memory, intelligence, digestive fire, semen and ojas, as counteracting vāta and pitta and poison, and as improved by age, so that ghee kept for years acquires special virtues. Honey is described as astringent and sweet, cooling, scraping and good for kapha, and is distinguished into several kinds according to the bees that produce it; it is not to be heated or taken hot. Both serve as vehicles for many drugs.

Water and drinks. The texts distinguish rain water, river water and water from wells, tanks and springs, and recommend boiled water in many conditions (on Suśruta’s methods of purifying water, see Chapter 4). Alcoholic drinks of many kinds are described; Caraka praises wine taken in moderation, with food and by suitable persons, but describes at length the disorders caused by drinking to excess (Ca.Ci. 24).

Rules of eating. One should eat warm, unctuous food, in proper quantity, after the previous meal has been digested, without incompatible combinations, in a pleasant place, neither too fast nor too slowly, without talking or laughing, and with attention (Ca.Vi. 1). The rules of incompatibility (Section 3.3) go further and forbid particular combinations, such as milk with fish, on grounds that the texts derive from the qualities of the foods rather than from any recorded experience of harm.

docs.title: 6.5.1 Diet in Practice and the Culinary Literature
docs.text:
The compendia treat diet as a matter of judgement, to be adjusted to the eater, the season and the place. The eight determinants of the effect of food in the Vimānasthāna (Table 3.4)—the nature of the food, its preparation, combination and quantity, the place, the time, the rules of eating and the eater himself—make the point that no food is good or bad in itself, and the doctrine of habituation (sātmya) allows one person to keep foods that would harm another. The regimen for each season (Table 2.10) is above all a diet, and the treatment of a disease usually begins with one: thin gruels in fever, buttermilk in disorders of digestion, meat soups in wasting.

The same knowledge appears outside the medical texts, in a Sanskrit literature on food that joins recipes to the physician’s theory of qualities. The encyclopaedia Mānasollāsa of the Cālukya king Someśvara III (1131) contains a long section on the pleasures of the table, with recipes for rice, pulses, meats and sweets. Later works devoted to food, such as the Bhojanakutūhala of Raghunātha (17th century), describe dishes together with their effects on the doṣas and draw on the medical lexicons. In these works the cook and the physician speak the same language, and a dish is described by its taste, its heaviness or lightness and its heating or cooling effect. K. T. Achaya’s history of Indian food draws on both literatures (Achaya 1994).

docs.title: 6.6 Animal and Mineral Substances
docs.text:
Animal products in the classical pharmacopoeia include milk and its products, honey, beeswax, fats and marrow, bile, musk, horn, shell, coral and pearl, and the urine of several animals. Caraka lists eight kinds of urine—of sheep, goats, cows, buffaloes, elephants, camels, horses and donkeys—for use mainly in purgation and in external applications (Ca.Sū. 1). Claims made today for the therapeutic value of cow’s urine have no reliable scientific support. The use of animal products also raises questions of supply, hygiene and, for some substances such as musk, the protection of endangered species.

Some animal products were prized and costly: musk from the musk deer, gorocanā (a concretion from the gall bladder of cattle, used as a pigment and medicine), civet, ambergris (known through Arab trade), lac, pearls and coral. The trade in some of these, such as musk and the products of endangered wild animals, is now illegal under Indian and international law, and their use in traditional medicine is a conservation problem.

Mineral substances in the older compendia include salts—among them rock salt (saindhava), sea salt and black salt—alkalis prepared from the ashes of plants, red ochre, collyrium minerals, mineral pitch (śilājatu) and some metals. In the medieval period the range of mineral and metallic substances expanded enormously with the growth of rasaśāstra (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 6.7 Compound Formulations
docs.text:
Classical treatment relies chiefly on compound formulae (yoga) of several or many ingredients. A few are household names in India. Table 6.4 gives their chief ingredients; it is not a guide to their use, and the products sold under these names today may differ from the classical recipes.
