Table 6.4. Some well-known classical formulae and their principal ingredients Formula Principal ingredients Triphalā the three myrobalans: harītakī, bibhītakī, āmalakī Trikaṭu the three pungents: dry ginger, long pepper, black pepper Daśamūla the roots of ten plants (five trees and five herbs) Cyavanaprāśa āmalakī with some forty other herbs, cooked in ghee and sesame oil with sugar and honey Brāhmī ghṛta ghee processed with brāhmī and other herbs Yogarāja guggulu, Kāñcanāra guggulu guggulu resin with various herbs Ārogyavardhinī vaṭī a “herbo-mineral” pill containing processed mercury and sulphur, iron, copper and mica, with kaṭukī and other herbs

The history of cyavanaprāśa illustrates how a classical formula became a modern product. Its name recalls the sage Cyavana, whose rejuvenation by the Aśvins is told already in the Vedic Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa: the aged sage, married to the young princess Sukanyā, is restored to youth after bathing in a pool to which the divine physicians lead him. Caraka’s recipe (Ca.Ci. 1.1) makes the confection from the emblic myrobalan with some forty other herbs, ghee, oil, honey and sugar. In the twentieth century it became the best-known Ayurvedic product in India, sold by many companies in versions that differ from one another and from the classical recipe. Most contain a large proportion of sugar. Claims for its effects on immunity and longevity are not supported by good evidence.

The last item in Table 6.4 illustrates an important point: many formulae in daily use contain metals and minerals, and the line between “herbal” Āyurveda and the metallic pharmacy of rasaśāstra (Chapter 9) is not sharp.

Health and Safety Note

Products containing processed mercury, lead, arsenic, copper or other metals are sold widely as Ayurvedic medicines, and heavy-metal contamination has been found even in products not made by rasaśāstra methods. The evidence is set out in Chapter 9, and practical advice in Section 12.7.

docs.title: 6.8 Pharmaceutical Forms (Kalpanā)
docs.text:
Caraka names five basic ways of preparing a drug (pañcavidha kaṣāyakalpanā, Ca.Sū. 4.7; see also Table 6.5): the expressed juice of the fresh plant (svarasa), a paste made by grinding it (kalka), a decoction (śṛta or kvātha), a cold infusion (śīta or hima) and a hot infusion (phāṇṭa). Each is “lighter” than the one before. Later works, especially Śārṅgadhara’s, describe many more: powders (cūrṇa), pills (vaṭī, guṭikā), confections (avaleha), medicated ghee (ghṛta) and oil (taila) made by long cooking of a fat with a paste and a liquid, and self-fermented preparations (āsava and ariṣṭa), which contain alcohol produced by fermentation. Preparations of metals and minerals—“ashes” (bhasma) and others—are the subject of rasaśāstra.

Table 6.5. Principal pharmaceutical forms of the classical and later texts Form Description svarasa juice expressed from the fresh plant kalka paste made by grinding fresh or dried drugs kvātha or śṛta decoction made by boiling and reducing hima or śīta cold infusion, the drug steeped overnight phāṇṭa hot infusion cūrṇa powder vaṭī, guṭikā pill or tablet avaleha, lehya confection or electuary, made with sugar or jaggery ghṛta, taila ghee or oil cooked with a drug paste and a liquid āsava, ariṣṭa fermented preparations, made respectively without and with prior boiling; they contain alcohol bhasma, piṣṭi calcined metals and minerals; finely ground gems and shells (Chapter 9)

Medicated oils and ghees were prepared by long, slow cooking in which water was gradually driven off, and the texts distinguish degrees of cooking—soft, medium and hard—by the consistency of the drug paste, each suited to a different use. The fermented preparations were made in sealed vessels left for a fixed period, and contain self-generated alcohol, sometimes in substantial amounts. Modern commercial āsavas and ariṣṭas are regulated as medicines, but their alcohol content can be significant, which matters for children, pregnant women, people who avoid alcohol for religious or medical reasons, and people with alcohol dependence.

The texts give careful attention to the vehicle (anupāna) with which a medicine is taken—water, milk, honey, ghee or a decoction—and to the time of taking it, arguing that the vehicle carries the drug and modifies its effect. A related concept is the yogavāhin, a substance such as honey or long pepper that takes on and enhances the properties of whatever it is combined with. Modern pharmacologists have shown that piperine, a constituent of black and long pepper, increases the absorption of some other compounds, including curcumin (Shoba et al. 1998). This is an interesting convergence, but it does not validate the classical rules of combination in general.

docs.title: 6.9 From Dispensary to Factory
docs.text:
For most of its history Āyurvedic medicine was made by the physician or under his eye. Caraka’s house of treatment (Chapter 3) has its store of drugs, implements and assistants. The physician gathered or bought the raw materials, prepared the decoctions, powders, ghees and oils, and gave them to the patient with instructions on the vehicle and the diet. Raw drugs came from collectors and from the druggists of the market—the gāndhika or dealer in fragrant substances of the Sanskrit texts, the pansārī and the ʿaṭṭār of later times—whose knowledge of names, grades and substitutes mattered as much as the physician’s. Caraka acknowledges that goatherds, shepherds, cowherds and forest-dwellers know plants by name and appearance, but holds that only one who knows how to use them deserves to be called a physician (Ca.Sū. 1). The medieval formularies, from Cakrapāṇidatta’s onwards (Chapter 5), were written for such physician-pharmacists. They give recipes for the physician’s own use, not specifications for products to be sold.

The change came in the late nineteenth century. Physicians in Calcutta began to prepare medicines in quantity and to sell them by post through printed catalogues, and pharmacies founded as businesses manufactured classical formulae in bulk: Dabur in Calcutta (1884), the Arya Vaidya Sala at Kottakkal (1902), Zandu in Bombay (1910) and Baidyanath (1917) were among the best known, with Hamdard (1906) on the Unani side (Chapter 11). Manufacture changed the medicines themselves. Decoctions that the texts require to be prepared fresh gave way to concentrates and tablets; preservatives and new packaging lengthened shelf life; and branded “proprietary” combinations, which no classical text describes, appeared beside the classical formulae. The patient increasingly bought a product rather than receiving a preparation, a shift that Madhulika Banerjee has studied in detail (Banerjee 2009).

The law then turned the texts into standards. Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, as extended to the Indian systems in the 1960s, an Ayurvedic drug is defined by reference to formulae described in a list of “authoritative books” attached to the Act: the great compendia, the medieval formularies and a number of later works. A recipe printed in a medieval formulary thus became a legal definition of a medicine. The Ayurvedic Formulary of India, published by the government from the late 1970s, selected formulae from these books and fixed their ingredients and methods of preparation, and the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (Section 6.10) set standards for the single drugs.

This arrangement has had consequences that the authors of the texts could not have foreseen. Differences between editions and manuscripts, once matters for commentators, became questions for regulators, who had to decide which version of a recipe was the “classical” one (Section 5.6). The label “classical” can lend the authority of antiquity to preparations containing mercury, lead or arsenic, which are listed in the authoritative books like any other formula. And because proprietary medicines were regulated more loosely, much of the market moved to products that have no classical basis at all. The history of Āyurvedic pharmacy is therefore also part of the history of its texts (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 6.10 Quality, Identity and Adulteration
docs.text: The quality of herbal medicines depends on correct identification, proper collection and processing, and freedom from contamination. The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, published by the government in a series of volumes since the late 1980s, gives monographs with botanical identity, microscopic characters and chemical tests for single drugs and some formulations. In the market, however, substitution and adulteration remain common: studies using microscopy, chemical profiling and DNA barcoding have found that many samples sold under a classical name are of a different species, sometimes deliberately substituted with a cheaper plant. Contamination with pesticides, microbes, fungal toxins and heavy metals from soil, water and processing has also been reported. These are problems of the modern supply chain rather than of the classical texts, but they affect anyone who uses the products.

docs.title: 6.11 Indian Drugs in World Trade
docs.text: Many Indian medicinal substances were also articles of long-distance trade. Black pepper, long pepper, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon-like barks, spikenard, costus, sandalwood and the myrobalans were exported to the Mediterranean world in Roman times, and appear in the Greek pharmacology of Dioscorides (first century CE), which also describes an Indian “lycium”—apparently the extract of Berberis called rasāñjana in Sanskrit. Arab and Persian merchants carried Indian drugs westward in the Middle Ages, and the myrobalans became standard remedies in Arabic and medieval European medicine. In the other direction, drugs and plants reached India from the Middle East, Central Asia, China and, after 1500, the Americas: opium, asafoetida, China root, and later tobacco, chilli, cinchona and others. The materia medica of Āyurveda is in part a record of these exchanges.

docs.title: 6.12 Collection and Storage
docs.text:
The compendia lay down rules for the collection and storage of drugs (Ca.Ka. 1; Su.Sū. 36). Drugs are to be gathered from good land—neither saline, nor stony, nor near cremation grounds or temples—in the proper season, from healthy plants of full maturity, and stored in clean, dry, protected places. The texts recognise that potency depends on habitat, season and age. Modern pharmacognosy agrees that the content of plant constituents varies with these factors, though it measures and explains the variation differently. The over-collection of medicinal plants from the wild is today a serious threat to several species, including guggulu and some Himalayan plants used in Āyurveda and Tibetan medicine.

Summary

Classical pharmacology explains the action of every substance, food or drug, by five properties—taste, quality, potency, post-digestive taste and specific action—and classifies drugs chiefly by what they do. Its names often cannot be matched securely with modern species, and modern evidence for most of its plants is limited, while several are toxic and some popular ones have been linked to liver injury. Since the late nineteenth century the physician’s own pharmacy has given way to the factory, and the law has turned the recipes of listed classical books into legal definitions of medicines.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Sharma’s Hindi Dravyaguṇa-Vijñāna is a standard modern textbook (Sharma 2006). On the evidence and safety of particular remedies see (Szapary et al. 2003; Saper et al. 2004, 2008); on drug development from Ayurvedic sources, Mukherjee and Wahile (Mukherjee and Wahile 2006). On the pharmaceutical industry and its effect on practice, see Banerjee (Banerjee 2009).

docs.title: Chapter 7: Pañcakarma: The Purification Therapies
docs.text:
doṣāḥ kadācit kupyanti jitā laṅghanapācanaiḥ jitāḥ saṃśodhanair ye tu na teṣāṃ punarudbhavaḥ Doṣas subdued by fasting and digestives may sometimes flare up again; but those subdued by purification do not arise again.

— Caraka Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 16.20

docs.title: 7.1 Purification and Pacification
docs.text:
Classical therapy has two main strategies. “Pacification” (śamana) restores balance within the body by diet, drugs and regimen. “Purification” (śodhana) expels the excess doṣas from the body by the nearest route: upwards through the mouth, downwards through the anus, or through the nose. The compendia regard purification as the more radical and lasting treatment, as the verse above claims, but also as the more dangerous, and they surround it with elaborate rules about who may receive it, how the patient is to be prepared, and how complications are to be recognised and corrected.

The “five actions” (pañcakarma) are counted differently by the two schools. For Caraka they are emesis (vamana), purgation (virecana), the decoction enema (nirūha or āsthāpana), the oil enema (anuvāsana) and nasal purgation (nasya or śirovirecana). The surgical school of Suśruta counts the two kinds of enema as one and adds bloodletting (raktamokṣaṇa). In modern practice the term “pañcakarma” is used loosely for a much wider range of procedures, including the oil therapies developed in Kerala.

docs.title: 7.2 The Stages of Treatment
docs.text:
A course of purification therapy has three stages, shown in Figure 7.1.

Figure 7.1. The three stages of a course of purification therapy.

docs.title: 7.2.1 Oleation (Snehana)
docs.text:
Before purification the patient is “oleated”. Internal oleation consists in drinking ghee, oil, marrow or animal fat, often medicated, over a period of days until the signs of adequate oleation appear: softness of the body, oily stools, aversion to fat. External oleation is massage with oil. Oleation is thought to loosen the doṣas from the tissues and to bring them towards the alimentary tract, from which they can be expelled. Caraka devotes a chapter (Ca.Sū. 13) to the four kinds of fat, the times, forms and indications of oleation, and the signs of its deficiency and excess.

The texts distinguish pure fat taken by itself (accha) from fat mixed into food, gruel or other preparations (vicāraṇā), which Caraka recommends for those who cannot tolerate pure fat. They describe the signs of adequate oleation—the expulsion of flatus, a kindled digestive fire, oily and unformed stools, softness and smoothness of the body and an aversion to fat—and the signs of excess, which include pallor, heaviness, numbness, indigestion, salivation and diarrhoea. Oleation is forbidden in a long list of conditions, among them indigestion, kapha disorders with excess fat, recent fever, pregnancy and certain forms of poisoning.

docs.title: 7.2.2 Sudation (Svedana)
docs.text:
After oleation the patient is made to sweat. Caraka describes thirteen kinds of sudation using fire and ten kinds without fire (Ca.Sū. 14), summarised in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1. Caraka’s kinds of sudation (Ca.Sū. 14) Kind Examples With fire (13) application of heated boluses (saṅkara); lying on a heated bed of grain (prastara); steam conducted through a tube (nāḍī); pouring of warm liquids (pariṣeka); immersion in a warm bath (avagāhana); a heated sweating-house (jentāka); lying on a heated stone slab (aśmaghna); a trench heated with embers beneath the bed (karṣū); a closed hut (kuṭī); heated ground (bhū); a pot of hot decoction beneath the bed (kumbhī); a heated pit (kūpa); and a bed heated by a smouldering fire below (holāka) Without fire (10) exercise, a warm room, heavy coverings, hunger, much drinking, fear, anger, poultices, fighting and the heat of the sun

Suśruta groups sudation into four kinds: by direct heat, by steam, by poultice and by warm liquids. The texts warn that sudation is dangerous for some patients, and that excessive sweating causes thirst, fainting and burning.

docs.title: 7.3 The Main Procedures
docs.text:
Table 7.2 summarises the classical scheme of the main procedures.

Table 7.2. The purification procedures: a summary of the classical scheme Procedure Route Chiefly for Examples of classical indications emesis (vamana) mouth (upwards) kapha cough, dyspnoea, nausea, some skin diseases and fevers purgation (virecana) anus (downwards) pitta jaundice, skin diseases, abdominal swellings, worms decoction enema (nirūha) rectum vāta disorders of vāta, distension, pain, retention oil enema (anuvāsana) rectum vāta dryness, wasting, chronic vāta disorders nasal treatment (nasya) nose head and senses headache, catarrh, diseases above the collar-bone bloodletting (raktamokṣaṇa) skin and vessels blood, pitta skin diseases, abscesses, swellings, gout-like joint disease

docs.title: 7.3.1 Emesis (Vamana)
docs.text: Emesis is the treatment for disorders of kapha, which is concentrated in the upper body. After preparation, the patient is given an emetic drug—the texts consider the fruit of madana (Catunaregam spinosa) the best—and the physician watches the vomiting, judging its adequacy by the number of bouts, the quantity and the appearance of pitta at the end. The Kalpasthāna of the Caraka Saṃhitā gives a chapter to each of six emetic drugs, most of them of uncertain identity (Section 3.9). Caraka’s list of conditions for which emesis is indicated includes cough, dyspnoea, some fevers, nausea, skin diseases, swellings and disorders of the throat; among those for whom it is forbidden are the weak, the very young and old, the obese, pregnant women, those with heart disease or bleeding disorders, and those exhausted by fasting, grief or sexual activity.

docs.title: 7.3.2 Purgation (Virecana)
docs.text: Purgation is the treatment for disorders of pitta. The purgative drugs of the texts include trivṛt (Operculina turpethum), āragvadha (Cassia fistula), castor oil and, for strong purgation, the latex of snuhī (Euphorbia). The physician judges the adequacy of purgation by the number of motions, their quantity and the appearance of kapha at the end. The Kalpasthāna devotes six chapters to purgative drugs (Section 3.9), and the texts rank purgatives by strength and warn that the strongest, such as the latex of snuhī, are to be used only in particular conditions and never on the weak. Purgation is described as the best treatment for pitta, and it was used, among other things, for jaundice, skin diseases, abdominal swellings, worms and fevers of pitta origin.

docs.title: 7.3.3 Enemas (Basti)
docs.text: The enema, administered originally with a bladder (basti) attached to a nozzle, is the treatment above all for disorders of vāta, whose chief seat is the colon. Caraka extols it: some physicians, he reports, call it half of all therapy, and some the whole of it (Ca.Si. 1.39–40). The texts distinguish the decoction enema (nirūha or āsthāpana), prepared from a decoction of drugs with other ingredients, from the oil enema (anuvāsana), which is retained for a longer time; courses of treatment alternate the two. The Siddhisthāna is largely devoted to enemas. It describes the apparatus—a nozzle of metal, bone or wood attached to the bladder of an animal—and the manner of administration, lists the faults of the nozzle, the bladder and the administration that cause injury or failure, and gives many formulae for enemas suited to particular disorders, including “nourishing” enemas of milk and meat soup. A small, daily oil enema (mātrābasti) was considered safe even for the weak and the aged. A separate procedure, the “upper enema” (uttarabasti), introduced medicated liquids into the bladder or the uterus.

docs.title: 7.3.4 Judging the Result
docs.text: For every procedure the texts distinguish three outcomes: proper action (samyagyoga), inadequate action (ayoga) and excessive action (atiyoga). After proper purgation, for example, the channels are clear, the senses refreshed, the body light, the digestive fire kindled and the disease relieved; after inadequate purgation the patient feels heavy, nauseated and uneasy, and the disease persists; after excessive purgation there is faintness, thirst, prolapse, bleeding, cramps and, at worst, death. The emphasis on judging the patient’s response, rather than following a fixed schedule, is characteristic of the compendia, and it reflects an awareness that these procedures could do real harm.

docs.title: 7.3.5 Nasal Purgation (Nasya)
docs.text: “The nose is the gateway to the head,” Vāgbhaṭa says (AH Sū. 20.1), and drugs introduced into it are thought to act on the head and the parts above the collar-bone. The texts distinguish purgative nasya with pungent drugs, which causes discharge, from nourishing and pacifying forms with oils, milk or ghee, and describe a light daily form (pratimarśa) as part of the regimen of the healthy. Caraka lists several ways of administering medicines through the nose—as drops of oil (navana), as the juice of a crushed paste (avapīḍa), as a powder blown into the nostril through a tube (dhmāpana), as smoke, and as the light daily application—and gives rules about the times of day and seasons when nasal treatment should and should not be given.

docs.title: 7.3.6 Bloodletting (Raktamokṣaṇa)
docs.text: The surgical school regards bloodletting as a primary therapy for disorders of the blood and of pitta. Suśruta describes the use of leeches (jalaukā; Chapter 4); of horns and gourds for suction; of scarification; and of venesection (sirāvyadha), which he calls “half the treatment” in surgery, as the enema is in medicine (Su.Śā. 8.23). The surgical texts lay down when and on whom bloodletting may be performed: not in very cold, very hot or cloudy weather, not on the weak, the very young or old, pregnant women or those with swelling of the whole body, and with careful attention to the quantity of blood removed and the signs of excess. They recognise that excessive bleeding causes weakness, fainting, convulsions and death. Bloodletting was also central to Greek, Arabic and early modern European medicine, where it has long since been abandoned except for a few specific conditions; medicinal leeches are still used in some reconstructive surgery.

docs.title: 7.4 Lesser Procedures
docs.text: Besides the five main purifications, the compendia describe many smaller procedures, some of them part of the daily regimen and some used as treatments. In medicated smoking (dhūmapāna), wicks made of drug pastes wrapped around a reed are dried, lit and smoked through a tube, inhaled through the mouth or the nose; the texts distinguish “unctuous”, “moderate” and “purgative” smoking and prescribe it after meals, bathing, sneezing and other activities to prevent disorders of vāta and kapha in the head. Liquids are held in the mouth without movement (gaṇḍūṣa) or swilled and spat out (kavala). Oil is applied to the head (mūrdhataila) in four forms of increasing strength—anointing, pouring, a soaked pad, and oil retained within a cap (AH Sū. 22)—and poured into the ears (karṇapūraṇa). The eyes receive collyria, eye-drops and the retention of ghee within a ring of dough (tarpaṇa).

docs.title: 7.5 After-care and Complications
docs.text:
Purification is thought to leave the digestive fire weak; Caraka compares it to a small fire that is built up gradually with grass and dung (Ca.Si. 1.12–13). The patient therefore returns to normal food gradually, through a sequence of thin rice gruel (peyā), thick gruel (vilepī), unseasoned and seasoned pulse soups (yūṣa) and unseasoned and seasoned meat soups (māṃsarasa), the number of meals at each stage depending on the strength of the purification (saṃsarjanakrama).

The compendia are frank about the dangers. Caraka’s Siddhisthāna (Ca.Si. 6–7) describes the complications of emesis, purgation and enemas: inadequate or excessive evacuation, exhaustion, thirst, fainting, bleeding, prolapse, pain, distension and others, with their correction. The texts also list the people for whom purification is unsuitable, among them the very young and the very old, the weak and emaciated, pregnant women, and patients with certain diseases.

Health and Safety Note

The purification procedures are invasive and carry real risks. This book describes them historically and gives no instructions for carrying them out; the risks are set out in Section 12.7.

docs.title: 7.6 Who Received Purification?
docs.text:
The elaborate procedures of the compendia—with their specially built houses, attendants, stores of drugs and weeks of preparation and recovery—were designed for kings and wealthy householders. Caraka’s description of the house of treatment (Chapter 3) makes this clear. Most people in pre-modern India could not have afforded such treatment, and the texts themselves recommend simpler measures for the poor. Purification in its full classical form was thus a therapy of the elite, and the large-scale provision of pañcakarma in hospitals and commercial centres is a modern development.

Today, pañcakarma is offered in the departments of government Āyurvedic hospitals and colleges, in private hospitals and clinics, and in resorts catering for tourists. Official bodies have issued guidelines for the procedures and for the facilities and staff required, but practice varies widely, and in the commercial sector there is little independent oversight.

docs.title: 7.7 Purification and the Seasons
docs.text: The compendia also recommend purification for the healthy at the appropriate seasons, to remove the doṣas before they cause disease: emesis in spring, when kapha is aggravated; purgation in autumn, for pitta; and enemas in the rains, for vāta. This is the basis of the modern practice of offering “seasonal pañcakarma” to healthy clients, a practice that has become an important part of health tourism in India.

docs.title: 7.8 The Kerala Therapies
docs.text:
Many of the procedures now advertised as pañcakarma come from the medical tradition of Kerala (Section 5.3), where they are known as keraḷīya cikitsā. They involve the prolonged application of warm oils, milk or medicated preparations to the body (Figures 7.2 and 7.3), and are distinct from the five classical purifications. In dhārā a continuous stream of oil, buttermilk or another liquid is poured over the body, or over the forehead in śirodhārā; in piḻiccil the body is bathed in streams of warm oil while it is massaged; in ñavarakkiḻi it is massaged with cloth boluses of rice cooked in milk and herbal decoction; in śirovasti oil is retained on the head inside a leather cap; and in local vastis warm oil is held over the lower back, a knee or another part within a ring of dough.

Much of this tradition was developed and transmitted in the families of Kerala physicians, and was organised and popularised in the twentieth century by institutions such as the Arya Vaidya Sala at Kottakkal, founded by P. S. Varier in 1902.

Figure 7.2. The vessel used for śirodhārā: a metal dhārā pot (dhārā-pātra) hung on chains above the forehead, from which a continuous stream of liquid is poured. Photo: Vijayanrajapuram, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 7.3. A wooden treatment table (droṇī) of the kind used in Kerala oil therapies; the raised rim and the outlet allow the oil to be collected. Photo: Vijayanrajapuram, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 7.9 Evacuation in Comparative Perspective
docs.text:
Treatment by evacuation was not peculiar to India. Greek, Roman and Arabic physicians, working with their own humoral theory, purged, induced vomiting, administered enemas and let blood to remove excess or corrupted humours, and these practices remained central to European medicine until the nineteenth century. Bloodletting was abandoned in Europe largely because early statistical studies, beginning with those of the French physician Pierre Louis in the 1830s, showed that it did not help patients with pneumonia and other fevers. The history is a reminder that a therapy may be practised by intelligent physicians for two thousand years, and be consistent with a coherent theory, and still be useless or harmful. The only way to find out is to test it.

Today, Āyurvedic purification is often marketed internationally as “detoxification”. The term is borrowed from modern medicine, where it refers to the treatment of poisoning and drug dependence. There is no good evidence that emesis, purgation, enemas or oil treatments remove unspecified “toxins” from healthy people, and the healthy body has its own effective means—the liver and kidneys—of eliminating waste.

docs.title: 7.10 Modern Evidence
docs.text:
Purification therapies and Kerala oil treatments have been studied in a number of clinical trials in India and elsewhere, for conditions such as psoriasis, arthritis, insomnia and anxiety. Most of these studies are small, many lack an adequate control group, the people assessing the results are often aware of the treatment, and few have been repeated independently. Some report benefit; for most conditions the evidence is not strong enough to support firm conclusions, and the risks are rarely reported systematically. Relaxing oil treatments such as śirodhārā may well be pleasant and calming, but that is a different claim from the claim that they cure disease. Good-quality research, with full reporting of adverse effects, is needed before these treatments can be recommended for any medical condition.

Summary

Purification expels the doṣas by the nearest route, after oleation and sudation have loosened them and before a graded return to ordinary food; the texts judge each procedure by its effect on the patient and describe its complications frankly. In its full classical form it was a therapy for the wealthy. Much of what is now offered as pañcakarma comes instead from the later oil therapies of Kerala, and modern evidence for either is limited.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The purification therapies are described in Caraka’s Sūtra-, Kalpa- and Siddhisthāna (see the translations of Sharma and Wujastyk (Sharma 1981–1994; Wujastyk 2003)). On the Kerala tradition and its modern development, see the essays in (Wujastyk and Smith 2008).

docs.title: Chapter 8: The Clinical Branches
docs.text:
śalyaṃ śālākyaṃ kāyacikitsā bhūtavidyā kaumārabhṛtyam agadatantraṃ rasāyanatantraṃ vājīkaraṇatantram iti Extraction, the use of probes, therapy of the body, the science of spirits, the care of children, the doctrine of antidotes, and the doctrines of rejuvenation and of virility.

— Suśruta Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 1.7

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction
docs.text: The eight branches of classical medicine (Table 1.3) were not separate professions in the modern sense: a single physician was expected to know them all, though the surgical school of Suśruta and the medical school of Caraka had different emphases, and some later physicians specialised in eye treatment, children’s diseases or snakebite. Surgery has been described in Chapter 4. This chapter surveys the other branches as the texts present them. It reports what the texts say; it does not recommend any treatment.

docs.title: 8.2 General Medicine (Kāyacikitsā)
docs.text:
Kāyacikitsā, “treatment of the body”, is the branch to which most of the Caraka compendium is devoted. The commentators explain kāya as the digestive fire, since disorders of digestion were thought to underlie most disease. The major diseases of the Nidāna- and Cikitsāsthānas (Chapter 3) belong here: fevers, bleeding disorders, abdominal swellings, urinary disorders, skin diseases, wasting, cough and dyspnoea, diarrhoea and disorders of digestion, anaemia and jaundice, swellings and abdominal enlargement, and the many disorders of vāta.

The texts describe each disease by its causes, premonitory signs, signs and course, distinguish varieties by the doṣas involved, and prescribe treatment that combines fasting or nourishment, purification or pacification, diet and compound drugs. Pallor (pāṇḍu) shows the approach. Caraka recognises five kinds: one for each doṣa, one due to all three, and one caused by eating earth (Ca.Ci. 16). Treatment includes purification, diet and preparations of iron, one of the classical prescriptions that seems to match a modern understanding, since iron deficiency is the commonest cause of anaemia; but the classical iron preparations were not standardised, and anaemia has many other causes. Āmavāta, first described as a separate disease by Mādhava (c. 700), is a painful, swollen condition of the joints attributed to āma carried by vāta to the joints, and its treatment begins with fasting and drugs to digest the āma. The “king’s disease” (rājayakṣman), a wasting disease with cough, fever and bloody sputum, is explained by the exhaustion of the bodily constituents and treated with nourishment, rejuvenating drugs and regimen; it includes, but is not identical with, tuberculosis.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Diarrhoea and Jaundice
docs.text: Diarrhoea (atisāra) is described in many forms, by the doṣas and by the presence of āma, blood or mucus, and its treatment begins with fasting followed by thin rice gruels, buttermilk and astringent drugs. The emphasis on fluids and gruels is of interest in the light of modern medicine, which since the 1960s and 1970s has shown that oral rehydration—with a solution of salts and sugar, or with rice-based fluids—can prevent most deaths from diarrhoeal disease; the classical texts, however, did not understand dehydration as such, and their astringent and purgative drugs could make it worse. Jaundice (kāmalā) is described as a complication of anaemia or of disorders of pitta, with yellowness of the eyes, skin, nails and urine, and is treated with purgation and bitter drugs.

docs.title: 8.2.2 Fevers
docs.text: Fever (jvara) is the first disease in every compendium, and Caraka’s account of it, with its periodic “irregular” fevers and its treatment by fasting before drugs, has been summarised in Chapter 3. Besides the doṣas and periodicity, he classifies fevers by whether they arise from within or from external causes such as injury, poison, curses or emotion, and by whether they affect the surface or the interior of the body. The tertian and quartan patterns point to malaria, which must have been one of the greatest causes of illness and death in ancient India. Modern antimalarial treatment, by contrast, depends on drugs—quinine from the cinchona tree of South America, and artemisinin, discovered in the 1970s by Chinese scientists working from a traditional Chinese remedy—that were unknown to the Indian classics.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Skin Diseases and Leprosy
docs.text: The classical category of kuṣṭha covers eighteen skin diseases, seven “major” and eleven “minor”. It includes leprosy, whose signs—anaesthetic patches, ulceration, loss of fingers and toes, collapse of the nose—are described, but also psoriasis, eczema and many other conditions. The texts treat kuṣṭha with purification, bloodletting, bitter drugs such as khadira and neem, and applications; they also attribute it in part to sin, and the Dharmaśāstra literature treated leprosy as a consequence of evil deeds in a past life. People with leprosy were long excluded from society in India as elsewhere. Leprosy is now curable with multidrug therapy, which India has provided free of charge since the 1980s, but stigma persists.

docs.title: 8.2.4 Contagion, Pox and Cholera
docs.text:
Caraka explains the sickness of whole communities by the corruption of air, water, land and season (Chapter 3). Suśruta records a different idea. At the end of his chapter on skin diseases (Su.Ni. 5) he observes that certain diseases pass from one person to another through close association (which the commentator Ḍalhaṇa takes to mean sexual intercourse), touch, breath, eating together, sharing a bed or a seat, and using another’s clothes, garlands and unguents. He names kuṣṭha, fever, wasting and inflammation of the eyes, together with the “communicable” diseases (aupasargika), as passing from one person to another. The passage names no agent of disease and no mechanism beyond contact, and the same chapter also traces kuṣṭha to sin. What it records is an observation of transmission between persons that the theory of the doṣas could not easily explain, and it fits the practices of avoidance that grew up around leprosy and other diseases.

Suśruta lists the pox diseases (masūrikā, “lentil-like” eruptions) among the minor diseases (Su.Ni. 13), and the later diagnostic literature, notably Mādhava’s handbook (c. 700), gives them a chapter of their own, with their fever and pain, their eruptions of different colours and their often fatal course. The category probably covered smallpox, chickenpox and other eruptive fevers. Popular religion treated smallpox as the presence of the goddess Śītalā (Chapter 11). Inoculation with smallpox matter, which European observers described in eighteenth-century Bengal, was performed by specialist inoculators rather than by physicians of the Sanskrit tradition (see Volume 24, Samanvaya).

Viṣūcikā is an acute disorder with vomiting, purging, cramps and pains “as if pierced by needles”, which Suśruta treats as a disease of indigestion and overeating, together with two related conditions, alasaka and vilambikā (Su.Utt. 56). Nineteenth-century writers identified it with cholera, and the identification is still common. Whether the epidemic cholera of modern medicine was present in India before the nineteenth century is debated. The classical descriptions fit many kinds of acute gastroenteritis, and they do not describe the explosive spread through a community that marked the cholera epidemics. Portuguese observers in Goa, Garcia da Orta among them, described in the sixteenth century a swiftly fatal disease with vomiting and purging, which they called mordexim after a local name; it may well have been cholera, though the identification cannot be proved. What is certain is that an epidemic that began in lower Bengal in 1817 spread across India and then far beyond it, the first of a series of cholera pandemics that reached Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas in the nineteenth century.

The epidemics of the colonial period posed problems that the classical texts did not address. Cholera, plague, which reached Bombay in 1896, and the influenza pandemic of 1918, which killed many millions in India, overwhelmed every medical system of the time. The colonial state answered plague with inspections, segregation camps, house searches and the Epidemic Diseases Act of 1897, measures that provoked widespread resistance. Vaidyas and ḥakīms published remedies and advice in pamphlets and newspapers, and some hospitals run by Indian communities during the plague offered treatment by indigenous practitioners to patients who feared the government’s hospitals. Historians have argued that these crises gave the indigenous practitioners a new public role and a political argument, that the state’s medicine did not reach most of the people (Arnold 2000). No indigenous remedy was shown to work against these diseases. The decisive advances came from sanitation, clean water, vaccination, antibiotics and, for cholera, oral rehydration.

docs.title: 8.3 Diseases of the Head and the Senses (Śālākya)
docs.text:
Śālākya, named after the probe (śalākā) used in many of its procedures, deals with the parts “above the collar-bone”: eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat and head. Its fullest treatment is in the first 26 chapters of Suśruta’s Uttaratantra (Table 8.1).

Table 8.1. Suśruta’s classification of diseases above the collar-bone Organ Number Notes eye 76 by the part affected: lids (21), junctions (9), white (11), black (4), the whole eye (17), the “seeing” part (12), with two more of external origin (Su.Utt. 1) ear 28 Su.Utt. 20 nose 31 Su.Utt. 22 mouth 65 in seven sites: lips, gums, teeth, tongue, palate, throat and the whole mouth (Su.Ni. 16) head 11 Su.Utt. 25

Suśruta’s ophthalmology is the most elaborate part of the branch. He describes the anatomy of the eye in terms of “circles” and “junctions” and of layers (paṭala); diseases of the lids such as styes, cysts and trichiasis, which he treats by excision, scraping and cautery; growths on the conjunctiva (arman, probably pterygium), which he excises; inflammations with discharge; and the disorders of the “seeing” part, among them timira (a progressive dimming of vision) and liṅganāśa (“loss of the sign”, blindness), one form of which corresponds to cataract. Diseases of the head (śiroroga) include a half-sided headache (ardhāvabhedaka) that has been compared with migraine.

Treatment combines systemic measures with local ones: collyria (añjana) and eye-washes, eye drops, retention of ghee in a ring of dough around the eye (tarpaṇa), fumigation, nasal medication, gargles and mouth-washes, as well as surgery—couching for cataract (Chapter 4), excision of growths of the conjunctiva, and operations on the lids. The daily application of collyrium to the eyes was part of the regimen of the healthy.

docs.title: 8.3.1 Ear, Nose and Throat
docs.text: Suśruta’s twenty-eight diseases of the ear include earache, discharge, deafness, ringing in the ears, foreign bodies, worms and swellings of the ear canal; the treatments include ear-drops of oil, fumigation, cleaning with probes and the extraction of foreign bodies with forceps or by suction. Among the thirty-one diseases of the nose are a chronic catarrh (pīnasa), bleeding, polyps (nāsārśas), which he removes surgically, and loss of the sense of smell. Diseases of the throat include swellings that obstruct swallowing and breathing; the texts recognise some of these as dangerous and recommend urgent surgical treatment.

docs.title: 8.3.2 The Mouth and Teeth
docs.text: Suśruta’s chapter on diseases of the mouth (Su.Ni. 16) describes disorders of the lips, gums, teeth, tongue, palate and throat, among them inflammation and abscess of the gums, loose teeth, caries attributed to “worms”, and growths in the throat that obstruct breathing and swallowing. Treatment includes scraping, cautery, the extraction of loose or decayed teeth with forceps, and medicated gargles and powders. The regimen of the healthy prescribes cleaning the teeth each morning with a twig of a bitter or astringent plant, chewed into a brush, and scraping the tongue.

docs.title: 8.4 Children, Pregnancy and Childbirth (Kaumārabhṛtya)
docs.text:
The care of children (kumāra; the branch is called kaumārabhṛtya, “the nurture of children”) included in classical practice the care of pregnant women, childbirth and the newborn. The compendia treat these topics in their Śārīrasthānas; there is also a specialised work, the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā. The main classical sources are listed in Table 8.2.

Table 8.2. Principal classical sources on conception, pregnancy, women’s diseases and children Work Chapters and subjects Caraka Saṃhitā Śā. 2–4 (conception, embryology); Śā. 8 (conception rites, pregnancy, birth, newborn, nursery); Ci. 30 (twenty yonivyāpad, breast milk, semen) Suśruta Saṃhitā Śā. 2–3 (semen and menstrual blood, conception, development of the embryo); Śā. 10 (pregnancy, birth, the newborn and the new mother); Ni. 8 and Ci. 15 (miscarriage, obstructed labour); Utt. 27–37 (the “seizers”); Utt. 38 (yonivyāpad) Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya Śā. 1–2 (conception and embryology; disorders of pregnancy); Utt. 1–3 (care of children, their diseases, the “seizers”); Utt. 33–34 (diseases of the genital organs) Kāśyapa Saṃhitā children’s medicine and the nurse throughout; examination of infants; dentition; phakka; diseases of the new mother

docs.title: 8.4.1 The Kāśyapa Saṃhitā
docs.text:
This work, also called the Vṛddhajīvakīya Tantra, presents itself as the teaching of Mārīca Kaśyapa, redacted by Vṛddhajīvaka and later by Vātsya. It was known only from quotations until a single, incomplete palm-leaf manuscript was found in Nepal and published by the royal preceptor Hemarāja Śarmā in 1938. In its present form it probably dates from about the seventh century CE (Meulenbeld 1999–2002). It discusses the examination of children, dentition, the qualities of breast milk and the choice of a wet-nurse, children’s diseases, preparations to be licked (lehana) by infants, and, at length, the “seizers” that attack children, among them the goddess Revatī.

The Kāśyapa Saṃhitā is notable for its attention to the stages of an infant’s devel­op­ment—the eruption of the teeth, the beginning of speech and walking, the change from milk to solid food—and to the examination of a child who cannot describe his symptoms. It devotes long passages to the choice of a wet-nurse (dhātrī), who should be of the same caste, healthy, of good character and with healthy children of her own, and to the examination of breast milk, whose purity is tested by its colour, taste and behaviour when dropped into water. The emphasis on wet-nurses reflects the practice of the elite households for whom the text was written.

The children’s diseases discussed in the compendia and in the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā include fevers, diarrhoea and vomiting, cough, disorders of teething, skin eruptions, eye infections, worms, wasting, convulsions, and disorders attributed to faulty breast milk. The texts insist that children be treated with milder drugs in smaller quantities, preferably given through the mother’s or nurse’s milk or in sweet and palatable forms, and that harsh procedures be avoided. Modern medicine agrees that children are not small adults, but it has also shown that many of the diseases the texts describe—diarrhoea, pneumonia, measles, neonatal infections—require prompt and specific treatment, and that vaccination prevents many of them.

docs.title: 8.4.2 Menstruation, Fertility and Conception
docs.text:
The gynaecology of the compendia rests on a theory of menstrual blood. Caraka counts menstrual blood and breast milk among the by-products (upadhātu) of the nutrient fluid (Table 2.8). Suśruta calls the menstrual flow ārtava and treats it as fiery in nature, the female counterpart of the man’s cool, “lunar” semen. According to Suśruta it begins at about twelve years of age and ceases at about fifty (Su.Śā. 3).

The days after menstruation are the “season” (ṛtu) in which conception is possible, usually reckoned as twelve nights from the onset of the flow, of which the first three are excluded. The texts hold that intercourse on an even-numbered night produces a son and on an odd-numbered night a daughter. The belief has no basis, but it shows how closely the theory was tied to the wish for sons (Section 1.8). Suśruta names four requirements for conception in an agricultural image: the season (ṛtu), the field (kṣetra, the womb), the water (ambu, the nourishing fluid) and the seed (bīja) (Su.Śā. 2). The picture of the woman as field and the man as sower is shared with the Dharmaśāstra and runs through the whole of this literature.

The texts discuss at length why a couple may fail to conceive: defects of semen or menstrual blood, disorders of the womb, wrong timing, and the conduct of the parents (Chapter 3). They prescribe purification and diet for both partners before the attempt. Rahul Peter Das’s detailed study of these theories shows how far they treat the woman’s body as the place in which the man’s seed and the incoming self are joined and nourished (Das 2003).

docs.title: 8.4.3 Pregnancy
docs.text: The compendia prescribe a regimen for each month of pregnancy (Ca.Śā. 8; Su.Śā. 10), consisting chiefly of milk, ghee, rice and other “sweet” and nourishing foods, with medicated preparations and, in the later months, oily enemas and vaginal tampons to prepare for delivery. They list things the pregnant woman should avoid—heavy exertion, sexual intercourse, fasting, anger and grief, riding in vehicles, looking at frightening things—and attribute congenital abnormalities to her behaviour, to the frustration of her cravings, or to the deeds of past lives. Rites to obtain a son (puṃsavana) are prescribed for the early months.

docs.title: 8.4.4 Miscarriage and the “Sleeping” Foetus
docs.text:
Suśruta distinguishes two kinds of pregnancy loss. Up to the fourth month the foetus is still fluid and is said to “flow out” (garbhasrāva). In the fifth and sixth months its body has become firm, and it is said to “fall” (garbhapāta) (Su.Ni. 8.10). The compendia list the causes of miscarriage—falls, blows, exertion, fasting, purgatives, suppression of natural urges, and the frustration of the pregnant woman’s longings. When bleeding threatens, they prescribe cooling, soothing and nourishing measures.

Caraka also describes conditions in which the foetus, deprived of nourishment, stops growing or “sleeps” in the womb and remains there beyond the normal term (upaviṣṭaka, nāgodara; Ca.Śā. 8.26). Belief in a dormant foetus that can later revive and be born is found in other pre-modern traditions as well. In Islamic law, for example, the doctrine of the “sleeping” foetus could protect a woman whose child was born long after her husband’s absence or death. Modern medicine knows nothing of the kind. A pregnancy that fails to grow needs examination, and the prolonged retention of a dead foetus is dangerous.

docs.title: 8.4.5 Childbirth and the Newborn
docs.text: The texts describe the preparation of a lying-in house, the signs of approaching labour, the assistance of experienced women, the management of the placenta, and the immediate care of the newborn: clearing the mouth and throat, rousing the child, cutting and tying the umbilical cord, bathing and the first feeding. If the newborn does not breathe, the texts recommend rousing it by striking two stones together near its ear, sprinkling it with cold or hot water and fanning it—an early recognition of the need to stimulate a newborn who fails to breathe, though modern newborn resuscitation is very different. In the birth rite (jātakarman) honey and ghee are given to the newborn with mantras; some texts add gold. Suśruta’s chapter on obstructed labour (Su.Ci. 15) has been described in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 8.4.6 The Mother after Childbirth
docs.text:
The new mother (sūtikā) was regarded as both vulnerable and ritually impure. The compendia prescribe for her a period of rest and seclusion in the lying-in house. Her care includes massage with oil, warm baths, binding of the abdomen and warmth, with a graded diet that begins with thin gruels prepared with digestive spices and returns gradually to ordinary food. Suśruta sets the period at about a month and a half, or until menstruation returns (Su.Śā. 10). The Kāśyapa Saṃhitā and later works add a class of “diseases of the new mother” (sūtikāroga), among them fevers, swellings and wasting after childbirth, many of which must have been puerperal infections.

The seclusion, the special foods, the warmth and the massage survive in household customs of postnatal care across South Asia, and anthropologists of childbirth have studied them closely (Jeffery et al. 1989). The idea that mother and newborn were ritually impure for a period after birth also determined who attended them. In much of northern India the cutting of the cord and the handling of the afterbirth fell to the dāī, whose low status was bound up with the polluting character of her work (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 8.4.7 Infant Feeding and the Nursery
docs.text:
The texts divide early childhood by diet: the infant fed only on milk (kṣīrapa), up to about one year; the child who takes milk and food (kṣīrānnāda), up to about two; and the child who lives on food (annāda) (Su.Sū. 35). Breast milk is the ideal food. The compendia describe its good qualities and its defects, attributing the defects to the doṣas and recognising them by colour, taste, smell and behaviour in water. They treat these defects by treating the nursing mother or wet-nurse (dhātrī), not the child.

For the first three days, before the milk was thought to have come in, Suśruta prescribes honey and ghee with herbs, and only then the breast (Su.Śā. 10). Modern advice is the opposite: breastfeeding should begin within the first hour, because the first milk, colostrum, protects the newborn against infection. Delayed breastfeeding and the giving of other substances in the first days, a custom the texts reflect and that survived widely, have been a cause of illness and death among newborns.

Caraka’s chapter on birth describes a nursery (kumārāgāra) that should be clean, airy and free of vermin, and the child’s bedding, clothing and amulets (Ca.Śā. 8.59–64). It also considers toys. They should be brightly coloured, make pleasant sounds and be light. They should have no sharp points and be too large to put in the mouth. And the child, it adds, should not be frightened with talk of demons.

The Kāśyapa Saṃhitā gives particular attention to the infant who cannot say where it hurts. One of its chapters explains how to infer the seat of pain from behaviour: crying, clenching the fists, rubbing a part of the body, or refusing the breast. The work also describes phakka, a disorder in which a child fails to walk at the normal age, attributed to faulty breast milk, to a new pregnancy of the mother, or to illness. Among other measures it recommends a small three-wheeled wooden cart (phakkaratha) to help the child learn to walk. The descriptions suggest the effects of malnutrition, including rickets, though diagnosis at this distance is uncertain.

docs.title: 8.4.8 Children’s Diseases and the “Seizers”
docs.text:
Many children’s diseases are attributed to “seizers” (graha), demonic beings who attack infants whose mothers or nurses have neglected cleanliness and ritual. Suśruta names nine, among them Skanda, Śakunī, Revatī and Pūtanā, describes the signs of each, and prescribes baths, oils, fumigations, amulets and offerings (Su.Utt. 27–37). The seizers are deities or demons of a type well known from Indian religion, and several—Skanda, Revatī, the bird-like Śakunī, the “stinking” Pūtanā—have counterparts in mythology and in protective rituals for children. Many of the conditions described are recognisable as fevers, convulsions, diarrhoea and wasting—the infections and malnutrition that killed so many children before modern medicine.

Health and Safety Note

The classical regimens for pregnancy, childbirth and infancy described in this section are historical, and some of them, such as delaying breastfeeding and giving honey to newborns, are now known to be unsafe. See Section 12.7.

docs.title: 8.4.9 Women’s Diseases
docs.text:
The compendia discuss the disorders of menstruation, the reproductive tract and breast milk at some length. Disorders of menstrual blood (ārtava) are classified by the doṣas; excessive bleeding (asṛgdara) is described as a separate disease. Caraka devotes the last chapter of the Cikitsāsthāna to twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract (yonivyāpad), and Suśruta discusses them in the Uttaratantra (Su.Utt. 38).

Caraka’s twenty disorders show what the texts cared about. Four are due to the doṣas singly and together. Others are named after their chief sign: painful, obstructed menstruation (udāvartinī), absence of menstruation (arajaskā), a narrow opening (sūcīmukhī), a dry passage (śuṣkā) and a “great” womb, apparently prolapse (mahāyoni). One, the “killer of sons” (putraghnī), is the repeated loss of pregnancies, which Caraka attributes to aggravated vāta. Another (ṣaṇḍhī) describes a woman who never menstruates and whose breasts do not develop, a condition the texts attribute to a defect in the parents’ seed and regard as incurable. Menstruation, sexual function and above all fertility dominate the list. Infertility is a recurrent concern, and although Caraka also discusses defects of semen (Section 8.8), the texts usually look for its cause in the woman. Excessive menstrual bleeding (asṛgdara, also called pradara) is treated with astringent and cooling drugs and with diet.

The texts also prescribe a regimen for women during menstruation, which forbids them, among other things, to bathe, to apply collyrium or to sleep by day, and which is closely connected to brahmanical ideas of ritual impurity. These passages tell us much about the medical understanding of women’s bodies in the period and about the social constraints placed on them; they are discussed further in Chapter 1.

docs.title: 8.4.10 Reading the Texts on Women and Children
docs.text:
These chapters are among the richest in the classical literature, and among the hardest to read fairly. Martha Ann Selby has read the narratives of conception, gestation and labour in Caraka, Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa side by side. She notes that they speak almost entirely from the position of the male physician and of a household that wants a healthy son, and that the woman appears as the field and vessel of the pregnancy rather than as its subject. Yet the same texts attend closely to her cravings, her comfort and her fear, and require that experienced women stay with her through labour (Selby 2005).

Much of what the texts prescribe for labour and the newborn was in practice done by women they do not name, and whose knowledge has to be reconstructed from ethnography rather than from manuscripts. The physician, a man of high caste, was usually called to a birth only when something had gone wrong.

Seclusion made matters harder. In households that kept women in seclusion, a male physician of any tradition might be allowed to examine a woman only partly, and the Unani physician sometimes had to feel the pulse through a curtain. In the late nineteenth century this became an argument for training women as doctors. The Countess of Dufferin’s Fund, founded in 1885, supported hospitals for women and the medical education of women. In 1886 Anandibai Joshi graduated in medicine in Philadelphia and Kadambini Ganguly in Calcutta, among the first Indian women to qualify in Western medicine. Neither Āyurveda nor Unani produced a comparable body of women practitioners until women entered their colleges in the twentieth century.

The setting of these texts was grim. Before modern obstetrics and public health, a large share of children died in infancy and early childhood, and childbirth was one of the commonest causes of death among young women. The many rites and amulets for protecting mother and child, and the “seizers” of children’s medicine, are the response of a society that lived with these losses. The texts’ achievements deserve recognition: close observation of pregnancy and infancy, concern for gentle treatment of children, and attention to the mother’s well-being after birth. That recognition does not mean bringing their regimens into modern care. Programmes marketed today as garbha saṃskāra promise to shape a child’s intelligence, character or sex through the mother’s diet, music and rites in pregnancy. They go far beyond anything the evidence supports, and sex-selection in any form is illegal in India.

docs.title: 8.5 Disorders of the Mind and Possession (Bhūtavidyā)
docs.text:
The branch called “knowledge of spirits” (bhūtavidyā) dealt with disorders attributed to possession by gods, demons, ancestors and other beings. It overlaps with the treatment of disorders that the compendia attribute to the doṣas acting on the mind. Together, these are the nearest classical equivalent of psychiatry (Table 8.3).

Table 8.3. Some disorders of the mind in the compendia Disorder Classical description unmāda (madness) Five kinds in Caraka: one for each doṣa, one for all three, and one caused by external agents (gods, sages, ancestors, demons and others); disturbance of mind, intellect, memory, conduct and behaviour (Ca.Ni. 7; Ca.Ci. 9) apasmāra (“loss of memory”; seizures) Four kinds; episodes of loss of consciousness with abnormal movements, foam at the mouth and other signs (Ca.Ni. 8; Ca.Ci. 10) atattvābhiniveśa “Clinging to what is not real”: persistent false judgement about what is beneficial (Ca.Ci. 10) madātyaya Disorders caused by excessive drinking of alcohol (Ca.Ci. 24)

The texts classify the beings that cause possession. Suśruta names eight kinds—gods, demons (asura), celestial musicians (gandharva), yakṣas, ancestors (pitṛ), serpents, rākṣasas and piśācas—each producing a characteristic pattern of behaviour, and prescribes offerings, mantras, fumigations, amulets and medicated ghee and nasal medicines for each (Su.Utt. 60). The physician is told to recognise the day and time at which each kind of being is likely to attack.

Caraka’s account of madness is remarkably observant. He describes the patient’s restlessness, confusion, inappropriate laughter, weeping and singing, sleeplessness, neglect of hygiene, wandering, and violence or withdrawal, and distinguishes the forms associated with each doṣa. Madness caused by gods, demons or ancestors is recognised by behaviour attributed to the possessing being—a person “seized” by a gandharva loves music, perfume and pleasure, for instance—and by its appearance at particular times. The physician is told to protect the patient from harming himself and others, to treat him with patience, and to employ every means, including the patient’s friends and family.

docs.title: 8.5.1 The Causes and Course of Madness
docs.text:
Caraka’s account of the causes of madness looks first at the person rather than the disease. Madness arises in someone whose mind (sattva) is timid or weak, when the doṣas are disturbed by unwholesome, impure or incompatible food, by irregular conduct of the body and of treatment, or by shocks to the mind from desire, anger, fear, joy, grief and anxiety (Ca.Ni. 7.4); the chapter on treatment adds disrespect towards gods, teachers and brāhmaṇas (Ca.Ci. 9). The aggravated doṣas reach the heart, the seat of the intellect, and obstruct the channels that carry the mind. The definition that follows (Ca.Ni. 7.5) lists what is then thrown into confusion: mind, intellect, awareness, knowledge, memory, inclination, character, conduct and behaviour. Madness is in this view a disorder of the whole person’s capacity to know and to act, not only of mood or of perception (Figure 8.1). (The psychological side of these ideas is discussed in Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā.)

Figure 8.1. Caraka’s account of how madness arises (after Ca.Ni. 7 and Ca.Ci. 9; schematic). The lower row shows the “external” form, which Caraka also traces to the patient’s own conduct.

Before the illness declares itself there are warning signs, among them a feeling of emptiness in the head, restless eyes, noises in the ears, quickened breathing, loss of appetite and disturbed dreams, and the physician is to watch for them so that treatment can begin early. Each doṣa then produces its own picture, from the restless, talkative and wasting patient of the vāta form to the angry and violent patient of the pitta form, who longs for shade and cool water, and the silent, sleepy and solitary patient of the kapha form. Madness from all three together is judged incurable (Ca.Ni. 7.7).

Suśruta’s Uttaratantra treats possession, epilepsy and madness in successive chapters (Su.Utt. 60–62), and adds forms caused by grief and by poison to those of the doṣas. Vāgbhaṭa, following both predecessors, gives four consecutive chapters of his Uttarasthāna to the recognition of possession, its treatment, madness and epilepsy (AH Utt. 4–7). The categories thus remained stable for more than a thousand years, though each author arranged them in his own way (Table 8.4).

Table 8.4. Where the three great compendia treat possession, madness and epilepsy Topic Caraka Suśruta Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya possession by spirits within madness (Ni. 7; Ci. 9) Utt. 60 Utt. 4–5 madness (unmāda) Ni. 7; Ci. 9 Utt. 62 Utt. 6 epilepsy (apasmāra) Ni. 8; Ci. 10 Utt. 61 Utt. 7

docs.title: 8.5.2 Possession and Responsibility
docs.text:
The fifth, “external” (āgantu) form of madness is attributed to gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas and other beings. Caraka distinguishes it from the forms due to the doṣas by its signs. The patient may show strength, energy, learning, eloquence or knowledge beyond anything he had before, and the onset and course of the illness are irregular, not tied to the causes and seasons that govern the doṣas.

Caraka then adds an important qualification. Gods, gandharvas, piśācas and rākṣasas, he says, do not afflict a person who has not already brought affliction on himself: the root of external madness is the patient’s own offence against wisdom, in this life or in an earlier one, which exposes him to attack (Ca.Ni. 7). The passage keeps the language of possession, which belonged to the world of patients and their families, while placing the cause in the moral and mental life of the person. It also explains why the same chapter recommends good conduct as the best protection against madness of every kind.

The theory had two sides. It let the physician work alongside the exorcist and the priest, sharing a vocabulary with them rather than opposing them. But it also tied mental illness to moral fault, a link that has added, in India as elsewhere, to the stigma borne by the mentally ill and their families.

docs.title: 8.5.3 Epilepsy (Apasmāra)
docs.text:
The name apasmāra means “loss of memory”. Caraka defines the disorder as a sudden loss of memory and awareness, with a sense of entering darkness and with abnormal, distressing movements, caused by disturbance of the intellect and the mind (Ca.Ci. 10). The aggravated doṣas, driven into the heart and the channels of the mind, bring on attacks in which the patient falls, trembles, grinds the teeth and foams at the mouth, and afterwards wakes as if from sleep. Four forms are distinguished, one for each doṣa and one from all three, the last again judged incurable. The texts noticed that attacks recur at intervals, with the patient apparently well between them, and explained this by the persistence of disturbed doṣas that flare up when circumstances favour them. Some of the warning sensations they describe resemble what modern neurology calls an aura, but the classical category also covers other kinds of fit and faint, and should not be equated with epilepsy as now defined. Suśruta likewise distinguishes four kinds (Su.Utt. 61).

The term passed into religious thought. In the iconography of Śiva as lord of the dance (Naṭarāja), the dwarf crushed beneath the god’s foot is named Apasmāra, the personification of ignorance and forgetfulness (see Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa). Epilepsy itself has long been among the most stigmatised of illnesses in India, as elsewhere. People with epilepsy have faced discrimination in marriage and employment; until an amendment of 1999, Indian marriage law listed epilepsy among the grounds on which a marriage could be annulled. The belief that seizures are caused by spirits or past sins persists. The classical texts, which treated apasmāra as a disease with recognisable causes, did not create this stigma, but neither did they remove it.

docs.title: 8.5.4 Treatment as the Texts Describe It
docs.text:
The treatment of madness in Caraka (Ca.Ci. 9) follows the general order of his therapeutics. For the forms due to the doṣas the physician first gives oleation and the appropriate purification—emesis, purgation, enema or nasal medicine—and then pacifying measures. Medicated ghee has a special place: the chapter describes several named compound ghees, and in the next chapter, on epilepsy (Ca.Ci. 10), Caraka praises old, long-kept ghee for this group of disorders. Collyria, fumigations, ointments and baths complete the bodily treatment. For the external forms he prescribes mantras, offerings, vows, protective rites and amulets, the therapy “relying on the divine” (Chapter 1). Epilepsy is treated on similar lines (Ca.Ci. 10).

Caraka traces many mental disorders to “offences against wisdom” (prajñāparādha)—knowingly doing what one knows to be harmful—as well as to the doṣas and to external beings, and his treatment answers each cause. Alongside drugs and rites stands “mastery of the mind” (sattvāvajaya): reassurance, instruction, the inducing of contrary emotions (fear to counter desire, joy to counter grief) and the cultivation of knowledge, fortitude and concentration. These psychological measures are among the most interesting parts of the chapters. Friends and well-wishers are to speak to the patient in words that comfort him and recall his duties and interests. Where madness has followed the loss of something dear, the physician should try to restore something like it and console the patient. Alongside these gentle measures stand harsh ones, which Caraka reserves for patients who do not respond: threats, binding, beating, confinement and deliberate frightening, justified as means of shocking the mind back into its place and now regarded as abuse. Both kinds of measure belong to the same theory, in which the mind can be moved by emotion as the body is moved by drugs.

The ḥakīms of India brought a second learned vocabulary to the same patients. Unani medicine explained melancholy (mālīkhūliyā) by an excess or corruption of black bile, distinguished it from frenzy and from other forms of madness (junūn), and, following Ibn Sīnā, treated even passionate love (ʿishq) as a disease akin to melancholy, to be recognised by the pulse and treated by regimen, diversion and, where possible, union with the beloved (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007). Its treatments, like Caraka’s, combined evacuation, diet, baths and soothing drugs with conversation, music and change of scene. Patients and families in India could move between vaidya, ḥakīm, shrine and exorcist, and many did.

docs.title: 8.5.5 Madness and Care in Indian History
docs.text:
The compendia say little about where the mad lived and who looked after them. For most of Indian history the answer was the family, which bore the burden of care, sought help from physicians, astrologers, exorcists and priests, and often travelled to temples and shrines with a reputation for healing. Sudhir Kakar’s study of the Hanumān temple at Mehandipur in Rajasthan, where afflicted people stay for weeks of ritual healing, and William Sax’s study of ritual healing in the Garhwal Himalaya, which treats affliction as a disorder of social relations as much as of the individual, show how much such places can offer in community, meaning and relief (Kakar 1982; Sax 2009). Sufi shrines across the subcontinent have played a similar part.

These places also have a darker history of chaining, beating and deprivation. In August 2001, according to the reports of the time, a fire at a private home for the mentally ill near the shrine at Erwadi in Tamil Nadu killed some twenty-eight inmates who were chained and could not escape. The disaster led to inquiries ordered by the Supreme Court and to the closing of many such homes. The colonial state, for its part, founded lunatic asylums from the late eighteenth century, first for Europeans and soldiers and later for Indians, and governed them under the Indian Lunacy Act of 1912; they offered custody more than treatment. India’s Mental Healthcare Act of 2017 sets out the rights of persons with mental illness and prohibits chaining in any form. Volume 22 discusses shrine healing and these reforms from the side of psychology.

The classical approach is of real historical interest: it treated mental disorder as a medical concern, considered the patient’s whole circumstances, and gave a place to what we might call psychological treatment. But comparisons with modern psychotherapy should not be overstated, and the classical categories do not correspond to modern diagnoses.

docs.title: 8.6 Toxicology (Agadatantra)
docs.text:
Toxicology (agadatantra) was a well-developed branch, important in a land of venomous snakes and in courts where poisoning was feared. Its classical treatises are the eight chapters of Suśruta’s Kalpasthāna (Section 4.10) and the chapter on poisons in Caraka’s Cikitsāsthāna (Ca.Ci. 23). The texts (Table 8.5) distinguish poisons of immobile origin (plants and minerals) from those of mobile origin (snakes, scorpions, spiders, insects, rabid animals); poisons compounded and administered by others (gara); and weakened poisons that remain latent in the body (dūṣīviṣa). They describe the signs of poisoning in its successive stages and prescribe a wide range of treatments: tourniquets, incision and suction, cautery, emetics and purgatives, antidotes (agada) taken internally or applied, nasal medication, and mantras.

Caraka describes poison as having ten qualities—dry, hot, sharp, subtle, quick-acting, pervasive, spreading, clear, light and indigestible—which are the exact opposites of the qualities of ojas; poison therefore attacks the vital essence directly and spreads rapidly through the body (Ca.Ci. 23). He describes the successive stages (vega) through which poisoning progresses, from thirst, numbness and horripilation to collapse and death, and lists twenty-four measures (upakrama) of treatment, beginning with mantras, the binding of the limb, incision, squeezing, sucking and cautery and ending with antidotes and the revival of the apparently dead.

Suśruta locates the poisons of plants and minerals in ten parts: root, leaf, fruit, flower, bark, milky sap, heartwood, resin, mineral and bulb. He divides snakes into hooded snakes (darvīkara, associated with vāta), snakes with circular markings (maṇḍalin, associated with pitta), striped snakes (rājimant, associated with kapha), non-venomous snakes and hybrids, and describes the stages of envenomation; attempts to match these classes exactly to the cobras, vipers and kraits of modern herpetology are tempting but uncertain. His later chapters deal with the bites of rats, insects, spiders, scorpions, leeches and rabid animals, each with its own signs and treatment, and with drums smeared with antidotes whose sound was thought to cure. His account of the bite of a mad dog is notable. He describes how the dog’s behaviour changes, how the bitten person may later behave like the animal, and how a patient who is terrified at the sight or sound of water is incurable—a description that corresponds to the hydrophobia of rabies, which is still incurable once symptoms appear.

Table 8.5. The classical classification of poisons (after Su.Ka. 2–8 and Ca.Ci. 23) Class Description in the texts immobile (sthāvara) poisons of plants and minerals, located in root, leaf, fruit, flower, bark, milky sap, heartwood, resin, mineral or bulb mobile (jaṅgama) poisons of snakes, scorpions, spiders, insects, rodents, frogs, fish, leeches and rabid animals compound (gara) mixtures of substances administered by others, often by women to win a husband’s affection, according to the texts, causing chronic illness latent (dūṣīviṣa) weakened poison that remains in the body and causes chronic disease when provoked by season, diet or other factors

The protection of kings against poisoners was a major concern. Suśruta’s first chapter on toxicology (Su.Ka. 1) tells the king to employ a physician in the royal kitchen, to have food tasted, and to watch for signs of poison: food that is poisoned is said to give off a blue flame and much smoke when thrown on the fire, to make flies that eat it die, and to make certain birds behave abnormally—the eyes of the cakora partridge, for example, are said to turn red at the sight of it. The same chapter describes the signs of poison in drinks, ointments, clothing, beds, ornaments, combs and mounts. Such passages reflect the court politics of ancient India, in which poisoning was a recognised political weapon, as the Arthaśāstra also shows.

The fear of poison also produced legends. The “poison maiden” (viṣakanyā), a girl supposedly raised on small doses of poison until her touch or embrace was deadly, appears in Sanskrit literature—most famously in Viśākhadatta’s political drama Mudrārākṣasa, where one is sent to kill Candragupta—and in medieval stories in Persian and European languages. The idea has no basis in toxicology, but it shows how poison figured in the imagination of court politics.

In Kerala and elsewhere, specialist “poison physicians” (viṣavaidya) maintained a living tradition of snakebite treatment, with its own literature in Sanskrit and Malayalam (Section 5.3). Snakebite remains a major cause of death in rural India. A nationally representative study of mortality estimated some 1.2 million snakebite deaths in India between 2000 and 2019, an average of about 58,000 a year, most of them in rural areas (Suraweera et al. 2020), and delay in reaching antivenom is a large part of the problem.

Health and Safety Note

None of the classical treatments for snakebite, scorpion sting or poisoning should be used; they can cause harm or fatal delay. First-aid guidance is summarised in Section 12.7.

docs.title: 8.7 Rejuvenation (Rasāyana)
docs.text:
Rasāyana, literally “the path of rasa” (the nutrient fluid, or the essence of the body), is the branch concerned with prolonging life, preserving youth and strengthening memory and intellect. Its classical account opens Caraka’s Cikitsāsthāna, in a chapter divided into four “quarters”, which lists the benefits that rejuvenation promises:

Caraka Saṃhitā, Cikitsāsthāna 1.1.7–8

dīrgham āyuḥ smṛtiṃ medhām ārogyaṃ taruṇaṃ vayaḥ prabhāvarṇasvaraudāryaṃ dehendriyabalaṃ param vāksiddhiṃ praṇatiṃ kāntiṃ labhate nā rasāyanāt From rejuvenation a man obtains long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, excellence of lustre, complexion and voice, the greatest strength of body and senses, success in speech, respect and beauty.

Caraka distinguishes treatment in which the patient lives in a specially built hut (kuṭīprāveśika) from treatment in which he goes about his life in wind and sun (vātātapika). The regimen “in the hut” was elaborate. The hut was to be built in an auspicious place, with three concentric chambers to protect the patient from wind, sun and disturbance. The patient first underwent purification and a graduated diet, and then took the rejuvenating preparation for a period under a strict regimen of diet and conduct, before gradually returning to ordinary life. The “wind and sun” form could be taken by people going about their normal lives. Rejuvenation was intended above all for the healthy, in youth or middle age, rather than for the sick; the commentators add a distinction between rejuvenation sought for a particular benefit (kāmya) and rejuvenation given to cure a disease (naimittika).

The best-known preparations of the chapter are herbal: the brāhma rasāyana, and the confection associated with the sage Cyavana, whom the Aśvins are said to have restored to youth—the ancestor of the modern cyavanaprāśa, whose later history is followed in Section 6.7. The same chapter lists four drugs “beneficial to the intellect” (medhya): the juice of maṇḍūkaparṇī, the powder of liquorice taken with milk, the juice of guḍūcī, and a paste of śaṅkhapuṣpī (Ca.Ci. 1.3.30–31). It also includes preparations of iron, the ancestors of the iron “ashes” of the later pharmacy (Section 9.2).

The chapter closes with a different kind of rejuvenation. Caraka describes a person who is truthful, free from anger, abstinent from alcohol and sex, non-violent, calm, pleasant in speech, devoted to recitation and cleanliness, compassionate, charitable and respectful to elders, and says that such a person obtains the benefits of rejuvenation without taking any drug (Ca.Ci. 1.4.30–35). This “rejuvenation by conduct” (ācārarasāyana) expresses an old and widely shared conviction that moral life and bodily health are connected (Section 2.11).

The concern with ageing extends beyond rasāyana.
