The compendia describe the signs of old age—decline of the senses, strength, memory and digestion, greying, wrinkles and weakness—as the natural predominance of vāta in the last stage of life, and recommend for the elderly gentle oleation, nourishing food, milk and ghee, massage, regular habits and the avoidance of exhausting treatments.

In the medieval period the word rasāyana came also to mean alchemy, and the alchemists’ search for an elixir of immortality based on mercury had a large influence on medicine (Chapter 9).

Modern writers often describe rasāyana drugs as “immunomodulators”, “adaptogens” or “anti-ageing” agents. These terms reflect laboratory research on plant extracts. There is no good clinical evidence that any rasāyana preparation prolongs life or prevents disease in human beings, and commercial products sold under classical names often differ from the classical recipes (Section 6.7).

docs.title: 8.8 Virility and Fertility (Vājīkaraṇa)
docs.text:
Vājīkaraṇa, “making (a man) like a stallion”, is concerned with sexual vigour and the begetting of children. Caraka’s chapter on the subject (Ca.Ci. 2) is addressed entirely to men. It praises sexual pleasure and progeny as goods of the householder’s life, describes the qualities of the ideal partner, and gives many preparations—of milk, ghee, eggs, meat, sugar and herbs—intended to increase semen and potency. A man without children, the text says, is like a tree with a single branch, without shade and with a bad smell. The texts assume that the purpose of sexual life is the birth of sons, and that infertility is chiefly a matter of the woman’s body or of the man’s semen. Modern medicine has very different and far more effective ways of investigating and treating infertility in both partners.

The texts’ theory of reproduction underlies this branch. Semen (śukra) is the last and most refined of the bodily constituents, produced from all the others, so that its loss was thought to weaken the whole body—an idea that also underlies the high value placed on continence in Indian religious traditions. Caraka describes eight defects of semen, attributed to the doṣas, and treats them with purification, diet and drugs; female infertility is treated in the chapter on gynaecological disorders. Modern studies of infertility have shown that male factors are as common as female ones, and that the causes are many and specific.

The concern of the medical texts with sexual vigour links them to the wider literature on erotics. The Kāmasūtra attributed to Vātsyāyana (probably third century CE) ends with a book of recipes for aphrodisiacs, charms and means of attracting a partner (Doniger and Kakar 2002), and later erotic manuals such as the Ratirahasya and the Anaṅgaraṅga also contain medical recipes. The overlap shows how medical knowledge circulated among the educated elite, and how closely medicine was tied to the ideals of courtly life.

Summary

The clinical branches show the compendia at their most observant: in the periodic fevers, the skin diseases, the eye, the infant who cannot say where it hurts, and the patient whose madness Caraka traces to his own conduct. They also show the limits of the theory and the society behind it, from the son-seeking theory of conception to the harsh measures used on the insane. Rejuvenation, virility and toxicology complete the eight branches, and each has a modern afterlife—in cyavanaprāśa, in fertility tonics, in the treatment of snakebite—that the texts alone cannot justify.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On conception, pregnancy and the female body in the medical texts see Das and Selby (Das 2003; Selby 2005); on childbirth and the work of birth attendants in modern north India, Jeffery, Jeffery and Lyon (Jeffery et al. 1989); on healing shrines and ritual treatment of affliction, Kakar and Sax (Kakar 1982; Sax 2009); on the classical categories of disease, Meulenbeld (Meulenbeld 1999–2002) and the translations of the compendia cited in Chapters 3 and 4.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Rasaśāstra: Mercury, Metals and Medicine
docs.text:
yogād api viṣaṃ tīkṣṇam uttamaṃ bheṣajaṃ bhavet bheṣajaṃ cāpi duryuktaṃ tīkṣṇaṃ saṃpadyate viṣam By right use even a sharp poison may become an excellent medicine; and a medicine wrongly used becomes a sharp poison.

— Caraka Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 1.126

Health and Safety Note: read before this chapter

This chapter is a history. It gives no dose, recipe, method of preparation, “purification” procedure, firing schedule or vehicle for any preparation, and nothing in it should be used to prepare or take one. Mercury, lead, arsenic, copper and the other metals and minerals discussed are toxic. “Purification” and “incineration” change their chemical form but do not make them safe, and the traditional tests cannot detect toxicity. Preparations containing them—whether called bhasma, rasa, sindūra, parpaṭī, vaṭī or anything else—can cause serious and sometimes permanent harm to the nervous system, kidneys, liver and blood, and are especially dangerous in pregnancy and for children; surveys have found such metals in about one Ayurvedic product in five (Section 9.5). Anyone who has taken them and has abdominal pain, anaemia, fatigue, numbness or a change in behaviour should see a doctor and say what they took; blood tests for lead and mercury are available.

docs.title: 9.1 Alchemy and Medicine
docs.text:
In medieval Sanskrit, rasa—which in the older medical texts means “taste” or “nutrient fluid”—came also to mean mercury, and “the science of mercury” (rasaśāstra or rasavidyā) became the name of a body of knowledge that combined alchemy, metallurgy, pharmacy and religious practice. Its practitioners sought two kinds of transformation: the transmutation of base metals into gold (lohavedha or lohavāda) and the transformation of the human body into an immortal, perfected body (dehavedha or dehavāda). Mercury, the liquid metal that “eats” other metals and can be “killed” and revived, was the agent of both. In the religious imagination of the tradition it was the semen of Śiva, and sulphur the menstrual blood of the goddess; their union in the alchemist’s vessel reproduced the union of the divine couple. David Gordon White’s The Alchemical Body is the standard study of these “Siddha” alchemical traditions and their links with Tantra and Haṭha Yoga (White 1996).

Over time the medical side of the tradition became dominant. By the later medieval period, metals, minerals and mercury compounds prepared according to the rules of rasaśāstra had become a regular part of Āyurvedic practice, and many of the formulae used today contain them. This chapter outlines the history of the tradition and its main ideas, and then explains why its products raise serious safety concerns. The history of Indian alchemy and metallurgy is treated more fully in Volume 14 of this series, Rasāyana: Chemistry and Metallurgy.

docs.title: 9.2 Historical Development
docs.text:
The early compendia make little use of metals in internal medicine. Caraka and Suśruta prescribe preparations of iron, and gold occurs in rites for the newborn, but their remedies are overwhelmingly vegetable and animal. Mineral substances such as salts, alkalis, mineral pitch (śilājatu) and arsenic sulphides occur, the latter mainly in external applications.

Iron had a special place. Caraka’s chapter on rejuvenation describes preparations in which thin sheets of iron were heated, quenched in decoctions and ground, and he recommends iron in pallor and as a rejuvenating drug; Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa also prescribe it. These preparations are the ancestors of the iron “ashes” (lauha bhasma) of the later pharmacy. Gold was given to newborns in the birth rite, and gold and silver were used in eye preparations and collyria. But the systematic internal use of mercury, lead, arsenic and many minerals belongs to the later period.

A distinct alchemical literature appears in Sanskrit from about the tenth century CE, within Śaiva and Siddha religious traditions, and the internal use of mercury and of incinerated metals spreads into medical works from about the same period. The Rasahṛdayatantra of Govinda Bhagavat (perhaps 10th–11th century) and the Rasārṇava (c. 11th–12th century) are among the earliest surviving alchemical works; later centuries produced a large literature that increasingly emphasised medicine (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. Some important works of rasaśāstra (dates approximate and in several cases disputed) Work Author and date Notes Rasahṛdayatantra Govinda Bhagavat; c. 10th–11th century Early systematic work on mercury and its eighteen “processes” Rasārṇava anonymous; c. 11th–12th century Śaiva alchemical tantra; detailed on apparatus Rasendramaṅgala attributed to Nāgārjuna; date uncertain Often confused with a “Rasaratnākara of Nāgārjuna”; see below Rasendracūḍāmaṇi Somadeva; c. 12th–13th century Rasaratnasamuccaya attributed to a Vāgbhaṭa (not the author of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya); c. late 13th–14th century The most influential systematic work; source of the standard classification of minerals Rasaratnākara Nityanātha; c. 13th–14th century Large compendium Rasaprakāśasudhākara Yaśodhara; c. 13th century Āyurvedaprakāśa Mādhava Upādhyāya; c. 17th century Integrates rasaśāstra with medical practice Rasataraṅgiṇī Sadānanda Śarmā; 20th century Modern textbook widely used in Āyurvedic colleges

docs.title: 9.2.1 Nāgārjuna and the “Alchemical Ghost”
docs.text: Popular histories often credit Indian alchemy to Nāgārjuna, the great Buddhist philosopher of the second or third century CE, and cite a Rasaratnākara by him. Dominik Wujastyk has shown that this text is an “alchemical ghost”: the work usually cited under that name is the Rasendramaṅgala attributed to a Nāgārjuna, which is a much later work, while the Rasaratnākara proper is by Nityanātha (Wujastyk 1984). The several Nāgārjunas of Indian tradition—philosopher, alchemist, redactor of Suśruta, author of a Rasavaiśeṣikasūtra on pharmacological “taste” (which is not an alchemical work)—should be kept apart unless there is evidence that they are the same.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Alchemy, Tantra and Yoga
docs.text: White has shown that Indian alchemy was closely bound up with the Tantric and yogic traditions of the Siddhas and Nāths, who were also the founders of Haṭha Yoga (White 1996). In their teaching, the transformation of mercury in the alchemist’s vessel, the transformation of the yogin’s body by breath control and the raising of internal energies, and the ritual union of Śiva and the goddess were parallel processes, each of which could lead to a perfected, immortal body (divyadeha). Legends of alchemists who turned iron to gold, or who lived for centuries, cluster around holy mountains such as Śrīśailam in Andhra Pradesh. The alchemical texts are therefore religious works as well as technical ones: they prescribe initiations, mantras, the worship of the rasaliṅga (a liṅga made of “bound” mercury), and the ritual purity of the laboratory.

docs.title: 9.2.3 Mercury in Other Medical Traditions
docs.text: India was not alone in using mercury and other metals in medicine, and the comparison is sobering. Chinese alchemists sought elixirs of immortality containing mercury, arsenic and lead, and the official histories record that several emperors of the Tang dynasty died, apparently of elixir poisoning. Islamic alchemists, such as those of the Jābirian corpus, developed laboratory chemistry and some mercurial medicines. In sixteenth-century Europe, Paracelsus and his followers championed chemical medicines, and mercury became the standard treatment for syphilis for some four hundred years, despite its well-known toxicity; “a night with Venus, a lifetime with Mercury” was the grim proverb. Indian physicians, too, adopted mercury for syphilis in the sixteenth century (Chapter 5). Mercury, arsenic and antimony were removed from Western pharmacopoeias in the twentieth century, as better and safer treatments became available and their toxicity was understood. Tibetan medicine, by contrast, still prepares a processed mercury sulphide for its most prestigious pills (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 9.3 The Materials
docs.text:
The Rasaratnasamuccaya established a classification of mineral substances that later works followed. Its main groups are the “great rasas” (mahārasa), the “lesser rasas” (uparasa), the “common rasas” (sādhāraṇarasa), metals (loha or dhātu), gems (ratna) and poisons (viṣa). Several of the modern identifications are uncertain or disputed. Table 9.2 lists some members of each group, with the main toxic element involved where there is one.

Table 9.2. Some substances of rasaśāstra and their toxic components (identifications partly uncertain) Sanskrit name Usual modern identification Main hazard Mercury and its compounds pārada mercury mercury hiṅgula cinnabar (mercuric sulphide) mercury kajjalī black mercuric sulphide, made from mercury and sulphur mercury rasasindūra red mercuric sulphide mercury rasakarpūra mercurous chloride (calomel) mercury Metals suvarṇa, rajata gold, silver contamination from processing with mercury and other metals tāmra copper copper lauha iron iron overload; contamination nāga or sīsa lead lead vaṅga tin tin; contamination with lead yaśada zinc (a late addition to the list) zinc Minerals abhraka mica contamination mākṣika copper or iron pyrites copper, arsenic impurities sasyaka or tuttha copper sulphate (blue vitriol) copper rasaka a zinc ore (calamine) zinc, lead impurities haritāla orpiment (arsenic trisulphide) arsenic manaḥśilā realgar (arsenic sulphide) arsenic gaurīpāṣāṇa or śaṅkhiyā white arsenic (arsenic trioxide) arsenic gandhaka sulphur combined with mercury and metals

The plant poisons used in rasaśāstra formulae—aconite, Datura, nux vomica and others—are listed in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 9.4 The Processes in Outline
docs.text:
The operations, apparatus and laboratory practice of the alchemists are described in detail, as history, in Volume 14 of this series, Rasāyana. A short summary of concepts is enough here; nothing in it is a description of a procedure.

The alchemical works describe eighteen “refinements” (saṃskāra) through which mercury was to pass, from steaming and grinding through “swooning”, “reviving” and “binding” to the “digestion” of other metals, transmutation and, finally, use in the body; the first eight were treated as preparatory and medical, the rest as transmutational alchemy. Metals and minerals were to be “purified” (śodhana) by repeated heating and quenching in various liquids, and then “killed” (māraṇa) by repeated firing with plant juices and other substances until they became a fine powder called bhasma, “ash”. Mercury was usually “bound” with sulphur as black or red mercuric sulphide, and sublimed preparations such as rasasindūra and makaradhvaja (which includes gold) became among the most esteemed medicines of the later tradition. Empirical tests—that the ash should not glitter, should lodge in the lines of the fingers, should float on water and should not revert to metal—were used to decide whether the process was complete. The alchemists worked in a consecrated laboratory with a characteristic range of crucibles, furnaces, sand-baths and distillation and sublimation apparatus; their production of metallic zinc by downward distillation, attested archaeologically at Zawar in Rajasthan, is discussed in Volume 14.

These processes are of real interest to the historian of chemistry: they show long experience of the behaviour of metals and their compounds under heat and with different reagents. But the tradition’s claim that śodhana and māraṇa remove toxicity rests on its own theory, not on toxicological evidence. They convert metals into oxides, sulphides and other compounds whose toxicity varies; lead and arsenic remain lead and arsenic. The classical tests measure fineness and appearance, not safety.

docs.title: 9.5 Rasaśāstra Today
docs.text:
The tradition did not die out. Families of physicians known for their mercurial preparations (rasavaidyas) continued to practise into the twentieth century. Rasaśāstra is now taught as a subject (together with pharmaceutics, as rasaśāstra and bhaiṣajyakalpanā) in Indian Āyurvedic colleges, and “herbo-mineral” products are manufactured on a large scale under government licence; they are among the most expensive Ayurvedic medicines on the market, and their prestige rests on the tradition’s own claims about processing. Supporters argue that properly prepared bhasmas are safe because of their processing, and point to analytical studies showing that some consist of very fine particles, in some cases in the nanometre range, and that mercury in rasasindūra is largely in the form of mercuric sulphide, which is less readily absorbed than many other mercury compounds. Some have gone further and called bhasmas an “ancient nanomedicine”.

Animal experiments with some bhasmas have been published, mostly by Indian laboratories, and some report little toxicity at the doses tested. Such studies are of limited value: they are often short, use small numbers of animals, test a single batch of a product, and do not measure the accumulation of metals in the body over months or years of use.

These arguments do not establish safety. Particle size says nothing about toxicity, except that very fine particles may be absorbed more easily. The toxicity of mercury sulphide preparations taken repeatedly is not well studied. Lead, arsenic and copper preparations have no safe level of use as medicines. Most importantly, the products actually sold are often contaminated or mislabelled, and their content varies from batch to batch.

The evidence from outside the tradition is consistent. In a study published in 2004, Robert Saper and colleagues bought seventy Ayurvedic products in shops in the Boston area and found that one in five contained lead, mercury or arsenic, at levels that, if the products were taken as recommended, could exceed regulatory safety limits (Saper et al. 2004). A larger study of products bought over the internet and made in both India and the United States, published in 2008, found detectable metals in about one in five products, and more often in rasaśāstra products than in others (Saper et al. 2008). Public health agencies have repeatedly reported lead poisoning in people taking Ayurvedic medicines, including pregnant women and children (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004).

docs.title: 9.6 Alchemy and the History of Indian Science
docs.text: The modern study of Indian alchemy began with the chemist Prafulla Chandra Ray, whose History of Hindu Chemistry (Ray 1902–1909) presented the Sanskrit texts as evidence that India had possessed a chemistry of its own, and later historians have emphasised their religious and tantric setting and corrected their dates (White 1996; Wujastyk 1984). That history, and the place of alchemy in the history of Indian chemistry and metallurgy, are the subject of Volume 14, Rasāyana.

docs.title: 9.7 Significance
docs.text:
The alchemical tradition of medieval India is a major chapter in the history of science and religion. It developed apparatus and techniques for distillation, sublimation and calcination; it built up empirical knowledge of the behaviour of metals, minerals and salts; it produced metallic zinc; and it expressed in its own idiom a striking vision of the human body as something that could be perfected. Its integration into medicine, however, introduced into the pharmacopoeia some of the most toxic substances known. To recognise both of these facts is to take the tradition seriously.

Summary

Rasaśāstra grew from about the tenth century within Śaiva and Siddha religious traditions, as an alchemy that sought both gold and an immortal body, and over time became a pharmacy whose metallic preparations entered everyday Āyurvedic practice. Its laboratory knowledge, including the distillation of zinc, belongs to the history of chemistry, and its attribution to the philosopher Nāgārjuna rests on confusion. Its claim that processing removes the toxicity of metals is not supported by evidence, and its products are a documented cause of poisoning.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: White’s The Alchemical Body is the essential study (White 1996); Ray’s History of Hindu Chemistry remains valuable for its texts and translations (Ray 1902–1909); on the “alchemical ghost” see Wujastyk (Wujastyk 1984). On heavy metals in Ayurvedic products see (Saper et al. 2004, 2008; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Diagnosis and Prognosis
docs.text:
rogam ādau parīkṣeta tato ’nantaram auṣadham tataḥ karma bhiṣak paścāj jñānapūrvaṃ samācaret The physician should first examine the disease, then the remedy; and only then, with knowledge, undertake treatment.

— Caraka Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 20.20

docs.title: 10.1 The Means of Examination
docs.text: The compendia insist that treatment must follow examination, and that the physician must examine both the disease and the patient. Each describes the means by which the physician gains knowledge in a slightly different way. Caraka applies his general theory of knowledge to medicine: a disease is known by authoritative instruction, by perception and by inference (Ca.Vi. 4). Perception uses all the senses, and inference reasons from signs to what cannot be perceived, such as the state of the digestive fire from the capacity to digest food. Suśruta names six means, the five senses and questioning (Su.Sū. 10), and Vāgbhaṭa reduces them to three: the patient is to be examined by sight, touch and questioning (darśana, sparśana, praśna) (AH Sū. 1.22).

docs.title: 10.2 Examination of the Patient
docs.text:
Caraka gives a tenfold scheme for the examination of the patient (Ca.Vi. 8.94; Table 10.1). Its purpose is to judge the patient’s strength, so that the strength of the treatment can be matched to it.

Table 10.1. The tenfold examination of the patient (Ca.Vi. 8.94) Factor What is assessed 1 prakṛti the patient’s natural constitution 2 vikṛti the disorder and its strength 3 sāra the “essence”: which bodily constituent is of the highest quality 4 saṃhanana compactness of the body 5 pramāṇa bodily measurements and proportions 6 sātmya habituation: what the patient is accustomed to 7 sattva strength of mind 8 āhāraśakti capacity to take and digest food 9 vyāyāmaśakti capacity for exercise 10 vayas age

Caraka adds that the physician must examine not only the patient but everything relevant to treatment: the cause (kāraṇa), the instrument (the physician himself), the drugs, the place and the time, the effort required and the expected result (Ca.Vi. 8). Drugs are to be examined for their origin, quality and suitability; places for their nature as dry, marshy or moderate land and for the diseases and habits of their inhabitants; and time both as season and as the stage of the patient’s illness. The examination of the patient is thus embedded in a much wider assessment of the circumstances of treatment.

docs.title: 10.2.1 Measurement and Proportion
docs.text: Caraka’s examination of “measure” (pramāṇa) assumes that each person’s body can be measured in units of his own finger-breadth (aṅgula). He gives the normal dimensions of many parts of the body in these units—the feet, shanks, knees, thighs, chest, neck, face and so on—and states that the height of a well-proportioned person is eighty-four finger-breadths, equal to the span of his outstretched arms (Ca.Vi. 8.117). A person whose proportions match these norms is said to enjoy long life, strength and prosperity. The idea of a body measured by its own units has parallels in Indian iconometry, the rules for the proportions of images, and in other ancient traditions.

docs.title: 10.2.2 The Use of All the Senses
docs.text: The compendia expect the physician to use every sense. Hearing detects the sounds of the joints, intestines and breathing and the quality of the voice; touch, the temperature and texture of the skin and the pulsation of the vessels; sight, colour, shape, growth and the appearance of excreta; smell, the odour of the body, breath, wounds and excreta; and taste—inferred, the texts say, from such signs as the attraction of ants or flies to the patient’s urine or body, since tasting directly is improper. Questioning supplies what the senses cannot: the patient’s history, sensations, habits and desires.

docs.title: 10.3 Examination of the Disease
docs.text: The disease itself is known through its cause, its premonitory signs, its manifest signs, the response to trial treatment and its course of development (nidānapañcaka, Chapter 3).

docs.title: 10.3.1 The Therapeutic Test (Upaśaya)
docs.text: The commentators classify the “therapeutic test” carefully. A measure may give relief because it is opposed to the cause of the disease, opposed to the disease itself, or opposed to both; and in each case the measure may be a drug, a food or a mode of conduct. To these Cakrapāṇidatta adds measures that act by producing an apparently similar effect—as when vomiting is treated by an emetic—giving eighteen kinds of upaśaya in all. A response to such a trial helps to identify the doṣa at work when the signs are ambiguous; failure to respond (anupaśaya) is equally informative.

docs.title: 10.3.2 The Stages of Disease (Kriyākāla)
docs.text:
The surgical school describes the development of a disease in six stages, each of which is a “time for action” (kriyākāla) (Su.Sū. 21; Table 10.2 and Figure 10.1). The scheme is often attributed to Caraka in modern books, but it is Suśruta’s.

Table 10.2. The six “times for action” (Su.Sū. 21) Stage Description 1 saṃcaya accumulation of the doṣa in its own seat 2 prakopa aggravation of the accumulated doṣa 3 prasara spread of the doṣa through the body 4 sthānasaṃśraya lodging of the doṣa in a particular place; premonitory signs appear 5 vyakti manifestation of the disease 6 bheda differentiation of the disease into its varieties; chronicity or complications Figure 10.1. Suśruta’s six “times for action” (kriyākāla) in the development of a disease (Su.Sū. 21).

The point of the scheme is therapeutic: the earlier the stage at which the physician intervenes, the easier the treatment. Later writers explain why a spreading doṣa lodges in one place rather than another by a weakness of that place (khavaiguṇya), caused by heredity, previous disease, injury or habit.

docs.title: 10.3.3 Signs, Tests and Differential Diagnosis
docs.text:
Caraka is aware that the same sign may belong to several diseases, and that one disease may produce another. In the first chapter of the Nidānasthāna he explains how the five means of knowing a disease work together, and how the physician should distinguish between diseases with similar signs. Where the signs remain ambiguous, the therapeutic test described above helps to decide. The detailed descriptions of the healthy constitution, of the normal measures of the body and of the excellence of its constituents (Chapter 2) serve the same purpose: only by knowing the normal can the physician recognise the abnormal.

Questioning (praśna) covers the patient’s country, season, habits, diet, previous illnesses, the onset and course of the present complaint, and the patient’s own sensations. The compendia insist that the physician should listen carefully and examine thoroughly before forming a judgement, and that he should not be misled by the appearance of a patient (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 10.3.4 Examining a Wound
docs.text: The surgical school developed its own methods of examination. Suśruta teaches the surgeon to examine a wound by its site, shape, size, colour, discharge, smell and pain, and to recognise from these the doṣas involved and whether the wound is clean, infected or healing. He describes the discharges of wounds at length—watery, bloody, purulent, oily and so on—and the smells associated with each doṣa, and lists signs that a wound will not heal: a foul cadaverous smell, extreme pain, a wound over a vital point, and others. Many of these observations correspond to what a modern surgeon would look for in an infected or non-healing wound.

docs.title: 10.3.5 Signs in Pregnancy
docs.text: The texts describe the signs of conception and pregnancy and claim to predict the sex of the child from the mother’s symptoms and preferences: a heaviness or enlargement on the right side, for example, was taken to indicate a son. Such predictions have no reliable basis and, given the history of sex-selection in India, should be regarded purely as part of the history of belief.

docs.title: 10.4 Prognosis
docs.text:
Before treating, the physician must decide whether a disease is curable. Caraka divides diseases into the easily curable (sukhasādhya), the curable with difficulty (kṛcchrasādhya), the “maintainable” (yāpya)—which can be held in check but not cured—and the incurable (anupakramya or asādhya) (Ca.Sū. 10). The Indriyasthāna (Chapter 3) is devoted to the signs of approaching death.

The factors that make a disease easy or hard to cure are listed in detail. A disease is easily curable when its causes, premonitory signs and signs are few, when it is not of the same nature as the patient’s constitution, the season or the patient’s age, when it affects one channel and one doṣa, when it is recent, and when the patient is young, strong, self-controlled and supplied with the four “feet” of treatment; the more of these conditions are reversed, the harder the cure (Ca.Sū. 10). The physician is warned that a disease which is curable may become incurable if neglected, and that a “maintainable” disease, kept in check by treatment, will return if treatment is stopped.

The compendia advise the physician not to undertake the treatment of incurable diseases. The reason given is partly the patient’s welfare, but largely the physician’s: failure would damage his reputation and expose him to blame. This is very different from modern medical ethics, which recognises a duty of care to the dying, including relief of pain and honest communication. The classical texts should be read in the light of the conditions of their time, when a physician’s livelihood depended on his reputation and treatment was a private contract; Dagmar Wujastyk discusses the rule and the commentators’ arguments about it (Wujastyk 2012).

docs.title: 10.5 The Eightfold Examination
docs.text: In modern Āyurvedic practice the best-known scheme of examination is the “eightfold examination” (aṣṭavidhaparīkṣā): of the pulse (nāḍī), urine (mūtra), stool (mala), tongue (jihvā), voice (śabda), touch (sparśa), eyes (dṛk) and general appearance (ākṛti). It is not found in the classical compendia. It is given in this form in the Yogaratnākara, a compendium from Maharashtra of about the seventeenth or eighteenth century, and became standard through it.

docs.title: 10.5.1 The Pulse (Nāḍīparīkṣā)
docs.text:
Pulse diagnosis, now regarded by many as the hallmark of the Āyurvedic physician, is absent from the works of Caraka, Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa. It appears first in Sanskrit medical literature in works of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries—in the Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā and in short treatises on the pulse attributed to Kaṇāda and others—and was elaborated in later works such as the Bhāvaprakāśa and the Yogaratnākara. Its late appearance has led historians to ask whether it was influenced by the pulse lore of Greco-Arabic (Unani) medicine, which was well established in India by then, or by the Tibetan and Chinese traditions, in which pulse diagnosis is highly developed. The question is not settled (Meulenbeld 1999–2002).

The texts describe feeling the radial pulse at the root of the thumb, usually on the right hand of a man and the left of a woman, with three fingers. The pulse under the index finger is associated with vāta, under the middle finger with pitta and under the ring finger with kapha, and the movement of the pulse is compared to the gaits of animals: a vāta pulse moves like a snake or a leech, a pitta pulse like a frog, crow or quail, a kapha pulse like a swan or peacock. The texts also describe pulses that signify approaching death.

Some modern books and practitioners attach to the Āyurvedic pulse a scheme in which particular finger positions and depths reveal the state of particular organs (lung, liver, kidney and so on). That scheme belongs to Chinese medicine, not to the Sanskrit sources.

docs.title: 10.5.2 Urine and the Oil-drop Test
docs.text: The later texts give urine an importance it lacks in the compendia. The Yogaratnākara describes the examination of a morning sample, and a test in which a drop of oil is placed on the urine and the way it spreads is observed: spreading like a snake indicates vāta, like an umbrella pitta, like a pearl kapha; rapid spreading is a favourable sign and sinking unfavourable. A similar test is used in Siddha medicine (Chapter 11). Uroscopy was also a central diagnostic method of Greco-Arabic and medieval European medicine.

docs.title: 10.5.3 Pulse and Urine in Comparative Perspective
docs.text: Pulse and urine were central to diagnosis in several medical traditions. Galen wrote a series of treatises on the pulse, distinguishing its size, speed, frequency and hardness; Arabic physicians developed this lore further, and it reached India with Unani medicine (Chapter 11). Chinese medicine developed an elaborate pulse diagnosis at three positions on each wrist, codified in the Classic of the Pulse (Maijing) of the third century CE, and Tibetan medicine adopted a related system. Inspection of urine (uroscopy) was the emblem of the physician in medieval Europe and the Islamic world. All these systems drew genuine information from the pulse and the urine—their rate, rhythm, colour and turbidity—but they also read into them far more than they could reliably show.

docs.title: 10.5.4 Tongue, Voice, Skin, Eyes and Form
docs.text:
The remaining items of the eightfold examination record signs that any attentive physician would observe: a coated tongue, a hoarse or weak voice, dry or moist skin, the colour of the eyes and the build of the body. The texts relate each to the doṣas.

None of these methods—pulse reading, urine inspection or the oil-drop test—has been shown to diagnose disease reliably. The few studies that have asked whether different practitioners examining the same patient reach the same conclusion have found agreement that varies widely and is often modest (Kurande et al. 2013), and nothing in them supports the claims made in popular books that the pulse can reveal pregnancy, cancer, diabetes or the state of particular organs.

docs.title: 10.6 Reasoning in Diagnosis
docs.text:
Caraka gives a special place among the means of knowledge to “reasoning” (yukti), the faculty that sees how many factors combine to produce a result. His example is agricultural: a crop results from the combination of water, ploughing, seed and season; in the same way, an embryo results from the combination of the six factors, and recovery from the combination of physician, drugs, attendant and patient (Ca.Sū. 11.23–25). Diagnosis, on this view, is not the recognition of a single sign but the weighing of many—constitution, season, age, strength, cause, signs and the response to treatment—to reach a judgement about what is happening and what will help. The commentators debated whether yukti is a separate means of knowledge or a form of inference, but the compendia’s emphasis on it captures something essential about clinical judgement in any tradition.

The texts are equally aware of the limits of judgement. They warn that a physician who does not know the disease, even if he knows the drugs, will fail; that a physician who acts in haste, without examining the patient, kills him; and that one who knows the disease and the patient but not the proper time and measure of treatment is no better. These warnings frame the long lists of signs and tests described in this chapter.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Experience and the Missing Case History
docs.text:
Among the four qualities of the good physician Caraka names wide practical experience, the physician’s having “often seen the work done” (Ca.Sū. 9.6). Yet the Sanskrit medical literature records almost none of that experience in the form of individual cases. The compendia describe diseases and treatments in general terms; they do not tell the story of a particular patient, with the course of the illness day by day and the outcome. The contrast with other traditions is striking. The Hippocratic Epidemics preserve dozens of case histories, many ending in death. Abū Bakr al-Rāzī kept notes of his own patients, which his pupils gathered after his death (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007), and Chinese physicians from the Song period onwards published collections of case records.

The nearest Indian equivalents lie outside the learned compendia. The Buddhist monastic code tells the stories of Jīvaka’s cures (Chapter 1), but as narratives that exalt a physician and teach a rule, not as clinical records. Later practitioners kept private lists of “tested” formulae (anubhūta yoga), and Persian-writing ḥakīms compiled collections of remedies they had tried; some of these record which patient a remedy was given to. Case reports in the modern sense appear in Āyurvedic journals only in the twentieth century, under the influence of Western medicine.

Why this should be so is not certain. The authority of the compendia rested on their claim to transmit a teaching handed down from the sages, and an individual physician’s cases would have added little to that claim. The prognosis of the texts, with its general rules for judging curability, also took the place that a record of outcomes might have filled. Whatever the reason, the absence of case histories means that historians know much more about what the texts prescribed than about what physicians actually did, and how often their treatments succeeded. Modern Āyurvedic research faces the same gap in another form: claims of efficacy based on a practitioner’s experience are hard to assess without systematic records of what happened to all the patients treated, not only to those who recovered.

docs.title: 10.7 Diagnosis in Modern Āyurvedic Practice
docs.text:
Āyurvedic physicians trained in modern colleges learn both the classical methods and the elements of modern clinical examination, and many routinely order blood tests, urine analysis and imaging. In practice, a modern Āyurvedic diagnosis often combines a biomedical diagnosis—diabetes, osteoarthritis, psoriasis—with an assessment of the patient’s constitution and the doṣas involved, which guides the choice of diet and remedies. Electronic devices that claim to read the doṣas from the pulse have been marketed; there is no good evidence that they measure anything meaningful about the patient’s health. At the other end of the spectrum, some hereditary physicians rely almost entirely on the pulse and on questioning.

The juxtaposition of the two systems in a single consultation raises practical questions. When the Āyurvedic and biomedical assessments point in different directions—for example, when a patient with diabetes is told by one system that his condition is under control and by the other that it is not—the patient needs to know which to trust. For conditions where effective modern treatment exists, the biomedical assessment must take priority.

docs.title: 10.8 Assessment
docs.text:
The diagnostic teaching of the compendia has real strengths: it insists that examination comes before treatment; it considers the patient’s constitution, age, habits, strength and mind as well as the disease; and it attends carefully to the history and course of an illness. These are the virtues of good clinical practice in any tradition. Its weakness is that its categories—the doṣas and their combinations—and its signs were never tested against independent evidence of what was wrong with the patient. Modern medicine has the means to do this, and has shown that many diseases cannot be detected without laboratory tests and imaging. Diagnosis is therefore the area in which the traditional and modern systems are least interchangeable.

Summary

The compendia require the physician to examine both patient and disease before he treats, to weigh constitution, strength, age and habit as well as signs, and to judge in advance whether a disease can be cured. The methods most associated with Āyurvedic diagnosis today, the pulse and the eightfold examination, are later additions of the thirteenth to eighteenth centuries and have not been shown to be reliable. The Sanskrit tradition’s lack of case histories means that we know far more about what physicians were told to do than about what they did.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Caraka’s Vimāna- and Indriyasthāna are the main classical sources (in the translations of Sharma and Wujastyk (Sharma 1981–1994; Wujastyk 2003)); Meulenbeld discusses the later works on pulse and urine (Meulenbeld 1999–2002).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Siddha, Unani, Sowa-Rigpa and Local Health Traditions
docs.text:
mikiṉum kuṟaiyiṉum nōyceyyum nūlōr vaḷimutalā eṇṇiya mūṉṟu The three that the authors of the treatises count, beginning with wind, cause disease when they are in excess or in deficiency.

— Tirukkuṟaḷ 941

docs.title: 11.1 A Plural Medical Landscape
docs.text: Sanskrit Āyurveda was never the only form of learned medicine in India, still less the only form of healing. Alongside it, and in constant exchange with it, there developed a Tamil medical tradition, now called Siddha; Greco-Arabic medicine, known in India as Unani (Yūnānī, “Greek”); and, in the Himalayan regions, the Tibetan medical tradition called Sowa-Rigpa. Beneath and around all of these lay the healing knowledge of households, midwives, bonesetters, snakebite healers and the herbalists of forest and hill communities. The Government of India now recognises Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Sowa-Rigpa, together with Yoga, Naturopathy and Homoeopathy, under the Ministry of AYUSH (Section 12.3). This chapter introduces Siddha, Unani and Sowa-Rigpa and the local traditions on their own terms. Each deserves fuller treatment than is possible here.

docs.title: 11.2.1 The Siddhars and the Literature
docs.text:
Siddha medicine (Tamil cittamaruttuvam) is the learned medical tradition of the Tamil-speaking south. It takes its name from the cittar (Sanskrit siddha), “perfected ones”: yogis, alchemists and poets who were believed to have attained bodily immortality and supernatural powers, and to whom a large body of Tamil verse on medicine, alchemy, yoga and religion is attributed. Tradition counts eighteen great Siddhars, though the lists differ from source to source. Agastya (Tamil Akattiyar), the sage who in Sanskrit and Tamil legend brought culture to the south, is regarded as the founder of the medical tradition; Bhogar (Pōkar), Tirumūlar, Yūki, Tēraiyar, Korakkar and Pulippāṇi are among the other names associated with medical works.

The dates of this literature are difficult to establish. The Tirumantiram attributed to Tirumūlar, an important early Tamil text on yoga and Śaiva doctrine (perhaps of the later first millennium CE), contains verses on the body and its preservation but is not a medical treatise. Most of the medical poems attributed to the Siddhars are written in a language and style that suggest composition in the second millennium, many of them probably between the fifteenth and the nineteenth centuries; some are known only from nineteenth- and twentieth-century printed editions. The attribution of works of several thousand verses to individual Siddhars—the “Agastya 12,000” or “Bhogar 7,000”—is traditional. Richard Weiss has shown how, in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Tamil physicians and publishers shaped this literature into a self-conscious “Siddha system” and presented it as an ancient Tamil science distinct from, and older than, Sanskrit Āyurveda, as part of the wider Tamil revival (Weiss 2009). Kamil Zvelebil’s study of the Siddha poets remains a useful introduction to the wider tradition (Zvelebil 1996).

docs.title: 11.2.2 Early Tamil Evidence
docs.text:
The earliest Tamil evidence for a learned medicine is indirect. The anthologies of early Tamil poetry mention healing herbs and the dressing of wounds only in passing. The Tirukkuṟaḷ, the collection of 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love (c. 5th century CE; the date is disputed), is more explicit. One of its chapters (ch. 95, Maruntu, “Medicine”) consists of ten couplets on health, most of them about moderation in eating and eating only when the previous meal has been digested. Its first couplet (Kuṟaḷ 941), quoted at the head of this chapter, says that the three beginning with wind, as the authors of the treatises (nūlōr) count them, cause disease when they are in excess or in deficiency. Another (Kuṟaḷ 949) tells the learned physician to weigh the patient’s condition, the extent of the disease and the time before he acts. The last (Kuṟaḷ 950) divides medicine into four parts: the patient, the healer, the remedy and the attendant at the bedside. These correspond to the three doṣas and to the “four feet” of treatment of the Caraka Saṃhitā (Ca.Sū. 9; Chapter 3).

The couplets show that by the middle of the first millennium a humoral medicine, which the poet attributes to the authors of books, was known in the Tamil country in terms that match the Sanskrit compendia. This evidence does not settle the modern argument in either direction. It does not show an independent Tamil humoral theory older than the Sanskrit, and it does not show that Tamil medicine was a mere copy, since it tells us nothing about what Tamil physicians themselves wrote.

docs.title: 11.2.3 The Medical Corpus
docs.text:
The medical works attributed to the Siddhars are almost all in verse. They are usually known by the name of their supposed author and the number of their verses. They range from general works on therapeutics (vaittiyam) to treatises on the pulse, on the examination of urine, on the preparation of metals and minerals, and on the properties of drugs; collections of single formulae circulated in great numbers. A work on diagnosis and the classification of diseases attributed to Yūki Muṉivar (the Yūki Vaittiya Cintāmaṇi) is regarded as the source of the traditional Siddha count of 4,448 diseases, a figure that modern textbooks still repeat.

Much of this verse is deliberately obscure. The poets use a coded technical vocabulary (paripāṣai), in which drugs and processes are named by allusive synonyms, so that a text could be understood only with a teacher’s key. The code kept knowledge within lineages and gave the teacher authority. It also makes many drug identifications uncertain today.

Manuscripts survive in family collections, in the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library in Chennai and in the Sarasvati Mahal Library at Thanjavur. There the Maratha ruler Serfoji II (r. 1798–1832) had medical works copied and the prescriptions of his court physicians collected. Most Siddha texts reached their present form only when they were printed, from the late nineteenth century onwards. Their editors were often practitioners who rearranged, supplemented and sometimes rewrote them; much of Weiss’s study is an account of this process (Weiss 2009). Modern college teaching relies on twentieth-century textbooks that arrange the material under headings borrowed partly from Western medicine, such as materia medica (kuṇapāṭam), physiology and pathology.

docs.title: 11.2.4 Theory
docs.text:
Siddha theory shares much with Āyurveda: the five elements; three humours (together mukkuṟṟam, “the three faults”); seven bodily constituents; the urges that must not be suppressed (fourteen in the Siddha lists); and the importance of diet, season and constitution. It also has distinctive features. The human being is described as composed of ninety-six principles (tattuvam), a scheme derived from Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy that includes the elements, senses and organs of action, the inner faculties, the vital airs and channels, the sheaths of the self, the bodily “supports” (ātāram), the humours, the qualities, the passions and the states of consciousness. The usual modern list is summarised in Table 11.1.

Table 11.1. The ninety-six principles (tattuvam) as usually listed in modern Siddha textbooks Group No. Group No. elements (pūtam) 5 sheaths of the self (kōcam) 5 sense organs (poṟi) 5 supports or centres (ātāram) 6 sense objects (pulaṉ) 5 regions (maṇṭalam: fire, sun, moon) 3 organs of action (kaṉmēntiriyam) 5 impurities (malam) 3 actions of these organs 5 humours (tōṭam) 3 inner faculties (karaṇam) 4 desires (ēṭaṇai) 3 knowledge (aṟivu) 1 qualities (kuṇam) 3 channels (nāṭi) 10 deeds (viṉai: good and bad) 2 vital airs (vāyu) 10 passions (rākam) 8 receptacles (ācayam) 5 states of consciousness (avattai) 5

The correspondence between the body and the universe—summed up in the Tamil phrase aṇṭattil uḷḷatu piṇṭattilum uṇṭu, “what is in the macrocosm is in the microcosm”—is a favourite theme of the Siddha poets.

docs.title: 11.2.5 Humours, Constituents and Tastes
docs.text:
In Tamil the three humours are called vaḷi (wind), aḻal (heat or fire) and aiyam (phlegm), or by the Sanskrit-derived names vātam, pittam and kapam. Siddha writers hold that in a healthy person the three stand in a fixed proportion, which modern textbooks give as one to one-half to one-quarter and which the physician is said to feel in the pulse. Vātam has ten forms, the ten vital airs of the yogic texts (Table 11.1). Pittam and kapam have five each, and these correspond closely to the five forms of pitta and kapha in the Sanskrit compendia (Chapter 2).

The seven bodily constituents (uṭal kaṭṭukaḷ) are chyle (cāram), blood (ceṉṉīr), flesh (ūṉ), fat (koḻuppu), bone (eṉpu), marrow (mūḷai) and the reproductive fluid (cukkilam in men, curōṇitam in women), the same sequence as the Sanskrit dhātus. There are six tastes (aṟucuvai): sweet, sour, salt, bitter, pungent and astringent. As in Āyurveda, each is formed from two of the elements.

The differences from Āyurveda lie less in these lists than in their setting. They include the ninety-six principles, the yogic physiology of channels and centres, the alchemical pharmacy described below, and a Tamil technical vocabulary that grew up alongside the Sanskrit one.

The Siddha poets also took a distinctive attitude to the body. Much Indian religious literature treats the body as impure and an obstacle to liberation. The Siddhars made its preservation a spiritual aim. In a verse of the Tirumantiram that modern Siddha writers often cite (verse 724 in the usual numbering), Tirumūlar says that when the body perishes the life perishes with it, and true knowledge cannot be reached; having learned how to foster the body, he fostered it, and so fostered life. Yoga, breath control, diet and alchemical medicines all served this end. A perfected, undecaying body was the goal of the most ambitious practitioners, and medicine in the ordinary sense was the lower application of the same knowledge.

docs.title: 11.2.6 Diagnosis
docs.text:
Siddha diagnosis uses an “eightfold examination” (eṇvakait tērvu) of pulse (nāṭi), touch (paricam), tongue (nā), colour (niṟam), speech (moḻi), eyes (viḻi), stool (malam) and urine (mūttiram). Siddha physicians place particular weight on the pulse and on the examination of urine, including the observation of a drop of oil placed on it (neykkuṟi), a test similar to that of the late Sanskrit texts (Chapter 10). Like the Sanskrit pulse and urine tests, these methods have not been shown to be reliable means of diagnosis.

Reading the pulse is the most prestigious diagnostic skill. The physician feels the radial pulse with three fingers, as in the late Sanskrit texts, reads vātam under the index finger, pittam under the middle finger and kapam under the ring finger, and judges the relation between the three against the healthy proportion. The examination of urine (nīrkkuṟi) considers colour, density, smell, froth and deposit in a sample collected early in the morning, before the oil-drop test is made. Works on the pulse and the urine are attributed to several Siddhars, among them Tēraiyar.

docs.title: 11.2.7 Three Kinds of Treatment
docs.text: Siddha writers divide treatment into three classes. “Divine” medicine (tēva maruttuvam) comprises the potent metal and mineral preparations, such as centūram, paṟpam and kaṭṭu; “human” medicine (māṉiṭa maruttuvam) the herbal preparations, such as juices, decoctions, powders and medicated oils; and “demonic” medicine (acura maruttuvam) incision, cautery, leeches, caustics and other surgical measures. The ranking shows the prestige of the alchemical tradition, in which the mineral medicines are the highest form of the art. It also explains why the safety debate about Siddha has centred on those medicines (see the note below).

docs.title: 11.2.8 Pharmacy and Alchemy
docs.text:
Siddha pharmacy is noted for its extensive use of metals and minerals. Medicines are classified into thirty-two forms for internal use and thirty-two for external use. The internal forms include, besides juices, decoctions, powders, pills, confections and medicated oils, preparations of metals and minerals such as centūram (red calcined preparations), paṟpam (white calcined preparations), kaṭṭu (“bound” preparations of mercury and other substances) and kaḷaṅku. The tradition recognises sixty-four pāṣāṇams, “stones” or mineral poisons, thirty-two natural and thirty-two prepared. Among the latter are vīram (mercuric chloride, corrosive sublimate), pūram (mercurous chloride, calomel) and kauri pāṣāṇam (arsenic trioxide). These are among the most toxic substances known.

Siddha alchemy also aimed at rejuvenation and immortality. The regimen called kāyakaṟpam (“making the body last an aeon”) combined yogic discipline with special diets and preparations, sometimes taken in seclusion; the legendary muppu, a “universal salt” whose composition was kept secret, was said to be its key. A celebrated legend attributes to Bhogar the image of Murukaṉ at the hill temple of Palani, said to be made of nine pāṣāṇams (navapāṣāṇam); the composition of the image has never been verified.

Health and Safety Note

Siddha preparations containing mercury, arsenic, lead and other metals or mineral poisons, including the pāṣāṇams, can cause serious poisoning. The modern hospital use of arsenic trioxide for one form of leukaemia, under specialist monitoring, does not make traditional preparations safe. See Chapter 9 and Section 12.7.

docs.title: 11.2.9 External Therapies
docs.text: Siddha practice includes a range of external therapies: medicated oil massage, a form of manipulative massage called tokkaṇam with several distinct techniques (pressing, squeezing, kneading, tapping and others), fomentation with heated bundles of herbs, poultices, medicated baths, fumigation, and the application of caustics, leeches and cautery. The thirty-two external forms of medicine in the Siddha classification include many of these.

docs.title: 11.2.10 Varmam
docs.text: Varmam (Sanskrit marman) is the Tamil lore of vital points, shared with the martial art varmakkalai and with the kaḷarippayaṟṟu tradition of Kerala. Modern Siddha texts usually speak of 108 points, of which twelve are “striking” points (paṭu varmam) whose injury may be fatal and ninety-six are “touching” points (toṭu varmam). Practitioners use pressure and manipulation at these points to treat injuries, pain and paralysis and to revive the unconscious. The tradition is old and was transmitted largely orally and within families, often among non-brahmin communities. Its therapeutic claims have not been adequately tested.

docs.title: 11.2.11 Siddha Today
docs.text:
Siddha medicine is taught in government and private colleges in Tamil Nadu and practised in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Puducherry, Sri Lanka and the Tamil diaspora. Its practitioners include both formally trained graduates and hereditary physicians, and much Siddha knowledge is still held in family palm-leaf manuscripts, many of them uncatalogued.

Institutional Siddha is largely a twentieth-century creation. In the Madras Presidency, after the report of the Usman Committee (1923; Chapter 12), a government School of Indian Medicine opened in Madras in the mid-1920s. It taught Āyurveda, Siddha and Unani together, with elements of Western medicine. A separate government college for Siddha was founded at Palayamkottai in 1964. Siddha later acquired its own pharmacopoeia and a National Institute of Siddha at Chennai (opened in 2005). Siddha research was administered jointly with Āyurveda by the Central Council for Research in Ayurveda and Siddha until 2010, when a separate Central Council for Research in Siddha was created. In Sri Lanka, Siddha forms part of the state system of indigenous medicine and is taught at the University of Jaffna.

Weiss’s study of the modern history of Siddha shows how its identity was shaped by the politics of language and caste in twentieth-century Tamil Nadu (Weiss 2009). Its advocates presented it as the original medicine of the Tamils, older than Sanskrit Āyurveda and free from brahmanical domination; Siddha physicians were often non-brahmins, and the Siddhar poets themselves had denounced caste and ritual. The government recognition of Siddha as a system separate from Āyurveda, in the decades after independence, was the result of this movement. Historically, the boundary between Tamil and Sanskrit medicine was more porous than these claims suggest: Siddha theory shares much with Āyurveda, and Tamil physicians long used Sanskrit texts. But the movement drew attention to a large body of Tamil medical knowledge that the Sanskrit-centred history of Indian medicine had ignored.

docs.title: 11.3.1 Origins
docs.text:
Unani (ṭibb-i yūnānī, “Greek medicine”) is the Greco-Arabic medical tradition. Its theoretical foundations are those of Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE) and Galen (129–c. 216 CE), which were translated into Arabic in Abbasid Baghdad in the eighth to tenth centuries and developed by physicians of the Islamic world writing in Arabic and Persian. Among them were Abū Bakr al-Rāzī (Rhazes, c. 854–925), whose al-Ḥāwī (“The Comprehensive Book”) is a vast collection of clinical notes and excerpts; Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna, 980–1037), whose al-Qānūn fī al-ṭibb (“The Canon of Medicine”) became the standard textbook from Central Asia to Europe; and Abū al-Qāsim al-Zahrāwī (Albucasis, d. c. 1013), whose al-Taṣrīf contains a celebrated illustrated treatise on surgery (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007). The Islamic medical tradition itself drew on Indian as well as Greek and Persian sources (Chapter 5).

Greek medicine reached the Islamic world through the translation movement of the eighth to tenth centuries, in which Christian, Jewish and Muslim scholars put most of the Greek medical corpus into Syriac and Arabic. The most prolific translator, Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq (d. 873), and his circle rendered almost the whole of Galen (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007). The same milieu took in Indian medicine. The Firdaws al-ḥikma (“Paradise of Wisdom”) of ʿAlī ibn Sahl Rabban al-Ṭabarī, completed about 850, is mainly an account of the Greek system, but it ends with a long summary of Indian medicine drawn from Caraka, Suśruta and other Sanskrit authorities (Ullmann 1978). The Unani that later came to India had therefore already absorbed some Indian learning.

Its most influential synthesis, Ibn Sīnā’s Canon, is in five books: general principles of physiology, pathology, hygiene and therapy; simple drugs; diseases particular to each organ, from head to foot; diseases not confined to one organ, such as fevers, swellings, wounds and poisons; and compound drugs. This progression, from principles to particular diseases and remedies, became the model for later Unani textbooks in India.

docs.title: 11.3.2 Unani in India
docs.text:
Physicians trained in this tradition came to India with the Ghaznavids and the Delhi Sultanate from the eleventh and thirteenth centuries, and the tradition flourished under the patronage of the Sultans, the regional Muslim kingdoms and the Mughals. Much of its Indian literature is in Persian. Indian physicians wrote major works, such as the Ṭibb-i Akbarī of Muḥammad Akbar Arzānī (early eighteenth century), and engaged with Āyurveda: the Maʿdan al-Shifāʾ-i Sikandar-Shāhī (1512) of Miyān Bhuwa presented Sanskrit medical learning in Persian, and Unani pharmacy absorbed many Indian drugs. Hindu physicians learned and practised Unani, and Muslim physicians used Āyurvedic remedies.

Interest in Indian drugs among Islamic scholars long predates the Delhi Sultanate. The polymath al-Bīrūnī, who travelled in India in the early eleventh century with the armies of Maḥmūd of Ghazna and learned Sanskrit, wrote both a celebrated description of India and a work on pharmacy (Kitāb al-ṣaydana) in which he recorded the Indian names of many drugs alongside their Greek, Arabic and Persian names.

The Persian medical literature of India is very large and still incompletely studied. It includes general compendia, pharmacopoeias, works on particular diseases and on the pulse, translations from Arabic and from Sanskrit, and medical sections in encyclopaedias compiled for rulers. Some of its authors were Hindus who wrote in Persian, the language of administration and high culture, and some works deliberately combined the two traditions, describing Indian drugs in Unani terms or presenting Āyurvedic diagnosis to Persian readers. The court physicians of the Mughals included Persians, Indian Muslims and Hindus, and European travellers such as François Bernier, himself a physician, left accounts of medical practice at the Mughal court.

Under the Mughals, Indian Unani reached its classical form. Physicians from Iran found employment at the courts of Akbar and his successors and wrote in Persian for Indian patrons. Nūr al-Dīn Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh Shīrāzī compiled two important works. The first is a dictionary of drug names, the Alfāẓ al-adwiya (1628), dedicated to Shāh Jahān; Francis Gladwin translated it into English in 1793, and it long served European physicians in India. The second is a vast medical compendium, the Ṭibb-i Dārā Shikōhī (also called ʿIlājāt-i Dārā Shikōhī). It was completed in the 1640s and dedicated to Shāh Jahān’s eldest son, the scholar-prince Dārā Shikōh. Both works give Indian drug names alongside Arabic and Persian ones. In the eighteenth century, as Mughal power declined, Delhi physicians such as Arzānī and Ḥakīm Muḥammad Sharīf Khān, from whom the Sharīfī family takes its name, wrote Persian works that remained in use into the twentieth century.

Seema Alavi shows how, in the nineteenth century, the loss of court patronage pushed Unani families towards new patrons, towards print and towards Urdu. She also shows how Unani came to be identified with Muslim identity in a way it had not been in Mughal times, when Hindu and Muslim physicians practised it alike (Alavi 2008).

In the colonial period Unani, like Āyurveda, lost official support but retained wide popular following, and in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it was reorganised and defended by reformers. The most important was Ḥakīm Muḥammad Ajmal Khān of Delhi (1868–1927), physician, nationalist and educator, who founded the Ayurvedic and Unani Tibbia College in Delhi, opened in 1921, to teach both systems together with modern sciences. Guy Attewell’s study traces how Unani was “refigured” in this period in dialogue with Western medicine and Āyurveda (Attewell 2007). India today has the largest Unani establishment in the world, with colleges, a research council, a National Institute of Unani Medicine at Bengaluru, and a major pharmaceutical industry.

docs.title: 11.3.3 The Unani Physician in Indian Society
docs.text: Unani physicians served the courts of Delhi, Agra, Lucknow, Hyderabad and the other Indo-Muslim states, and families of ḥakīms, such as the Sharīfī family of Delhi to which Ajmal Khān belonged, maintained hereditary traditions of learning and practice over many generations. They taught in their homes and in madrasas, wrote in Persian and later in Urdu, and served patients of all communities. In the princely state of Hyderabad, Unani received official support and was taught in government institutions well before independence. The Hamdard company, founded in Delhi in 1906 by Ḥakīm Ḥāfiẓ ʿAbd al-Majīd, became the largest manufacturer of Unani medicines, and its founders’ family established educational institutions in both India and Pakistan (below).

docs.title: 11.3.4 Reform, Nationalism and Partition
docs.text:
Ajmal Khān’s career shows how closely Unani reform was bound up with nationalism. Besides founding the Tibbia College, he was a leader of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements. He presided over the Ahmedabad session of the Indian National Congress in 1921 and was the first chancellor of the Jamia Millia Islamia. He also wanted Unani drugs to be studied with the methods of modern chemistry. The research department he planned at the Tibbia College brought the chemist Salimuzzaman Siddiqui to Delhi. In 1931 Siddiqui isolated alkaloids from Rauvolfia serpentina and named one of them ajmaline after Ajmal Khān. This was an early step in the story told in Chapter 12 (see also Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna).

Colonial medical legislation gave the reformers a common cause. In 1910, as provincial governments prepared bills to register medical practitioners, Ajmal Khān founded the All-India Vedic and Unani Tibbi Conference, which brought practitioners of both systems together in their defence. The Acts that followed, beginning with Bombay’s in 1912, created registers of practitioners qualified in Western medicine. They did not forbid indigenous practice, but they denied vaidyas and ḥakīms official standing (Attewell 2007).

Elsewhere reform took similar forms. In Lucknow the ʿAzīzī family of physicians founded the Takmīl al-Ṭibb College early in the twentieth century, and in Hyderabad the Nizam’s government taught Unani in state institutions. Attewell shows how the reformers standardised teaching and pharmacy and adopted the language of science. They also argued over how much Western anatomy and physiology Unani should absorb, while defending humoral theory as its core (Attewell 2007).

The partition of 1947 divided the Unani world. Many ḥakīm families moved to Pakistan, and Hamdard was split. In India, Ḥakīm ʿAbdul Ḥamīd, the founder’s elder son, turned the company into a charitable trust (waqf) and used its income to build educational institutions in Delhi that grew into the Jamia Hamdard university. His younger brother, Ḥakīm Muḥammad Saʿīd, founded Hamdard in Karachi. In independent India, Unani was placed with Āyurveda and Siddha under the Indian Medicine Central Council Act of 1970, acquired its own research council and pharmacopoeia, and is now taught in many colleges. In recent years Ajmal Khān’s birthday, 11 February, has been marked as Unani Day.

docs.title: 11.3.5 Theory
docs.text:
Unani physiology is built on seven “natural matters” (umūr-i ṭabīʿiyya): the elements (arkān), temperament (mizāj), humours (akhlāṭ), organs (aʿḍāʾ), spirits or vital pneumata (arwāḥ), faculties (quwā) and functions (afʿāl). There are four elements—fire, air, water and earth—and four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist and dry. Every person, organ, food and drug has a temperament, a particular mixture of these qualities.

Table 11.2. The four humours of Unani medicine Humour English Qualities Associated element dam blood hot and moist air balgham phlegm cold and moist water ṣafrāʾ yellow bile hot and dry fire sawdāʾ black bile cold and dry earth

Health depends on the balance of the humours (Table 11.2) and on the proper management of six “essential factors” (asbāb-i sitta ḍarūriyya): air, food and drink, bodily movement and rest, sleep and wakefulness, evacuation and retention, and the emotions—the “six non-naturals” of Galenic medicine. The body’s own power of self-preservation and healing is called ṭabīʿat (“nature”), and the physician’s task is to assist it.

Temperament (mizāj) is the central idea. It is the quality that results when the opposed qualities of the elements act on one another in a mixture. The physicians recognised one ideally balanced temperament, which exists only as a norm, and eight unbalanced ones: four simple (hot, cold, moist, dry) and four compound (hot and moist, hot and dry, cold and moist, cold and dry). Every person, organ, age, sex, season and region has its own temperament, so that what is health for one person may be disease for another. The physician therefore judges a patient against that patient’s own normal temperament, much as the Āyurvedic physician judges against the patient’s prakṛti (Chapter 2).

The body is governed by three faculties. Each has its seat in a principal organ and is carried by a “spirit” (rūḥ), a subtle vapour formed from the finest part of the humours (Table 11.3).

Table 11.3. The three faculties (quwā) of Galenic and Unani physiology Faculty Seat Carried by Functions natural (ṭabīʿiyya) liver veins nutrition, growth, reproduction vital (ḥayawāniyya) heart arteries life, the pulse and the passions psychic (nafsāniyya) brain nerves sensation, voluntary movement, thought

The humours themselves are produced by digestion (haḍm), which takes place in four stages: in the stomach, where food becomes chyle; in the liver, where chyle is turned into the four humours; in the vessels; and in the organs, where nutriment is finally assimilated. Each stage leaves a residue that the body must expel. The scheme recalls the successive transformations of the Āyurvedic dhātus (Chapter 2), but it grew independently out of Galen’s physiology.

For the Unani physician, disease is a contest between the morbid matter and the body’s nature. Its turning point is the crisis (buḥrān), which the Hippocratic tradition expected on particular “critical days”. Treatment follows the principle of contraries (ʿilāj bi’l-ḍidd): a hot disease is treated with cooling drugs and regimen, a moist one with drying measures. Morbid matter is first “ripened” with concoctive drugs (munḍij) and then evacuated with purgatives (mushil), a sequence that parallels the Āyurvedic preparation for purification (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 11.3.6 Diagnosis and Treatment
docs.text:
The Unani physician (ḥakīm) diagnoses by the pulse (nabḍ), the urine (bawl) and the stool, as well as by history and examination; pulse and urine lore are highly elaborated in the Greco-Arabic tradition. Treatment is of four kinds: by regimen (ʿilāj bi’l-tadbīr), including exercise, baths, massage, cupping (ḥijāma), venesection and leeches; by diet (ʿilāj bi’l-ghidhāʾ); by drugs (ʿilāj bi’l-dawāʾ), mostly herbal but including mineral preparations; and by surgery (ʿilāj bi’l-yad). Unani pharmacy includes calcined metallic preparations (kushta), to which the same safety concerns apply as to Āyurvedic bhasmas.

Regimental therapy has a long history. Cupping (ḥijāma), with or without small incisions, was practised throughout the Islamic world and is associated in Muslim tradition with the Prophet’s approval, which has contributed to its popularity; venesection followed elaborate rules about which vein to open for which condition; and the Turkish bath (ḥammām), exercise, massage and changes of air were prescribed for health. Like bloodletting in the Āyurvedic and European traditions, these practices rest on humoral theory and have little modern evidence in their favour, though cupping is popular today in many countries.

Unani pharmacy classifies drugs by their temperament and its degree, from the first degree (mild) to the fourth (strong enough to be dangerous), and prepares them in characteristic forms: electuaries (maʿjūn), confections made with honey or sugar (khamīra, jawārish), syrups (sharbat), distilled waters (ʿaraq), pills (ḥabb), powders (safūf), decoctions (joshānda) and oils. The Persian and Urdu pharmacopoeias of India include many Indian drugs alongside those inherited from the Greek and Arabic tradition, such as poppy, saffron, rose and the myrobalans, which the Arabic writers themselves had taken from India.

Ibn Sīnā’s Canon lays down conditions under which the action of a drug may be judged from experience. The drug must be free from accidental change. It must be tried on a simple, not a compound, disease, and in contrasting cases. Its strength must be matched to the strength of the disease. Its effect must be observed over time, so that it is not confused with the natural course of the illness, and it must act consistently. And it must be tested on human beings, not only on animals. These rules are often cited as an early statement of the logic of drug trials. In practice the Unani pharmacopoeias rested mainly on authority and accumulated experience, and modern controlled trials of Unani preparations are still few.

docs.title: 11.3.7 Unani Surgery and Hospitals
docs.text: Surgery (ʿilāj bi’l-yad) had an important place in the classical Arabic tradition, above all in al-Zahrāwī’s treatise, with its illustrations of instruments; cautery, bloodletting and the setting of fractures were practised by Unani surgeons in India. The Islamic world developed large public hospitals (bīmāristān) in Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo from the ninth century onwards (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007), and similar institutions were founded by Indian rulers: the fourteenth-century Sultan Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq, for example, is recorded to have founded a hospital (dār al-shifāʾ) in Delhi where the sick were treated free of charge. In the Deccan, the Quṭb Shāhī ruler Muḥammad Qulī Quṭb Shāh built at Hyderabad, in 1595, a large hospital known as the Dār al-Shifāʾ, which also served as a place of teaching; its building still stands. Among the ordinances that the Mughal emperor Jahāngīr issued at his accession in 1605 was an order to found hospitals in the great cities and appoint physicians to them, paid from the treasury. How far such orders were carried out is uncertain, but they show that the public hospital was an established ideal of Indo-Islamic kingship.

docs.title: 11.4.1 Origins and Texts
docs.text:
Sowa-Rigpa (Tibetan gso ba rig pa, “the science of healing”) is the medical tradition of Tibet, practised also in Bhutan, Mongolia, Nepal and the Himalayan regions of India. Its foundational text is the Four Tantras (rGyud bzhi), which tradition regards as the teaching of the Medicine Buddha, transmitted through the physician Yuthog Yönten Gönpo. Historians date its compilation to the twelfth century and associate it with a later physician of the same name, Yuthog Yönten Gönpo “the Younger”. The Four Tantras draws heavily on Indian medicine, above all the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (Chapter 5), and also on Chinese, Greco-Persian and indigenous Tibetan sources; its pulse diagnosis and some of its anatomy and therapy reflect these non-Indian influences.

In the late seventeenth century, Desi Sangye Gyatso, regent of the Fifth Dalai Lama, wrote the authoritative commentary on the Four Tantras known as the Blue Beryl, commissioned a celebrated series of medical paintings to illustrate it, and founded the medical college on Chakpori hill in Lhasa. Janet Gyatso’s study of this period shows Tibetan physicians debating the relation between Buddhist doctrine and empirical observation in strikingly critical terms (Gyatso 2015). From the fifteenth century two schools of interpretation, the Northern (Byang) and the Southern (Zur), had developed rival commentaries and pharmaceutical traditions. Desi Sangye Gyatso’s work was in part an attempt to settle their disagreements with an authoritative text and images. Physicians on both sides sometimes appealed to what could be seen with the eyes, including the anatomy visible in corpses at sky-burial grounds, to question or defend descriptions of the body inherited from the texts.

docs.title: 11.4.2 Indian Sources and the Question of Origins
docs.text:
Tibetan histories of medicine tell that the early emperors of the seventh and eighth centuries invited physicians from India, China and the lands to the west, and that the meeting of their teachings laid the foundations of Tibetan medicine. These accounts were written down centuries later, and they should be read as tradition rather than history.

What is certain is that Sanskrit medical works were translated into Tibetan in the period of the “later diffusion” of Buddhism. The great translator Rin chen bzang po (958–1055) translated the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya with an Indian collaborator. The canonical collection of translated treatises (bsTan ’gyur) also contains Candranandana’s commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, the Yogaśataka attributed to Nāgārjuna, and several shorter medical works. The Tibetan Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya is a careful, literal translation. Modern editors of the Sanskrit text use it as a witness to readings older than many surviving Sanskrit manuscripts.

The Four Tantras opens with a Sanskrit title, as if it were translated from an Indian original. No Sanskrit text has ever been found, however, and much of its content cannot be derived from Indian sources, including its pulse diagnosis, its moxibustion and much of its terminology. Tibetan scholars disputed the work’s status for centuries. Gyatso has shown that the sixteenth-century physician Zurkharwa Lodrö Gyelpo argued, with careful qualifications, that it had been composed in Tibet by Yuthog rather than spoken by the Buddha (Gyatso 2015). Most modern historians regard it as a Tibetan composition of the twelfth century. It reworks Indian material, above all Vāgbhaṭa’s, together with Chinese and other elements, and is neither a translation nor an independent invention.

docs.title: 11.4.3 Theory and Practice
docs.text:
Its physiology closely parallels the Indian model: seven bodily constituents (lus zungs), from nutritional essence to reproductive fluid, and three waste products (faeces, urine and sweat). Like Āyurveda, Sowa-Rigpa describes three “faults” or humours—rlung (wind), mkhris pa (bile) and bad kan (phlegm)—whose balance is health; but it relates them explicitly to the three Buddhist mental poisons of desire, hatred and delusion. Diagnosis relies heavily on pulse and urine examination and on questioning; treatment uses diet, behaviour, medicines—mostly multi-ingredient herbal pills—and external therapies such as moxibustion, bloodletting and baths.

Each of the three humours has five forms, and these correspond closely to the five forms of each doṣa in the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya. The “life-sustaining” wind seated in the head, for example, corresponds to Vāgbhaṭa’s prāṇa.

The Explanatory Tantra’s embryology follows the Indian pattern: conception comes from the father’s seed, the mother’s blood and a consciousness driven by past action. But it groups the weeks of gestation into three phases named after the fish, the tortoise and the pig. Frances Garrett has traced how this account was elaborated in Tibetan medical and religious literature (Garrett 2008).

Tibetan medicine also gave sustained attention to disorders of the mind. Many of these were attributed to a disturbance of the “life-wind” (srog rlung) and treated with diet, rest, warmth, massage and calming medicines, as well as with ritual (Clifford 1984).

Diagnosis has a characteristic form. The physician reads the radial pulse on both wrists with three fingers.
