Each fingertip is divided into two halves, so that twelve positions in all report on particular organs, a scheme close to Chinese practice. Urine is examined in a white vessel, ideally at dawn: it is stirred and observed as it cools for colour, vapour, smell, bubbles, sediment and the film on its surface.

docs.title: 11.4.4 Pharmacology
docs.text:
Tibetan pharmacology analyses drugs, like Āyurveda, by taste, potency and post-digestive taste, but it counts eight potencies and seventeen qualities and organises the materia medica somewhat differently. Its medicines are usually compound pills of many ingredients, including plants of the high Himalaya and the Tibetan plateau, imported spices and woods from India, minerals and animal products. The most prestigious, the “precious pills” (rin chen ril bu), contain metals and minerals and are prepared by elaborate procedures that include the processing of mercury into a mercury sulphide preparation called btso thal, which Tibetan physicians regard as having been detoxified. Barbara Gerke’s study of this preparation shows how Tibetan physicians understand its toxicity and the processing that is meant to “tame” it, and how these ideas meet modern toxicology and regulation (Gerke 2021). As with rasaśāstra, independent evidence for the safety of such preparations is lacking, and the same cautions apply.

Most Tibetan medicines, however, are plant-based compounds given as decoctions, powders, pills, medicated butters or pastes. Many of their ingredients are named after their Indian originals. For centuries they were prepared by the physician himself, or in monastic and institutional pharmacies, from plants he collected or bought. In the late twentieth century production moved increasingly to factories in India, Nepal, Bhutan, Mongolia and China. Rules of standardisation, licensing and “good manufacturing practice” changed what was made and how. Craig has studied how Tibetan physicians understand and defend the efficacy of their medicines while working within these regulatory systems (Craig 2012).

docs.title: 11.4.5 Sowa-Rigpa and Āyurveda
docs.text: The relationship between the two traditions is close but not simple. The Four Tantras adopts the three humours, the seven constituents, the six tastes and much of the therapeutic framework of Āyurveda, and Tibetan physicians have long regarded India as the land from which their medicine came. But Tibetan medicine developed its own anatomy (including a system of channels influenced by Buddhist tantric yoga), its own pulse and urine diagnosis, its own pharmacy adapted to the plants of the Himalaya, and its own institutions, above all the monastic medical colleges. It also integrated Chinese elements, such as aspects of pulse diagnosis and moxibustion. Tibetan medicine is therefore best understood as an independent tradition that drew on Indian sources, not as a branch of Āyurveda.

docs.title: 11.4.6 Sowa-Rigpa in India
docs.text:
In India Sowa-Rigpa is practised by amchi physicians in Ladakh, Lahaul and Spiti, Sikkim, the Darjeeling hills and Arunachal Pradesh, as well as in the Tibetan exile community, whose Men-Tsee-Khang (Tibetan Medical and Astro-Science Institute) was refounded at Dharamsala in 1961. In 2010 Parliament recognised Sowa-Rigpa as one of the Indian systems of medicine, and a National Institute of Sowa-Rigpa has since been established at Leh.

The full name of Men-Tsee-Khang (sman rtsis khang, “house of medicine and astro-calendrical science”) reflects a link that runs through Tibetan medicine. Physicians were often trained in calendrical science (rtsis) as well as medicine. Its Indian part derives largely from the astronomy of the Kālacakra Tantra. The calendar governed the timing of collecting and compounding medicines and of some treatments, and an astrological reckoning could form part of a consultation. The connection resembles the late medieval Indian combination of medicine and astrology described in Chapter 5.

Sowa-Rigpa has also received international recognition as cultural heritage: in 2018 the Lum medicinal bathing tradition of Sowa-Rigpa, nominated by China, was inscribed on UNESCO’s list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Its classical texts are shared across national borders, and practitioners in India, Nepal, Bhutan, Mongolia and the Tibetan regions of China maintain distinct institutions and debates about the future of the tradition.

In the villages of Ladakh and Spiti, the amchi was traditionally a hereditary practitioner, often a member of a respected family, who collected and prepared his own medicines from the plants of the high Himalaya, treated patients in return for gifts and services, and combined medicine with Buddhist practice. Anthropologists have documented how this role has changed with the arrival of government health services, roads and markets, and with state recognition and certification (Pordié 2008; Craig 2012). The amchis’ dependence on wild plants, many of them slow-growing high-altitude species now heavily harvested for the commercial Tibetan medicine industry, has made the conservation of medicinal plants a pressing concern.

Recognition has also changed how practitioners are trained. The name chosen for the system, Sowa-Rigpa, rather than “Tibetan medicine” or “amchi medicine”, presents it as one of India’s own systems with Himalayan roots, and not only as the medicine of a refugee community. Formal teaching is offered by Men-Tsee-Khang, by the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies at Leh and by the Central University of Tibetan Studies at Sarnath, and their degrees have become the basis of state registration. As with Āyurveda, the move from household apprenticeship to college degree has changed who practises and how. The hereditary village amchi now works alongside graduates, manufacturers and town clinics.

docs.title: 11.4.7 The Structure of the Four Tantras
docs.text:
The Four Tantras is presented as a dialogue between two emanations of the Medicine Buddha. It has 156 chapters in four parts (Table 11.4).

Table 11.4. The four parts of the Four Tantras (rGyud bzhi) Part Tibetan Ch. Main contents Root Tantra rTsa rgyud 6 summary of the whole system; the tree of medicine Explanatory Tantra bShad rgyud 31 embryology, anatomy, physiology, causes of disease, regimen, diet, drugs, the physician Oral Instruction Tantra Man ngag rgyud 92 diagnosis and treatment of particular diseases Subsequent Tantra Phyi ma rgyud 27 pulse and urine, preparation of medicines, purification and external therapies

The four parts are the short Root Tantra, which summarises the whole system with the image of a tree whose roots, trunks, branches and leaves represent the body in health and disease, diagnosis and treatment (in the usual count, three roots, nine trunks, forty-seven branches and 224 leaves, with flowers and fruits standing for health, long life and the goals of a good life); the Explanatory Tantra, on anatomy, physiology, embryology, the causes of disease, regimen, diet, drugs and the conduct of the physician; the long Oral Instruction Tantra, on the diagnosis and treatment of particular diseases; and the Subsequent Tantra, on pulse and urine diagnosis, the preparation of medicines and external therapies. The illustrated medical paintings commissioned by Desi Sangye Gyatso, which show anatomy, plants, instruments, the causes of disease and the ethics of the physician, are among the most remarkable works of Tibetan art; a complete set has been published with translations of its inscriptions (Parfionovitch et al. 1992).

docs.title: 11.5 Exchanges Between the Traditions
docs.text:
The modern institutions separate Āyurveda, Siddha, Unani and Sowa-Rigpa into distinct “systems”, each with its own colleges, councils and pharmacopoeias. Historically the traditions were in constant contact, and the evidence of exchange runs in every direction.

Āyurveda and Unani. Sanskrit medicine absorbed drugs and ideas from Islamic medicine. Opium and other new drugs entered the Sanskrit pharmacopoeia in the medieval and early modern periods (Chapter 5). Pulse diagnosis, absent from the classical compendia, may owe something to Greco-Arabic pulse lore (Chapter 10). A late Sanskrit work on distilled medicinal waters (arka), the Arkaprakāśa, takes as its subject a form of pharmacy that is generally thought to have reached Indian physicians from Islamic practice, where such distillates were called ʿaraq. In the early modern period, some authors set out the principles of Unani medicine in Sanskrit verse for Hindu physicians. In the other direction, Persian authors translated and summarised Sanskrit works for Muslim readers, Unani pharmacy took in many Indian drugs, and Hindu physicians practised Unani at the Mughal and later courts (Section 11.3).

Siddha, Āyurveda and Unani in the South. Tamil physicians used Sanskrit texts and Sanskrit physicians used Tamil formularies. Tamil-speaking Muslim physicians practised Unani alongside both. The first government school of indigenous medicine in Madras taught all three together, and many twentieth-century Tamil practitioners moved between them in practice even as the institutions drew boundaries.

Sowa-Rigpa and Indian medicine. Tibetan physicians obtained many of their drugs from the Indian plains through the trans-Himalayan trade, and the shared materia medica is visible in iconography. The Medicine Buddha holds in his hand a myrobalan (a ru ra, Sanskrit harītakī), which Tibetan pharmacology calls the “king of medicines”. Its place in Āyurveda is described in Chapter 6. In Ladakh and Spiti, amchis have long treated patients who also consulted Āyurvedic vaidyas, ritual healers and, more recently, government doctors.

Patients, then as now, have moved freely between practitioners, choosing according to cost, reputation, the kind of illness and the advice of family. Anthropologists describe this as medical pluralism and have studied how patients combine traditional and biomedical care, and how the state’s categories shape what practitioners may legally do (Leslie 1976; Sujatha and Abraham 2012). The comparison in Section 11.7 should be read with this history of exchange in mind.

docs.title: 11.6 Local, Folk and Tribal Health Traditions
docs.text: Most healing in India has always taken place outside the learned systems. Households have their own remedies and dietary rules; villages have their midwives (dāī), bonesetters, snakebite healers, exorcists and herbalists; Adivasi communities possess detailed knowledge of the plants of their forests. These practitioners rarely wrote books, and much of their knowledge was transmitted orally, within families, castes or communities. The Sanskrit compendia themselves acknowledge such knowledge: Caraka says that herdsmen, shepherds, forest-dwellers and others know plants by name and form, though only the learned physician knows how to use them properly (Ca.Sū. 1.120–121).

docs.title: 11.6.1 Healing and Religion
docs.text: Much local healing is inseparable from religion. Smallpox, for example, was understood across northern and eastern India as the presence of the goddess Śītalā, “the cool one”, and treated by worship, cooling measures and the avoidance of certain foods, rather than by medicine. At the same time, Bengali practitioners called ṭīkādārs practised variolation—the deliberate inoculation of material from smallpox pustules to produce a milder infection and lasting immunity—as the British surgeon J. Z. Holwell described in 1767, before Jenner’s introduction of vaccination with cowpox in 1796. The colonial government later banned variolation in favour of vaccination, a policy that met long resistance. Spirit possession, the evil eye, sorcery and the anger of local deities were, and remain, common explanations of illness, and healing at shrines and by ritual specialists is an important part of the medical landscape. Sudhir Kakar’s study of healers in India, and William Sax’s study of ritual healing in the Himalaya, explore these practices with sympathy and critical attention (Kakar 1982; Sax 2009).

docs.title: 11.6.2 Recording and Appropriation
docs.text:
Much of what outsiders learned about Indian medicinal plants came from such local experts, often without acknowledgement. The Portuguese physician Garcia da Orta’s Colóquios dos simples e drogas da Índia (Goa, 1563) drew on Indian informants. The twelve-volume Hortus Malabaricus (Amsterdam, 1678–1693), compiled under the Dutch governor Hendrik van Rheede, was based on the knowledge of the Kerala physician Itty Achuden, of the Īḻava community, and of Konkani brahmin collaborators, whose testimony is printed in the first volume.

The colonial period produced many catalogues of Indian drugs that relied on local informants. Whitelaw Ainslie, a surgeon of the Madras establishment, published a Materia Indica (1826) that recorded Tamil, Sanskrit, Persian and other names of hundreds of drugs; William Roxburgh’s Flora Indica and later the multi-volume Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (1889–1896) edited by George Watt included extensive medical information gathered from Indian practitioners. These works are valuable records of nineteenth-century practice, though they rarely name the people from whom the knowledge came.

In recent decades the question of who owns traditional knowledge has become a legal and political issue. A frequently cited example is that of the Kani people of the Western Ghats in Kerala, whose knowledge of the plant ārōkyappacca (Trichopus zeylanicus) led scientists at the Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute in Thiruvananthapuram to develop a commercial herbal product in the 1990s, with an agreement, as the case is usually described, to share fees and royalties with the community—an arrangement often cited as an early model of benefit-sharing, though not without controversy. India’s Biological Diversity Act of 2002 and the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (Chapter 12) are attempts to protect such knowledge from misappropriation.

docs.title: 11.6.3 Kinds of Local Healer
docs.text:
The range of local healers is very wide, and varies from region to region. Among the most widespread are:

  • Birth attendants (dāī and their regional equivalents), usually women of low caste status, who attended most births in India until recent decades. Their knowledge of normal labour was considerable, but some customary practices—delayed breastfeeding, unclean cutting of the cord, the application of substances to the cord stump—contributed to maternal and newborn deaths. Programmes since the 1970s have tried to train them, and the shift to births in health facilities has transformed their role.

  • Bonesetters, who treat fractures and dislocations by manipulation and splinting, sometimes with great skill and sometimes with serious complications.

  • Snakebite healers, who use mantras, herbs and rituals; in Kerala, specialist viṣavaidyas maintained a learned tradition in Sanskrit and Malayalam.

  • Herbalists of Adivasi and rural communities, whose detailed knowledge of local plants has been documented by ethnobotanists since the colonial period.

  • Ritual healers, exorcists and shrine-based healers, to whom many people take mental illness and misfortune; studies of such shrines have shown both the comfort they provide and the abuses—chaining, beating, neglect—that sometimes occur.

docs.title: 11.6.4 Value and Limits
docs.text: Organisations such as the Foundation for Revitalisation of Local Health Traditions in Bengaluru, and scholars working with them, have argued that “local health traditions” are an important resource for primary health care and should be documented and supported (Shankar and Unnikrishnan 2004). Local healers are often the first and sometimes the only source of care in remote areas, and they possess genuine knowledge of plants and of their communities. They also, like all healers, sometimes do harm: through delay in the treatment of serious illness, through harmful practices in childbirth and snakebite, and through the use of toxic substances. Respect for local knowledge and insistence on safety are not in conflict.

docs.title: 11.7 Comparison
docs.text:
Table 11.5. The learned medical traditions of India compared Āyurveda Siddha Unani Sowa-Rigpa Language of the classics Sanskrit Tamil Arabic, Persian, Urdu Tibetan Foundational texts Caraka, Suśruta, Vāgbhaṭa poems attributed to the Siddhars Hippocrates, Galen, Ibn Sīnā Four Tantras Elements five five four five Humours three three four three Characteristic diagnosis (later) pulse, eightfold examination pulse, urine and oil-drop test pulse and urine pulse and urine Metallic preparations bhasma, rasa preparations centūram, paṟpam, pāṣāṇams kushta precious pills with processed mercury

The traditions compared in Table 11.5 share a broadly humoral understanding of the body, a reliance on diet and regimen, a rich materia medica and, in each case, a prestigious but hazardous use of metals and minerals. They have borrowed from one another for centuries, and the boundaries between them were more fluid in practice than the modern institutional categories suggest.

Each tradition also has its own picture of the good physician, to set beside the Sanskrit ideal described in Chapter 1. The Explanatory Tantra of the Four Tantras closes with a chapter on the physician, which lists the qualities he needs—among them intelligence, compassion, fidelity to his vows and his teacher, skill, diligence and right conduct among people—and, like Caraka, ranks the physician who works out of compassion above the one who works for gain. In the Unani tradition the ninth-century physician Isḥāq ibn ʿAlī al-Ruhāwī wrote one of the earliest books devoted entirely to medical ethics, Adab al-ṭabīb (“The Conduct of the Physician”), on the physician’s own regimen and piety, his behaviour towards patients and their visitors, and the examination of physicians; in later Islamic cities the market inspector (muḥtasib) was expected to test physicians and pharmacists and to check their drugs (Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007). The Siddha texts stress instead the bond between teacher and pupil and the secrecy of knowledge, promising effective remedies only to the worthy disciple and warning against revealing them to the unworthy. These ideals differ. They share a concern that the power of medicine be used for the patient’s good, and a conviction that the physician’s character matters as much as his learning (Section 1.8).

Summary

Siddha, Unani and Sowa-Rigpa are learned traditions in their own right, each with its own texts and languages, though all three share with Āyurveda a humoral understanding of the body and a prestigious but hazardous use of metals. Their modern identities—Siddha as the ancient medicine of the Tamils, Unani as the medicine of Indian Muslims, Sowa-Rigpa as one of India’s own systems—were shaped in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, while their history is one of constant exchange. Around and beneath all of them, local healers have always provided much of the care, with real knowledge and real risks.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On Siddha medicine see Weiss and Zvelebil (Weiss 2009; Zvelebil 1996); on Islamic medicine, Ullmann and Pormann and Savage-Smith (Ullmann 1978; Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007); on Unani in modern India, Attewell and Alavi (Attewell 2007; Alavi 2008); on Tibetan medicine, Gyatso, Garrett and the Blue Beryl paintings (Gyatso 2015; Garrett 2008; Parfionovitch et al. 1992); on local health traditions, Shankar and Unnikrishnan (Shankar and Unnikrishnan 2004).

docs.title: Chapter 12: Āyurveda in the Colonial and Modern World
docs.text:
kṛtsno hi loko buddhimatām ācāryaḥ śatruś cābuddhimatām For the wise the whole world is a teacher; for the foolish, an enemy.

— Caraka Saṃhitā, Vimānasthāna 8.14

docs.title: 12.1 Introduction
docs.text: The Āyurveda practised today is not simply the medicine of Caraka and Suśruta carried unchanged into the present. It is the product of two centuries of encounter with Western biomedicine: of colonial neglect and selective interest, of nationalist revival, of the making of colleges, pharmacopoeias and a pharmaceutical industry, of state recognition after independence, and, more recently, of a global market in “wellness”. Historians and anthropologists have studied this history closely (Leslie 1976; Leslie and Young 1992; Arnold 2000; Ernst 2002; Langford 2002; Alter 2005; Wujastyk and Smith 2008; Banerjee 2009). This chapter outlines it, and then asks what modern research has and has not shown, and what safety questions the use of Ayurvedic medicines raises.

docs.title: 12.2.1 Early Exchanges
docs.text: In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries European physicians and naturalists in India learned eagerly from Indian practitioners, as the works of Garcia da Orta and the Hortus Malabaricus show (Chapter 11). Indian drugs entered European pharmacopoeias, and in the eighteenth century European surgeons in India observed Indian practices, such as the operation for rebuilding the nose reported in 1794 (Chapter 4) and inoculation against smallpox, which was practised in Bengal before the introduction of vaccination.

docs.title: 12.2.2 The Native Medical Institution and Its Closure
docs.text:
In 1822 the East India Company government in Calcutta founded the Native Medical Institution to train Indians as medical assistants for its army and dispensaries. Teaching was in Hindustani, and Western medicine was taught alongside Indian medicine; classes in Āyurveda were also held at the Sanskrit College, and in Unani at the Calcutta Madrasa. The experiment was short-lived. In 1835, following the decision of Governor-General Bentinck’s government to support only Western learning in English, the Native Medical Institution and the indigenous medical classes were abolished and the Calcutta Medical College was founded to teach Western medicine alone. Madhusudan Gupta, who had taught Āyurveda at the Sanskrit College, moved to the new college and in 1836 performed the first human dissection there—an event later celebrated as a break with tradition, although Suśruta had himself prescribed dissection (Arnold 2000).

From then on, the colonial state recognised and regulated only Western-trained practitioners. Āyurveda and Unani lost official patronage and access to public institutions, though they continued to be practised by the great majority of healers and used by the great majority of Indians.

docs.title: 12.2.3 Revival
docs.text:
In the later nineteenth century Āyurveda was reorganised by its own practitioners. Sanskrit medical texts were printed for the first time, many in Calcutta and Bombay, making the classics widely available. Bengali kavirājs, such as Gaṅgādhara Rāy, wrote new commentaries and trained large numbers of students. Ayurvedic pharmacies began to manufacture medicines on an industrial scale—Dabur in Calcutta from 1884 and the Arya Vaidya Sala at Kottakkal from 1902 are well-known early examples—and to sell them through advertisements and by post. Practitioners founded associations, among them the All-India Ayurvedic Congress (1907), journals and colleges.

Some Indian rulers supported Āyurveda before the British provinces did. The state of Travancore opened a school of Āyurveda at Thiruvananthapuram in 1889, which later became a government college, and Mysore and other princely states also founded Āyurvedic schools and dispensaries in the early twentieth century. In British India, private colleges were founded by practitioners’ associations and philanthropists, and in 1927 Banaras Hindu University, under Madan Mohan Malaviya, opened an Āyurvedic college that taught both Sanskrit texts and modern sciences.

The revival was closely linked to nationalism. Āyurveda was presented as an Indian science, equal or superior to Western medicine, whose decline was due to foreign rule. Its leaders disagreed, however, about how it should relate to Western medicine. Some argued for “pure” (śuddha) Āyurveda taught from the Sanskrit texts; others for an “integrated” curriculum that included modern anatomy, physiology and pathology. The debate, analysed by Charles Leslie in a classic essay (Leslie 1976), has shaped Āyurvedic education ever since. Nationalist leaders were not uncritical. Mahatma Gandhi, while sympathetic to indigenous medicine and opposed to much of Western medical practice, told Āyurvedic and Unani physicians that they had neglected research and relied too much on the authority of old texts. Provincial governments, under pressure from the nationalist movement, began to support indigenous medicine in the 1920s, beginning with Madras.

docs.title: 12.2.4 The Usman Committee
docs.text:
The first full official inquiry into the Indian systems was made in Madras. In 1921 the government of the Madras Presidency, then run in its “transferred” departments by ministers of the Justice Party under the reforms of 1919, appointed a committee on the indigenous systems of medicine. Its chairman was Muhammad Usman, and its secretary was G. Srinivasa Murti, a physician with a Western medical qualification who became one of the most articulate defenders of Indian medicine. The committee sent a questionnaire to practitioners and scholars across India and printed their replies in its report of 1923, together with Srinivasa Murti’s long memorandum on the scientific character of Āyurveda, Siddha and Unani.

The report argued that the indigenous systems were rational, that they served most of the population, and that the state should support them by founding schools, registering qualified practitioners and encouraging research. Its recommendations led to the opening of a government school of Indian medicine in Madras in the mid-1920s, which taught Āyurveda, Siddha and Unani together with Western subjects (Chapter 11). The replies to the questionnaire are an important source for the state of Indian medicine at the time. The questions the committee posed—whether the Indian systems should be taught in their own terms or alongside modern science, and how the state should recognise their practitioners—dominated the next half-century.

docs.title: 12.2.5 New Textbooks and Colleges
docs.text:
The colleges of the revival needed textbooks, and one of the most ambitious answers came from Calcutta. Gaṇanāth Sen (1877–1944), a kavirāj who had studied Western medicine as well as the Sanskrit texts, published from 1913 the Pratyakṣaśārīra, “the body as directly seen”. It is an anatomy written in Sanskrit that follows modern anatomy and coins Sanskrit terms for structures the classical texts do not name. He followed it with the Siddhāntanidāna, a work on pathology in the same spirit. Sen’s books set out to show that Sanskrit could carry modern science, and that an Āyurvedic physician could know the body as precisely as a Western-trained doctor without ceasing to be a vaidya; they turned Suśruta’s call for direct observation (Chapter 4) into a curriculum. Projit Bihari Mukharji has studied this generation of Bengali physicians, who adopted the thermometer and other small instruments, and modern anatomy, while reworking them within Āyurvedic ideas, and he describes the result as a “braided” science rather than a simple borrowing (Mukharji 2016). In an earlier study he showed how Bengali practitioners of Western medicine (ḍākṭārī) used print and the medical market to make that medicine their own, in competition with the kavirājs for the same patients (Mukharji 2009). In the same years Jāminībhūṣaṇ Rāy founded the Aṣṭāṅga Āyurveda Vidyālaya in Calcutta, one of several colleges in which students learned the Sanskrit texts alongside dissection and clinical work in an attached hospital. In Kerala, P. S. Vāriyar, the founder of the Arya Vaidya Sala at Kottakkal, also founded a school to train physicians in a regular course.

In north India the revival took a different colour. Rachel Berger has shown how in the United Provinces Āyurveda became tied to the Hindi movement and to Hindu nationalist politics, how its advocates sought state recognition in the provincial legislatures, and how regulation turned on the question of who could call himself a vaidya (Berger 2013). In the Punjab, Kavita Sivaramakrishnan has traced how practitioners recast their medicine through print, associations and competition with Unani and Western medicine, and how questions of language and religious community shaped the result (Sivaramakrishnan 2006).

docs.title: 12.2.6 Registration
docs.text: From the 1910s the provinces of British India registered doctors trained in Western medicine, and so excluded indigenous practitioners from official recognition (Chapter 11). The associations of vaidyas and ḥakīms answered by seeking registers of their own. During the 1920s and 1930s several provinces and princely states set up boards or faculties of Indian medicine that registered practitioners, recognised colleges and held examinations. Registration gave status and some protection to college-trained vaidyas and ḥakīms. It also turned into “unqualified” practitioners the many hereditary physicians who had learned in a family or from a single teacher and held no diploma. The same process pushed further to the margins the midwives, bonesetters, snakebite healers and other local practitioners described in Chapter 11, who had never belonged to the learned systems at all.

docs.title: 12.2.7 “Pure” and “Integrated” Āyurveda
docs.text: The debate between śuddha and integrated Āyurveda was fiercest between the 1940s and the 1960s. Its best-known champion on the “pure” side was Pandit Shiv Sharma, the son of a royal physician of Patiala, who had taught at the Dayanand Ayurvedic College in Lahore, later worked in Bombay, and became a leading figure of the All-India Ayurvedic Congress. In his book The System of Āyurveda (Bombay, 1929) and in many later addresses he argued that Āyurveda was a complete science that should be developed from its own principles, and that the integrated colleges produced graduates who were neither true vaidyas nor competent modern doctors and who drifted into practising Western medicine. The integrationists answered that no physician, of whatever system, could ignore anatomy, physiology, pathology and pharmacology, and that the classical theory had to be tested and supplemented. Paul Brass’s study of Āyurvedic education in Uttar Pradesh shows how these positions were bound up with the politics of language, religion and professional interest, and how governments swung between them (Brass 1972). The two camps shared more than they admitted. Both accepted the college, the examination, the diploma and the register as the proper forms of a modern medical profession, and both changed Āyurveda in the process of defending it.

docs.title: 12.2.8 Indigenous Drugs and Colonial Science
docs.text: Even as the colonial state withdrew support from Indian practitioners, it took an interest in Indian drugs as possible cheap substitutes for imported medicines and as sources of new ones. Officials compiled catalogues of Indian medicinal plants, and the Pharmacopoeia of India of 1868 included a number of Indian drugs. In the twentieth century, scientific study of these drugs was organised by Indian scientists. At the Calcutta School of Tropical Medicine, founded in 1921, Ram Nath Chopra led a long programme of research on Indian medicinal plants and published Indigenous Drugs of India (Chopra 1933), which tried to separate the useful from the useless by laboratory and clinical study. After independence, the Central Drug Research Institute at Lucknow (1951) and other laboratories screened large numbers of plants. These programmes yielded much knowledge but few new drugs; reserpine (below) was the outstanding success.

docs.title: 12.3 Āyurveda in Independent India
docs.text:
After independence the Indian state gave Āyurveda and the other “Indian systems of medicine” official recognition, while making Western medicine the basis of the public health system. A series of committees considered their place: the Chopra Committee (1948) recommended integrating them with modern medicine; later committees debated standards of education and practice (Table 12.1).

Table 12.1. Some landmarks in the institutional history of Āyurveda in India Year Event 1923 Report of the Madras committee on the indigenous systems (Usman Committee) 1927 Āyurvedic college founded at Banaras Hindu University 1948 Report of the Committee on Indigenous Systems of Medicine (Chopra Committee) 1954 Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act prohibits advertisements claiming to cure specified diseases 1967 Gujarat Ayurved University, Jamnagar 1970 Indian Medicine Central Council Act; Central Council of Indian Medicine set up to regulate education and practice 1978 Central Council for Research in Ayurveda and Siddha constituted from an earlier combined council (renamed the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences when Siddha received its own council in 2010) 1995 Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy in the Ministry of Health 2003 Department renamed AYUSH 2014 Ministry of AYUSH created 2016 First National Ayurveda Day 2017 All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi, inaugurated 2020 National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Act replaces the Central Council of Indian Medicine 2022 WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine established at Jamnagar

docs.title: 12.3.1 Committees and Curricula, 1946–1970
docs.text:
The Health Survey and Development Committee chaired by Joseph Bhore, whose report of 1946 set out the plan for India’s public health services, gave the indigenous systems little attention. A separate Committee on Indigenous Systems of Medicine, chaired by Ram Nath Chopra, the pharmacologist whose work on Indian drugs is described above, reported in 1948. It recommended a “synthesis” of Indian and Western medicine through integrated training, research on Indian drugs and the inclusion of indigenous practitioners in the health services. Research was given an institutional home at Jamnagar in Saurashtra, where a research institute and, in the mid-1950s, a postgraduate training centre in Āyurveda were set up; Jamnagar later became the seat of the Gujarat Ayurved University (Table 12.1).

Further committees, chaired by D. T. Dave (1955) and K. N. Udupa (1958), examined the standards of teaching and practice. For a time the central and several state governments supported courses in “pure” Āyurveda alongside the integrated colleges, under pressure from the śuddha camp. The Indian Medicine Central Council Act of 1970 brought this period of experiment to an end. The Central Council of Indian Medicine set a common minimum curriculum and kept a central register, and the degree course that resulted, described below, keeps the classical texts and the modern subjects side by side. The questions of the 1920s were thus settled administratively rather than intellectually, and they continue to be argued.

docs.title: 12.3.2 Homoeopathy, Naturopathy and Yoga
docs.text: Two of the systems now grouped with Āyurveda under AYUSH did not originate in India but took deep root there. Homoeopathy, devised by the German physician Samuel Hahnemann at the end of the eighteenth century, reached India in the early nineteenth century and spread rapidly in Bengal, where the physician Mahendralal Sircar adopted it in the 1860s. It was given statutory recognition by the Homoeopathy Central Council Act of 1973, and India now has more homoeopathic practitioners than any other country. Systematic reviews, among them a comprehensive assessment by Australia’s National Health and Medical Research Council, have found no reliable evidence that homoeopathic remedies, which are usually diluted beyond the point at which any molecule of the original substance remains, work better than placebo (National Health and Medical Research Council 2015). Naturopathy, or “nature cure”, also came from Europe; Mahatma Gandhi was a lifelong advocate of it and founded a nature-cure centre at Uruli Kanchan near Pune in 1946. Yoga therapy developed at institutions such as Kaivalyadhama at Lonavla, founded by Swami Kuvalayananda in 1924 (see Volume 5 of this series). Their place in the same ministry as Āyurveda is an administrative grouping of the “non-allopathic” systems, not a sign of a shared history.

docs.title: 12.3.3 Āyurveda in the Health System Today
docs.text:
From the 2000s the government began to bring AYUSH practitioners into the public health system on a larger scale. Under the National Rural Health Mission, launched in 2005, AYUSH doctors were posted to primary health centres and community health centres, often alongside or in place of doctors of modern medicine, and the Ayushman Bharat programme of 2018 included AYUSH health and wellness centres. These policies have been defended as a way of extending health care to underserved areas and criticised as a substitute for training and posting enough doctors of modern medicine.

India today has several hundred Āyurvedic colleges, which award a five-and-a-half-year degree (B.A.M.S.) that includes modern anatomy, physiology and pathology as well as the classical texts, and postgraduate degrees in the various branches. Hundreds of thousands of registered practitioners work in government dispensaries and hospitals, in private practice and in industry. Many Āyurvedic graduates in fact practise modern medicine, especially in rural areas where qualified doctors are scarce—a long-standing and contested feature of Indian health care. The courts have repeatedly been asked to rule on such “cross-practice”. In Poonam Verma v. Ashwin Patel (1996), for example, the Supreme Court held that a practitioner registered in one system who treated a patient with the drugs of another, in which he was not qualified, was negligent; the permissions that several state governments have since given to practitioners of the Indian systems to prescribe some modern drugs have been challenged in turn. Ayurvedic medicines are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, which was extended to them in the 1960s, and official pharmacopoeias set standards for single drugs and formulations. Rules on good manufacturing practice for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani medicines were added to the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules in 2000, and later rules required the testing of products for heavy metals, at least for export. Enforcement of these standards, however, has been uneven.

docs.title: 12.3.4 Industry, Advertising and Regulation
docs.text:
The Ayurvedic pharmaceutical industry, which began in the late nineteenth century, has grown into a large sector of the Indian economy, ranging from multinational companies to small local manufacturers. Its products include “classical” formulations made according to the recipes of authoritative texts, and “proprietary” medicines—new combinations sold under brand names—which make up much of the market. Madhulika Banerjee has studied how this industry has reshaped Āyurveda, turning a practice based on individual prescription into one dominated by branded products sold directly to consumers (Banerjee 2009). Advertising has always been central to the industry, and claims to cure serious diseases have repeatedly brought it into conflict with the law of 1954 against objectionable advertisements and with the courts.

The law of 1954 lists a number of serious diseases—among them cancer, diabetes, heart disease, epilepsy and others—for which advertisements claiming a cure are prohibited, whatever the system of medicine. Enforcement has been weak, and in 2024 the Supreme Court of India publicly censured a large Ayurvedic company and the regulatory authorities over misleading advertisements, a case that drew national attention to the problem.

The relationship between Āyurveda and modern medicine within the Indian health system remains contested. Government policy since the 2010s has promoted “integration”—co-location of AYUSH services in hospitals, and in 2020 a notification permitting postgraduates in Āyurvedic surgery to perform a list of common operations. The latter was strongly opposed by the Indian Medical Association, which criticised what it called “mixopathy”. Behind such controversies lie real questions about training, standards, patient safety and the shortage of doctors in rural India.

docs.title: 12.3.5 Medicinal Plants and Conservation
docs.text: Most of the plants used in Āyurvedic and other traditional medicines are still collected from the wild, often by poor and tribal collectors who receive a small share of the final price. Growing demand, in India and abroad, has put a number of species under severe pressure, among them guggulu, kaṭukī and several Himalayan plants also used in Tibetan medicine. The National Medicinal Plants Board, set up in 2000, promotes cultivation and conservation. Sustainable supply is now one of the central practical problems of the industry.

docs.title: 12.3.6 Education and the Place of Sanskrit
docs.text: The Āyurvedic degree course has been a subject of debate since the revival. Its curriculum combines the study of the classical texts—often in Sanskrit, with commentaries—with modern anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, surgery and obstetrics, and clinical training in both systems. Critics from within the tradition have argued that the modern subjects crowd out the classical learning and produce graduates who are neither good vaidyas nor good doctors; critics from modern medicine argue that the classical subjects teach an outdated theory of the body. Surveys of Āyurvedic graduates have found that many practise modern medicine, wholly or partly, after qualifying. The question of what an Āyurvedic physician should know—and what he or she should be allowed to do—remains unresolved.

docs.title: 12.4 International Recognition and the Global Market
docs.text:
The World Health Organization has encouraged member states to make use of traditional medicine in primary health care since the Declaration of Alma-Ata (1978). Its Traditional Medicine Strategy 2014–2023 called on states to integrate traditional medicine into health systems where it is safe and effective, to regulate products and practitioners, and to support research (World Health Organization 2013). WHO has published benchmarks for training and practice in Āyurveda, and in 2022 established its Global Centre for Traditional Medicine at Jamnagar, with funding from the Government of India. The eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases includes a supplementary chapter for traditional-medicine diagnoses; its first module covered traditional medicine of Chinese origin, and a second module for Āyurveda, Siddha and Unani was added in 2024. These steps are recognitions of the importance of traditional medicine in health systems; they are not endorsements of the efficacy of particular treatments.

Outside South Asia, Āyurveda became widely known from the 1970s and 1980s, partly through the “Maharishi Ayur-Ved” promoted by the Transcendental Meditation movement and through popular authors in the United States and Europe. It is now part of a large international market in wellness, spa treatments, health tourism and supplements. Regulation varies widely. In the European Union, the Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products Directive of 2004 allows the registration of herbal medicines on the basis of long traditional use and evidence of safety, but most Ayurvedic formulae, especially those containing minerals, do not qualify. In the United Kingdom, Ayurvedic practitioners are not statutorily regulated. In the United States, most Ayurvedic products are sold as dietary supplements, which do not require proof of efficacy before marketing, and the Food and Drug Administration has repeatedly warned consumers and detained imports because of heavy-metal contamination.

docs.title: 12.4.1 Sri Lanka and Nepal
docs.text: In Sri Lanka, Āyurveda has a long history alongside indigenous medicine (deśīya cikitsā) and Siddha and Unani, and the island’s chronicles record royal hospitals from an early period. After independence the Ayurveda Act of 1961 established a department, a medical council and a research institute, and Āyurveda became an official part of the national health system, with its own hospitals and colleges. In Nepal, too, Āyurveda received state patronage, and Kathmandu became an important repository of medical manuscripts: the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā and an early manuscript of the Suśruta Saṃhitā survived there (Chapters 4 and 8). In both countries Āyurveda is practised alongside modern medicine, and the relationship between them raises the same questions as in India.

docs.title: 12.4.2 Health Tourism
docs.text:
Since the 1990s, Kerala in particular has promoted Āyurveda as an attraction for foreign and domestic tourists, through resorts, spas and treatment centres offering “rejuvenation” packages and Kerala oil therapies. Health tourism has brought income and employment, but critics have pointed to the commercialisation of a medical tradition, to treatments offered by poorly trained staff, and to the promotion of unproven claims. The state government has introduced classification schemes for Āyurvedic centres in an attempt to maintain standards.

Anthropologists who have studied this “global Ayurveda” have noted how much it differs from practice in India (Wujastyk and Smith 2008). In Europe and North America it is often presented as a gentle, vegetarian, spiritual system of self-care centred on the three doṣas as personality types, on diet and on oil massage, while the surgery, toxicology, meat-based dietetics and mineral pharmacy of the classical and medieval texts are largely absent. In India itself, Āyurveda is practised in government hospitals and dispensaries, in private clinics, by hereditary physicians and by graduates who also prescribe modern drugs; it is used chiefly for chronic illness, digestive complaints, skin diseases and conditions where patients feel that modern medicine has failed them, and most patients use it alongside modern medicine rather than instead of it. Jean Langford’s ethnography of Āyurvedic practitioners in North India shows how they reinterpret the tradition in dialogue with modern medicine and nationalist ideas (Langford 2002).

docs.title: 12.5.1 A Success Story: Rauvolfia
docs.text: The best example of a traditional Indian drug that passed into modern medicine is Rauvolfia serpentina, known in Sanskrit as sarpagandhā and long used in Indian folk and learned medicine, among other things for insanity. In 1931 the Calcutta physicians Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose reported its use in insanity and high blood pressure, and in 1949 the Bombay cardiologist Rustom Jal Vakil published in the British Heart Journal a study of its effect in essential hypertension that drew international attention (Vakil 1949). Its active alkaloid, reserpine, was isolated in 1952 and became one of the first effective drugs for hypertension and an important tool in the development of psychopharmacology. It is rarely used today, because better-tolerated drugs have replaced it; its side effects include depression. The story shows that traditional knowledge can lead to valuable drugs—and that the path runs through rigorous testing.

docs.title: 12.5.2 The State of the Evidence
docs.text:
Since the 1950s a great deal of laboratory and clinical research has been carried out on Ayurvedic plants, formulae and procedures, much of it in India. Reviews of this research reach broadly similar conclusions (Mukherjee and Wahile 2006; Patwardhan et al. 2005). Many plants contain biologically active compounds and show effects in laboratory and animal studies. Clinical trials are fewer; most are small, short, inadequately controlled or unblinded, and few have been replicated independently. Where larger and better trials have been done, results have often been disappointing: the American trial of guggulipid for high cholesterol is an example (Szapary et al. 2003). There are encouraging findings in some areas—for example, the alkaline-thread treatment of fistula-in-ano (Chapter 4)—but for most uses of most Ayurvedic treatments there is not yet good evidence of benefit.

Table 12.2 summarises, in very general terms, the state of the evidence for some of the most widely used Ayurvedic plants and procedures as of the mid-2020s. It is necessarily simplified, and the evidence changes as new studies are published.

Table 12.2. The state of clinical evidence for some widely used Ayurvedic treatments (simplified) Treatment Main claimed uses Clinical evidence and safety Rauvolfia (reserpine) hypertension, psychosis effective; the active compound became a standard drug, now largely superseded because of side effects Guggulu (guggulipid) high cholesterol, obesity, arthritis a good-quality trial found no benefit for cholesterol; skin reactions Turmeric (curcumin) inflammation, arthritis, many others many small trials, inconsistent results; poor absorption; liver injury reported with concentrated supplements Aśvagandhā stress, sleep, vigour small trials of limited quality; liver injury and thyroid effects reported Brahmī (Bacopa) memory small trials with modest effects on some tests Guḍūcī fever, “immunity” little good clinical evidence; liver injury reported Triphalā bowel function limited evidence of a laxative effect Alkaline thread (kṣārasūtra) fistula-in-ano controlled trials comparing it with surgery; used in some surgical units Purification therapies many chronic diseases small, mostly uncontrolled studies; risks under-reported Rasaśāstra preparations many diseases no adequate trials; heavy-metal toxicity documented

Some argue that the randomised controlled trial is unsuited to a system that individualises treatment. Trials can, however, be designed to test individualised “whole-system” treatment against a control, and some have been. The real obstacles have been lack of funding for large independent trials, the variability of products, and a tendency in some quarters to treat the antiquity of a remedy as evidence of its value.

docs.title: 12.5.3 Research Ethics and Method
docs.text:
Research on traditional medicine raises the same ethical questions as any medical research, and some particular ones. Participants must give informed consent and must not be denied effective treatment for serious conditions. Products tested must be of known composition and free of contamination; several trials of Ayurvedic preparations have used products whose metal content was not measured. Results must be reported in full, including negative results and adverse effects, and trials should be registered in advance—in India, with the Clinical Trials Registry–India, established in 2007. A recurrent problem in the field has been the publication of small positive studies in low-quality journals and the neglect of negative ones, which together give a misleadingly favourable impression.

Some Indian researchers have proposed a “reverse pharmacology” approach: starting from remedies that experienced practitioners believe to be effective, documenting their use carefully, and then testing them clinically and investigating their constituents, rather than screening plants at random in the laboratory. The approach is sensible, provided that the final step—rigorous clinical testing—is not skipped.

docs.title: 12.5.4 Animals and Plants
docs.text: Traditional medicine for animals also continues. Livestock keepers throughout India use local remedies for their cattle, goats and other animals, and “ethnoveterinary” knowledge has been documented by researchers and some development organisations as a cheap and accessible resource, especially where veterinary services are scarce. The classical traditions of horse and elephant medicine (Chapter 5) survive in some places, notably in the care of temple elephants in Kerala. As with human medicine, the value of such remedies has to be established case by case, and some are harmful.

docs.title: 12.5.5 Research Institutions
docs.text: Research on Āyurveda in India is carried out by the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences and its network of institutes, by the national institutes and Āyurvedic universities, by laboratories of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research and the Indian Council of Medical Research, by universities and by industry. A number of journals publish this research, of very variable quality. The quality of much of it has been criticised by both Indian and foreign reviewers: small samples, lack of randomisation and blinding, unregistered trials, poorly characterised products and selective reporting are common. In recent years there have been efforts to improve standards, including the registration of trials, collaboration with institutions of modern medicine, and the publication of protocols in advance.

docs.title: 12.5.6 Constitution and Genetics
docs.text: Research on the genetic and biochemical correlates of prakṛti (Chapter 2) has attracted wide interest under the name “Ayurgenomics”. The early findings are intriguing but preliminary, and they do not yet show that constitutional assessment can guide the treatment of disease (Prasher et al. 2008; Aggarwal et al. 2010).

docs.title: 12.5.7 The COVID-19 Pandemic
docs.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2022), Ayurvedic and other traditional preparations were widely promoted in India as “immunity boosters”, and some were advertised as cures. There was no reliable evidence that any of them prevented or treated the disease, and claims of cure led to regulatory and legal action. In the following months Indian hepatologists reported cases of liver injury associated with heavy use of guḍūcī and other herbal products (Nagral et al. 2021). The episode showed both the public trust that traditional medicine enjoys and the dangers of claims that run ahead of evidence.

docs.title: 12.6 Āyurveda and Science
docs.text:
The relationship between Āyurveda and modern science has been argued over for more than a century. Three broad positions can be distinguished. The first holds that Āyurveda is a complete science in its own right, with its own epistemology, and that it should be judged by its own standards rather than those of biomedicine. The second holds that Āyurveda is a valuable storehouse of observations and remedies, from which modern science can extract what is useful—particular drugs and practices—by testing them in the ordinary way. The third, now common in Indian policy, calls for “integration” of the two systems in education, research and practice.

Each position has its difficulties. Every medical system has its own concepts, but claims that a treatment works for patients are claims about the world, and the methods for testing them—comparison with a control, measures against bias, honest reporting—are not the property of any one culture; the compendia themselves insist on examination and reasoning. Extracting individual drugs from Āyurveda can neglect the context of diet, regimen and individual assessment in which they were used. And “integration” raises hard questions about which concepts are retained and how disagreements between the systems are to be resolved. The historian’s task is not to settle these debates but to make sure that they are conducted on the basis of an accurate account of what the tradition actually contains.

docs.title: 12.7 Safety
docs.text:
This section gathers the practical warnings to which the shorter notes in earlier chapters refer. It is not medical advice for any individual: anyone who is ill should consult a registered medical practitioner.

Health and Safety Note

The single most important fact for a modern reader about Ayurvedic medicines is that “natural” and “traditional” do not mean safe. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about every traditional medicine or supplement you take, avoid products containing metals or minerals, be especially careful in pregnancy and with children, and never stop prescribed treatment without medical advice.

Metals and minerals. Studies of Ayurvedic products sold in the United States and online found lead, mercury or arsenic in about one product in five, often at levels that could exceed safety limits if the products were taken as directed (Saper et al. 2004, 2008), and many cases of lead poisoning from Ayurvedic medicines have been reported, including in pregnant women and children (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004). Products whose ingredients include bhasma, rasa, sindūra or named metals and minerals are best avoided, and products bought online or abroad, whose content is least controlled, call for particular caution. Traditional eye cosmetics and collyria (añjana, surmā, kājal) are often made from lead compounds and are a recognised cause of lead poisoning, especially in children (Section 8.3; Chapter 9).

Poisonous plants. Some classical formulae contain aconite, Datura, nux vomica and other poisonous plants (Section 6.4). Deaths from aconite poisoning after the use of traditional medicines continue to be reported, and classical “purification” does not reliably remove the toxicity of these plants.

Liver injury, interactions and other adverse effects have been reported with several popular herbs and multi-ingredient products, among them aśvagandhā and guḍūcī (Björnsson et al. 2020; Nagral et al. 2021). Herbal medicines can interact with prescribed drugs and affect laboratory tests. Anyone who develops jaundice, abdominal pain, unusual fatigue, numbness or a rash while taking a traditional medicine should stop it and see a doctor.

Purification procedures. Emesis, purgation, enemas, nasal treatments and bloodletting are invasive and carry real risks: dehydration and dangerous disturbances of body salts, inhalation of vomit, injury to the bowel, fainting, bleeding and infection. Large amounts of ghee or oil taken by mouth may harm people with heart, liver or metabolic disease. The procedures are unsuitable for pregnant women, children, the elderly and the frail without assessment by a qualified doctor, and claims that they remove “toxins” have not been substantiated (Chapter 7). Anyone considering them should ask about the qualifications of those treating them and about the risks of the procedures proposed.

Pregnancy, childbirth and infancy. Purification therapies and many herbs are unsafe in pregnancy. Breastfeeding should begin within the first hour after birth, without other feeds; honey must not be given to infants under twelve months, because of the risk of infant botulism; and “gold” and other metal preparations given to infants (suvarṇaprāśana) have no established benefit and carry risks of contamination. Sex-selection is illegal in India. Heavy bleeding, fever or severe pain after childbirth, and any illness in a newborn or young child, need prompt medical attention, and immunisation protects against many of the diseases of childhood (Section 8.4).

Snakebite, animal bites and poisoning. The classical treatments must not be used. The first-aid advice in the World Health Organization’s guidelines for South-East Asia is to keep a person who has been bitten still and calm, to immobilise the bitten limb, to remove rings and tight clothing, not to cut or suck the wound or apply a tourniquet or ice, and to take the person to hospital at once for assessment and, if needed, antivenom (World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia 2016). A bite or scratch from any animal that may carry rabies should be washed at once with soap and water for about fifteen minutes, and needs urgent medical care for vaccination and, where indicated, immunoglobulin; rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms develop, and no traditional remedy prevents it. For any suspected poisoning, emergency care should be sought at once. Such guidance is revised from time to time, and the current advice of national health authorities should be followed (Section 8.6).

Delay. The greatest harm often comes from delaying effective treatment of serious conditions—tuberculosis and other infections, diabetes, anaemia, jaundice, cancer, heart disease, epilepsy and mental illness—or from stopping a prescribed treatment, for high blood pressure, HIV or any of these conditions, in favour of a traditional remedy. Severe diarrhoea and vomiting need prompt oral rehydration and medical care. Restraint, ritual treatment or purification should never take the place of care for mental illness, epilepsy or alcohol dependence, for which effective treatments exist (Section 8.5).

India has a pharmacovigilance programme for Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani and homoeopathic medicines through which adverse effects can be reported; reporting them helps others.

docs.title: 12.8 Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property
docs.text: In the 1990s Indian scientists and activists challenged patents granted in the United States and Europe on traditional uses of Indian plants. A United States patent on the use of turmeric to heal wounds was revoked in 1997 after the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research showed that the use was already described in Indian texts, and a European patent on a neem-based fungicide was revoked after a long challenge. To prevent such patents, the Government of India created the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) in 2001. It records formulations from the classical texts of Āyurveda, Unani, Siddha and Yoga, translated into English, French, German, Japanese and Spanish and classified in a form usable by patent examiners, and access is given to major patent offices for the purpose of searching “prior art”. The TKDL has been widely praised as a defensive tool, though some have pointed out that it protects the knowledge of the textual traditions more effectively than that of oral, local and tribal ones.

docs.title: 12.9 Conclusion
docs.text:
Āyurveda is one of the great medical traditions of the world. Its classical texts are among the most important scientific works of ancient India: rich in observation, systematic in theory, humane in ethics, and remarkable in the range of their concerns, from the regimen of the day to the reconstruction of the nose. Its later history shows a living tradition that absorbed new diseases, new drugs, alchemy and pulse diagnosis, and that adapted to colonial rule, nationalism and the global market. Its historical achievements deserve to be known and studied.

They are honoured best by accuracy. The compendia are not timeless; they were composed and revised over centuries and reflect the societies that produced them. Their theory of the body is not a hidden anticipation of modern science. Their remedies must be judged, like any others, by careful testing, and some of them are dangerous. The tradition’s own founders insisted on examination and reasoning before action. Applied to Āyurveda itself, that principle is the best guide to its future.

Summary

The Āyurveda practised today was made in the last two centuries: by colonial withdrawal and nationalist revival, by print, pharmacies, colleges and committees, by the debate between “pure” and “integrated” teaching, and by the registers, councils and ministry of independent India. Modern research has found biologically active compounds in many of its plants and one outstanding drug in Rauvolfia, but good evidence of benefit for most of its treatments, and evidence of harm from some. The tradition is honoured best by accurate history and by the examination and reasoning that its own founders demanded.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On the colonial period see Arnold (Arnold 2000); on the revival and modern Āyurveda, Leslie, Langford, Banerjee and the essays edited by Wujastyk and Smith (Leslie 1976; Langford 2002; Banerjee 2009; Wujastyk and Smith 2008); on the professionalisation of Āyurveda in Bengal, the United Provinces and the Punjab, Mukharji, Berger and Sivaramakrishnan, and on the politics of Āyurvedic education, Brass (Mukharji 2016; Berger 2013; Sivaramakrishnan 2006; Brass 1972); on WHO policy, (World Health Organization 2013); on research, (Patwardhan et al. 2005; Mukherjee and Wahile 2006); on safety, (Saper et al. 2004, 2008).

docs.title: Plants of the Classical Materia Medica

This appendix gives the usual modern identifications of plants frequently named in the classical and medieval medical texts. It is meant to help in reading the texts and the scholarly literature. It is not a guide to the use of any plant. Many identifications are uncertain or disputed, and the same Sanskrit name may refer to different plants in different regions; where a plant is notably toxic, this is indicated. The poisonous plants of the pharmacopoeia are discussed in Chapter 6.

docs.title: A Guide to Further Reading
docs.text: This guide is a short, annotated selection from the works listed in the Select Bibliography, arranged by topic, for readers who wish to go further. Full details are given in the bibliography.

docs.title: The Classical Texts
docs.text: The Sanskrit texts of the great compendia are most conveniently read in the editions of Jādavjī Trikamjī Ācārya, which print the standard commentaries of Cakrapāṇidatta on Caraka and of Ḍalhaṇa on Suśruta (Trikamji Acharya 1941; Trikamji Acharya and Acharya 1938). Complete English translations are those of Priyavrat Sharma for Caraka (Sharma 1981–1994), Kunja Lal Bhishagratna for Suśruta (Bhishagratna 1907–1916) and K. R. Srikantha Murthy for Vāgbhaṭa’s Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (Srikantha Murthy 2012). Translations made for practitioners sometimes modernise the text; readers should compare them with the Sanskrit where possible. The best starting point for the general reader is Dominik Wujastyk’s The Roots of Āyurveda, which translates key chapters of the major works, including the Bower Manuscript, with a clear and reliable introduction (Wujastyk 2003a). The Bower Manuscript itself was edited and translated by Hoernle (Hoernle 1893–1912).

docs.title: Histories and Surveys
docs.text: G. Jan Meulenbeld’s History of Indian Medical Literature is the indispensable reference for authors, texts, commentaries and dates; it is arranged as a work of reference rather than a narrative (Meulenbeld 1999–2002). Older surveys by Jolly (Jolly 1951), Filliozat (Filliozat 1964), Kutumbiah (Kutumbiah 1962) and Zimmer (Zimmer 1948), and the collaborative volume edited by Subbarayappa (Subbarayappa 2001), remain useful, though their dates should be checked against Meulenbeld. Wujastyk’s essay on “the science of medicine” is a concise modern overview (Wujastyk 2003b). M. S. Valiathan’s three volumes on the legacies of Caraka, Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa retell the great compendia, section by section, for the modern Indian reader (Valiathan 2003, 2007, 2009), and Meulenbeld’s annotated translation of the first chapters of the Mādhavanidāna with its chief commentary shows how a diagnostic handbook was read (Meulenbeld 1974).

docs.title: Origins: Veda, Buddhism and the Ascetics
docs.text: Kenneth Zysk’s two books—on healing in the Vedic hymns and on medicine in the early Buddhist monasteries—are the fundamental studies of the period before the compendia, and develop the influential but still debated thesis that rational medicine emerged among the heterodox ascetics (Zysk 1985, 1991). On the transmission of Indian medicine to China, see Salguero (Salguero 2014); on a Sanskrit handbook carried into Tibetan and Khotanese, Emmerick’s edition of the Siddhasāra (Emmerick 1980–1982).

docs.title: Surgery and Anatomy
docs.text: Guido Majno’s The Healing Hand places Suśruta’s surgery in the context of wound care across the ancient world (Majno 1975). Hoernle’s study of the bones and Mukhopadhyaya’s study of the surgical instruments are pioneering works that are still consulted (Hoernle 1907; Mukhopadhyaya 1913–1914). Wujastyk discusses how the body was pictured in premodern India (Wujastyk 2009).

docs.title: Body, Gender and Society
docs.text: Rahul Peter Das’s The Origin of the Life of a Human Being is a detailed study of the medical and sexological texts on conception and the female body (Das 2003); Martha Ann Selby’s article reads the classical narratives of conception, gestation and labour (Selby 2005), and Jeffery, Jeffery and Lyon’s ethnography describes childbirth and the work of birth attendants in modern north India (Jeffery et al. 1989). Francis Zimmermann’s The Jungle and the Aroma of Meats is the classic study of the ecological theme in classical dietetics and pharmacology (Zimmermann 1987), and Dagmar Wujastyk’s Well-Mannered Medicine the fullest study of medical ethics and etiquette in the compendia (Wujastyk 2012); K. T. Achaya’s history of Indian food sets the medical dietetics beside the culinary literature (Achaya 1994). Olivelle’s translation of Manu’s law code shows the place of physicians in brahmanical law (Olivelle 2005), and his translation of the Arthaśāstra the place of medicine in statecraft (Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: Alchemy and Rasaśāstra
docs.text: David Gordon White’s The Alchemical Body is the essential study of the Siddha alchemical traditions (White 1996); P. C. Ray’s History of Hindu Chemistry remains valuable for its texts (Ray 1902–1909); Wujastyk’s article on the “alchemical ghost” corrects a persistent error (Wujastyk 1984). Volume 14 of this series, Rasāyana, treats the subject in detail.

docs.title: Siddha, Unani, Sowa-Rigpa and Local Traditions
docs.text: On Siddha medicine and its modern history, see Weiss (Weiss 2009) and, for the wider Siddha poetic tradition, Zvelebil (Zvelebil 1996). On Islamic medicine generally, see Ullmann’s concise survey and Pormann and Savage-Smith (Ullmann 1978; Pormann and Savage-Smith 2007); on Unani in India, Alavi and Attewell (Alavi 2008; Attewell 2007). On Tibetan medicine, Gyatso’s intellectual history and the anthropological studies of Craig and of the contributors to Pordié’s volume (Gyatso 2015; Craig 2012; Pordié 2008); Garrett on embryology, Clifford on mental illness, and the published set of the Blue Beryl paintings (Garrett 2008; Clifford 1984; Parfionovitch et al. 1992); Gerke on the Tibetan mercury preparation and its safety (Gerke 2021). On medical pluralism in India today, see the volume edited by Sujatha and Abraham (Sujatha and Abraham 2012). On healing and religion, Kakar and Sax (Kakar 1982; Sax 2009); on local health traditions, Shankar and Unnikrishnan (Shankar and Unnikrishnan 2004).

docs.title: Colonial and Modern Āyurveda
docs.text: The essays in Leslie’s Asian Medical Systems and in Leslie and Young’s Paths to Asian Medical Knowledge remain classic (Leslie 1976; Leslie and Young 1992). Arnold surveys medicine in colonial India (Arnold 2000); Ernst’s volume and Alter’s discuss plural medicine and globalisation (Ernst 2002; Alter 2005); Langford’s ethnography and Banerjee’s study of the pharmaceutical industry are essential for modern practice (Langford 2002; Banerjee 2009); and the essays edited by Dagmar Wujastyk and Frederick Smith survey “modern and global Ayurveda” (Wujastyk and Smith 2008). The making of Āyurveda into a modern profession is studied regionally by Mukharji for Bengal (who has also studied the Bengali practitioners of Western medicine (Mukharji 2009)), Berger for the United Provinces and Sivaramakrishnan for the Punjab, and Brass analyses the politics of Āyurvedic education after independence (Mukharji 2016; Berger 2013; Sivaramakrishnan 2006; Brass 1972).

docs.title: Evidence and Safety
docs.text: On heavy metals in Ayurvedic products, see the studies of Saper and colleagues and the report of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Saper et al. 2004, 2008; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2004); on liver injury, the case series of Björnsson and colleagues and of Nagral and colleagues (Björnsson et al. 2020; Nagral et al. 2021); on the reliability of Āyurvedic diagnosis, the overview of Kurande and colleagues (Kurande et al. 2013); and on snakebite in India, the mortality study of Suraweera and colleagues and the WHO guidelines (Suraweera et al. 2020; World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia 2016). Examples of rigorous clinical research include Vakil’s study of Rauvolfia and the trial of guggulipid (Vakil 1949; Szapary et al. 2003). Broader discussions of research on Ayurvedic drugs are given by Patwardhan and colleagues and by Mukherjee and Wahile (Patwardhan et al. 2005; Mukherjee and Wahile 2006); the policy context is set out in the WHO strategy (World Health Organization 2013).

docs.title: A Guide to the Principal Medical Works
docs.text:
This appendix lists the principal works mentioned in the volume, with their approximate dates and contents. Dates follow Meulenbeld’s History of Indian Medical Literature unless otherwise stated, and many are uncertain; attributions to legendary authors are given as traditional. Works are in Sanskrit unless otherwise indicated.
